THE BEST ESTATE. Art thou thy own heart's conqueror? Strive ever thus to be; That is the fight that is most sore, The noblest victory. Art thou beloved by one true heart? • 0 prize it ! it is rare? There are so many in the mart, So many false and fair. Art thou alone ? 0 sok not so ! The world is full, be sure; There is so much of want and woe, • So much that thou canst cure. Art thou in poverty thyself? Thou still canst help a friend; Kind words are more than any pelf, Good deeds need never end. Art thou content in youth or age? Then let who will be great; • Thou haat the noblest heritage, Thou hast the best estate! '6—Cassell's Magazine.
F. E. WEATHERLY.

IN OUR SQUARE. Last night again we saw him there, Beneath the plane-tree in the square, Our student neighbour. He watches every evening now, While we play tennis; but, somehow, It seemed a labour. The runnings round, and futile stretching, At random balls, while he was sketching That foolish Polly. Who quietly stood with arm upraised. The while her junior partner praised Her style of " I went quite near him as we played, He looked so peaceful in the shade, Amid our bustle.
He draws and sketches all the day, , And studies through the night, they say, Some bone or muscle. And that is why his eheek is pale, And why he looks so thin and frail. But is such labour
The reason why his coat is bare And worn, and marks him everywhere Our student .neighbour? I know that I shall almostsry To-morrow- when we pass him by, All Cound together
For Cornish seas; while he—but there Miss Polly's always in the square This sumneer weather. —Londoie Socky.

It has been proved, over and over again, in England, Germany, and America, that children under twelve learn as much in four hours a day as in six. One way of making a child conscientious and trust- worthy is to entrust him with small duties. These,-of course, should not be boo arduous: they should be easy of accomplishment and agreeable in their nature, but the parent er teachershould see that they are punctually and faithfully performed. , A rich man in Brattleboro' had been applied to for a contribution towards building an iron fence round a cemetery in that town. But he declined, on the rather irreverent, but witty, plea that the cemetery does not need a fence, as those inside cannot get out, and those outside de cot want to get in. GERMAN VERSUS Exerusa HOME LIFE.—The museum, the town club, the centre of modest, cheap, and reason- able amusement for whosoever pleases, is an admirable • invention for a little country town. The balls cost no- thing, save for supper, which the guests order as pleases them. The hall is very handsome, prettily lighted, with a capital door, and very good music. The youths and maidens have known each other from their cradles. There is a homely, friendly air about the place. The same kind of people in an English town of correspond- ing pretensions would prefer to turn out their own little rooms for a poor little party once a year or so, and to elevate Air. Mudie into the most gigantic of _monopolists and most irresponsible of rulers. It is a very curious question-to know why.—The English Rlustrated.gagazint. A. COMMON ERROR ABOUT SUGAR.—It is a prevalent, though mistaken, notion that sugar injures the teeth;! but, so far from thisbeing the case, it is—in moderate quantities—one of the most valuable of our commodi- ties. It is, indeed, nothing short of cruel to deprive children of sweets, dithough it is quite as great a mis- take to allow &free consumption of them, for the chief reason that the appetite will be spoiled for more sub- stantial food. But it should be borne in mind that without sugar a ehild would soon starve, and,that in nature's product—the human milk—it exists in a greater, proportion than in that of cows or goats. This is un- doubtedly one of the reasons why many infants brought up "by hand" do not thrive as they ought to do. One of the chief causes of had teeth in children is their par- taking of .food,toolot, thus causing indigestion, a fore- runner of decayed teeth, though it is the harmless sugar that is often blamed for their early loss. DANGEBS OE CHEMICAL EXPERIMENTS.—M. Rouelle, an eminent French chemist, was not the most cautious of operators. One day, while performing some experi- ments, he observed to ids auditors, "Gentlemen, you see this cauldron upon this brazier; well, if I were to cease missing a single moment, an explosion would ensue which would blow Ilk all in the air !" The company had smrcely time rto reflect on this comfortable piece of in- t .'lligenee before the operator did forget to stir his mix- ture, and his prediction was accomplished. The explo- sion took plaoewith a terrible crash; all the windows of the laboratory were smashed to pieces, and two hundred auditors thrown about the building and out of it in con- fusion. fortunately none received any very serious injury, the greatest violence of the explosion having been done in -the direction of the chimney, and the demonstrator escaped without further harm than the loss of his wig.—The World of Wonders. HIS PAIiBPORT.—A story is told of Tetrarch, the poet, that once when a number of witnesses were being sworn, of whom he was one, the officiating magistrate administered the oath as usual until he came to the poet, when he passed himitt once with the remark, "As for you, Petrarel, your word is sufficient." This was an extraordinary tribute to character. Here follows an ex- ample to genius quite as pronounced and quite as re- markably deserved.:—lt is related of Gustave Dore that many years ago, while on a tour in Switzerland, he hap- pened to lose his passport. Arriving at Lucerne, he asked to be allowet to speak to the Mayor, to whom he gave his name. "You say you are M. Gustave Dore," replied the Mayor," and I believe you; but," he added, producing pencil and apiece of paper, "you can easily prove it." Dore looked around him and perceived some women selling potatoes in the street. With a few touches he cleverly reproduced the homely scene, and, appending his name to the sketch, presented it to the Mayor. "Your passport is perfectly in order," remarked the official, "but you .must allow me to keep it as a souvenir, and to offer you in return one in the ordinary form." Tan BIGGEST HORSE-jUMP ON RECORD.—What distance and what height can a ,horse jump is another inquiry which comes within the scope of this article, and if the reader will carefully measure out thirty-nine feet, an idea of the horse's capacity in this direction will be gatherecL Such a distance a steeplechase horse called Old Chandler is reported to have covered at Warwick some years ago; and there is more than one apparently authentic record of a horselclearing seven feet in height. The scene of one such exploit was at the Pheenix Park, and the horse was an animal descended from a famous winner named Pottlos, himself called Turnip. The animal belonged to Sir E. Crofton, and the Duke of Richmond, then Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland, wagered £5OO that this height could not be &eared. A wall of the requisite dimensions was built, and when finished Turnip was ridden at it. He did what was asked of him in perfect style but it happened that his grace, not knowing that tke feat was ready for performance, was -not looking when the jump was made; and Turnip was therefore ridden over it again not only successfully but .easily. The wail of Hyde Park, opposite Grosvenor 'Place, six and a half feet on the inside with a drop of seight feet into the road beyond, has also been cleared.— English Illustrated Magazine. CULTIVAtE A SWET VOlCE.—There is HO power of love so hard to keep as a kind voice. A kind hand is deaf and dumb. It may be rough in flesh and blood, -yet do the work of a soft heart, and do it with a soft touch. But there is no one thing it 80 much needs as a sweet voice, to tell what it means and feels, and it is hard to get and keep it in the right tone. One must _start in youth, and be on the watch night and day, at work and while at play, to get and keep a voice that shall spea.k at all times the thoughts of a kind heart. But this is the time when a sharp voice is most apt to be got. You often hear boys and girls say words at play with a quick, sloarp tone, as if it were the snap of a whip. If any of them get vexed you will bear a voice that sounds as if it were made up of a snarl, a whine, and a bark. Such a voice often speaks worse than the ' heart feels. It shows more in tone than in words. It is often in mirth that one gets a voice or a tone that is sharp, and sticks to him through life, and stirs up will and grief, and falls like a drop of gall on the sweet joys at home. Such as these get a sharp home voice for use and keep their best voice for those they meet else- where, just as they would save the best cakes and pies for guests and all their sour food for their own bard. I would say to all girls and boys, " Use your best' voice at home." Watch it day by day as a pearl of_great pried, for it will be worth more to you in the days to come than the best pearl hid in the sea. A kind voice is a lark's song to heart and home. It is to the heart what light is to the eye. A girl at scbool would like to have two birthdays 1 every year. When she grows up to be a woman, she I often objects to having one. " Men often jump at conclusions," says the proverb. So do dogs. We saw a dog jump at the concrusion of a cat, which was sticking through the opening of a partly-closed door. How doth the small defective flue improve each mid- night hour, to show insurance companies its full destmc- tive power. How silently he sits aloft, in attic, or still higher, and in the dead Of night proclaims himself the fiend of fn.& _

"Don't you think you have a good mamma, to spread such nice large slices of bread-and-jam for your said an old lady to a little boy who was enjoying his tea. "Yes," was the reply; "but she would still be better if she'd let Me spread on the jam myself." How we always loathed that instructor of our youth who:told us, in the face of our better judgment, that a pound of feathers weighed as heavy as a pound of lead! How we always longed to get his head under a fourth- storey window and experiraent thereon with both. During the warn lady pissing from cotto cot through the wards of a hospital, Vas shocked to hear one fellow laugh at her. She stopped to reprove the wretched patient. "Why, ma'am," says he, "you have given me a tract on the sin of dancing, when both legs have been shot off." - Children should have several hours of play ever day in the open air, when possible. Vigyous and spontane- ous action of this sort is better than. gymnastics for the general run of children: and if girls were allowed by social feelings toy as boys do, they would cease to be so subject to spinal deformities.

Children—both-boys and girls—should be taught to sew. If they begin by making pretty things—not hum- drum useful things—they will soon get to be fond of the work. Many a man who has travelled far away from mother and sisters has felt the desirability of knowing how to sew on a button, or to put the necessary stitch in linen: while girls, of course, ought to be taught needlework, and the sooner they begin the more likely they are to become proficient in the art._

PLEA FOR THE PROTECTION OF WILD FLOWERS.— There is a statute for the protection of wild birds; and, between ourselves, wild birds are by no means so inno- cent as wild flowers. Gulls, solan geese, herons, and various other sea and water fowl have prodigious appe- tites, and when they get among a shoal of young fry work wholesale havoc. Still the Act is a good one— only I should like to see it extended. The brute who shot thegast Great Auk on our coast cannot have been more hopelessly wicked than the wretches who extir- .

pated the Killarney fern. And unless some such Act as I suggest is speedily passed, we shall be familiar with the Osmmada and its kindred only as we are familiar with the Great Auk and the Dodo. The poacher who is found on the public highway with a, hare or a pheasant up his sleeve is sharply purushed—as he deserves to be, no doubt; but the rascal who has stolen the only root of Woodsia hyperborea in a county escapes scot-free. What is a hare or pheasant more or less in comparison with a crested lastrea or a plant of Cystopteris montalut? —" Shirley," in Good Words.

.„ A TALE OF AR OXFORD PROCTOR-A famous young orator was returning one night from the Union De- bating Society, and solacing himself with a pipe on his waythotne. Meeting a Proctor within a few yards of the Union, and suspecting that uncompromising zeal had led his foe to lie in ambush till the close of the de- bate-4n unpardonable atrocity in the eyes of the under- graduates—he determined to be even with him. So having given up his name and College, and made the usual morning appointment, he spent the rest of the evening in making a round of the public- houses, and returned to his rooms with his pockets nearly bursting, and a smile of triumph on his brow. Next morning he celled upon his captor, bearing in his hand a fat calico bag tied up with red tape. " Mr. Spouter, I think ?" Spouter bows assent "Ah ! you were smoking in the Corn Market last night, Mr. Spouter. I must trouble you for ten shillings." Spouter unties his bag, and out rushes a torrent of halfpence. "Will you oblige me by counting them, sir? I can only make two hundred and thirty-nine." Spouter left Ox- ford next morning, and did not return till the following terrn.—CasaelPs lamily lifagazine.

CITY MISSIONARIES AND PUBLIC-110119E9.—T0 have per- severed amid such early discouragements until, at the present time the Society has sevehteen missionaries almost wholly devoted to this special visitation of public-houses and beer-shops, reflects the highest honour on the moral courage and Christian tact and patience of its missionaries. Truly, a grander field for mission work than the public-house could not exist. That this scat- tering broadcast the Divine salt of Christianity saves society from utter corruption, and, as Lord Shaftesbury puts it, prevents London from becoming a city of devils, even though the City Mission has not yet succeeded in making it a city of angels, must be manifest to every Christian mind. One incident connected with this de- partment of the mission's work must suffice. "Why, them missionary fellows," said a man in a public-house, "walk bang into the beer-shops now; and one's been in 'here, taking his religion and his tracts with him, and he Ikas so worked on the landlord's mind that he has quite turned it. He won't serve you now if you're only a bit tight; and if you let slip a word he says, 'Now, then, that won't do in this.house.' "—!' Well, he wasn't always so," said another; "he used to be as good a chap as any, and could swear a bit; I've heard him."—"Ah ! ' said a third, "he's not fit to be a publican now."—"Forty years," said a man on another occasion, "1 have been in and out of these cribs, and never heard a spouter before. What next. I wonder, after this ! "—Surely the men who do this brave work are worthy not only of Christian sympathy and support, but even of the Victoria Cross. —"The Quiver for October. -.

' A YOUNG ROMAN'S SACRIFICE.—A TRUE STORY.—Once ' upon a time, many hundred years ago, when Romp was -mistress of the world, and the Romans were braver and -stronger than anyone else, there lived a boy of thirteen whose name is still remembered. Lucius Valerius was fond of his lessons, but most of all did he love 'poetry; so, although he was only thirteen years old, he made up his mind that he would try to win the gold medal and ivory lyre which were given every five years to the boy who should write the best poem. Lucius not only tried, but he succeeded, and one day, before all the school and a number of visitors, the prizes were presented to him. Now, besides the medal and lyre which every one who gained them valued very much, there was something else which they thought far grander. A statue of the prize-winner was placed in the school and crowned with laurel. You may imagine how the boy's heart beat with joy as he saw the judge step forward to crown his statue, but just at that moment Lucius caught sight of a young man who had also tried for the prize, and who looked most downcast and miserable. Lucius sprang, forward, seized the laurel crown and put it on the head of the poor fellow who had been unsuccessful. "You are more deserving of it than I am," be said; "I obtained it more on account of my youth than my merit, and rather as an encouragement than AS a reward." Then the people set up a great shout of joy, for they knew that a noble heart was worth more than all the poems in The world, and they gave a new name to Lucius Valerius in memory of that day. So Lucius was always called Pudens, which means Modest, and you may be sure he valued his new title as much as he deserved it, for "Kind hearts are more than coronets."—" Little Folke" Magazine. INTEMPERANCE AND Wsmrs.—ln order to understand fully the influence of alcohol upon health we must con- sider not only its direct influence upon the body and the mind of the drunkards and their offspring, but we must take into consideration the effect it has upon their cir- cumstances. A disproportionate part of their earnings being spent in drink, they are unable to afford for them- selves and their families such good food, clothing, and lodging as they might otherwise have. At a certain stage of degradation, the drunkard may be still alive to all his own requirements while regardless of those of his family, and may leave them to be hungry and cold, while he is warm, and comfortable at the public-house. But as his drinking habits continue, and years advance, his power of earning is diminished; instead of working the whole week he works only a part of it, and his labour during that time becomes less and less valuable. A few years ago a master tailor told me that he had sometimes great difficulty in getting orders completed in time, because some of his best men only worked for about half the week. They were paid on Saturday, they were drunk on Sunday and Monday, and ill on Tuesday, and only began to work on Wednesday. Nor is the work so good after a debauch of this sort, although its imper- fections may not be so manifest in tailoring as in trades where the work is very delicate, as, for example, in grinding lenses for microscopes. In this process the glass used for making the lenses is Axed in a holder and pressed against a rapidly revolving disc. It requires to be held with the utmost steadiness, and gradually turned in such a manner that it shall be equally ground over the whole surface, as the least inequality greatly diminishes or completely destroys the value of the lens. The quality of the lens can only be ascertained after it has been fitted up so that a test object can be examined through it. A celebrated microscope maker in Paris, while showing* me this process, informed me that the lenses made by workmen who were perfectly sober, but had .been indulging in liquor the day before, were of greatly less value than those made by them at other times ; and where men were at all addicted to intoxica- tion, it did not pay to keep them, as the loss of time in examining the lenses was so great. As years pass, in- temperate workmen become more idle and less able to labour, so that unless they are carried off by disease. they find their way into the workhouse.-7he Book of Health..

The ibur-year-old Duchess cow; Grand Duchess 13rd, recently taken, out to America by Mr. J. Hill, St. .Paul, Minnesota, was burned to death in the cars whilst being brought from the quarantine station at Waltham to Chicago on August 28th. The two two-year-old heifers, Grand Duchess 27th and Duchess of Wappenham, were also badly injured, but are expected to recover. A RIDICULOUS PAOSECUTION.—An officer of the Inland Revenue, more zealous than wise, last week summoned a labourer for carrying a gun without a license on the highway. It seems that the man was employed by his master, a farmer, to scare rooks, and was merely cros- sing the road to his cottage with the gun, in order to clean it. He was convicted, and ordered toy a penny fine; but the magistrates very properly showed their sense of the triviahty of ' the charge by condemning the Crown in costs. The man had a right to carry the gun on his master's farm, but not on the highway without a license.

ANEW HORSE DRENCHAR.—A very admirable and in- genious appliance for giving horses medicine was exhi- bited at the recent Amsterdam exhibition by the firm n of Valk and de Bussy, of Utrecht. It is called a Paarden- trechter or horse drencher. A bit made of plain hollow pipe rather larger than an ordinary plain bar, and in the centre of which is a small hole, is put into the mouth. This is fixed to a bar on either side, which fits to the cheek and is strapped to the bridle. On one side of this bar a conical tube is fitted, and which is not very unlike a horn used for drenching, except that it is straight. When the bridle is put upon the horse, and the animal's head held up, .the medicine is poured into the tube and, finding its way through the bit, is swallowed without any difficulty whatever. THE YIELD OF MILK IN JEStshrs.—Mr. F. M. Carryl, Avondale, N.J., sends to the Albany Cultivator the record of the milk yield of his herd of five Jersey cows for the year 1883 as follows:— No. Last Calf Calved in 1883. Milk Yield. 10,034 9,300 ...... Jan. 23, 1883 ...... Jan. 23 7,122 ... z. Feb. 11, 1882 8,627 N0v.27, 1882 7,091 .1

The first two were four years old in April, 1883; the third five years inTebruary, and the last two six years respectively in March and May. This gives an average age of five years. On the Ist of January, 1883, the aver- age interval since previous calving was 4 months, and from that date to the birth of the next calves, the aver- age was seven months. The average yield was 5,8151b5. 130 z., or 684 gallons and a fraction. ' A TRICK or THE CORN TRADE.—Theie are ticks in all trades, and millers and', merchants are not immaculate. But is it not just a little bit too.mean to try to change the custom of the trade for one season only, as some buyers appear to be doing, when to do so will be an ad- vantage to buyers and a loss to growers of wheat? At Mark Lane for some years past buyers have in reality bought their wheat by weight, though nominally by the imperial quarter. That is to say they have insisted on getting 4041 b. per quarter, or 63tb. per bushel. But this year, as the natural weight of the wheat is exceptionally great, and a measured bushel commonly weighs over 631 b., buyers have found out that it is the custom of the trade to buy by imperial measure. Sellers have often had to add several pounds to each sack of wheat to make it of the required weight. Let them now sell at the same weight, and take toll out of each measured Ilack.---Mark Lane Express. TEE MERTON Smos.—A writer who has just visited Ithe silos at Merton of Lord Walsingham says that his new silos are built of clay lumps, and he had been able to put them up at a cost of only £6 each. The cost of labour required to build the first silos was sufficient to pay the building of the second lot, and this economy was effected by substituting the clay lumps for bricks. The total cost of the three new silos was therefore only £lB, and their storage capacity was about 28 tons each. Of course, as Mr. Woods pointed out, the silos would have cost more if they had not been built inside the barn; but where a barn can be put up for the purpose the divided walls can be put up and the :silos cemented inside for that figure. The Merton silos are made with sharp angles, and they are able with the aid of rammers to pack away the ensilage as closely in the corners as any other part of the silos. About &wt. of salt were used to the 28 tons of ensilage, not for the preservation of the ensilage, but to make it more tasty.., The ensilage was brought up In sacks, hoisted by a small derrick worked by a young man. The chaff cutter delivered the chopped mane into sacks, which were immediately con- veyed to the barn, hoisted by the crane, and their con- tents scattered evenly along the surface of the 'silo. Some of the men carried iron rammers weighing 211b5., with which they rammed the maize, being particularly careful to do it effectually round the, sides and in the corners of the silo. Mr. Woods estimates the crop of maize he has recently put into the silos at 30 tons an acre.

GAME PR.BSERVINLL—Numerous dogs having been poisoned near Llanfair-Caereinon, an indignation meet- ing has been held of farmers and others to protest against their continued destruction. Loud complaints were made of over preserving of game by persons who held leases of shooting. Mr. Marshall, during the pro- ceedings, volunteeted the following extraordinary state- ment. He said :—" I am lessee, and have the exclusive right of shooting over the Hirhoss Hall Estate. I took It from Mr. Moore on a 14 years' lease, and have the ground game reserved for me. Mr. Moore, the agent, agreed to let me the game. He knew what he was doing, and I can assure you I pay double what I ought to pay for my rights. There are, I know, three farms already untenanted on the estate—viz., Hirhoss, at a rental of £300; Caerbache, £62; and Ceinugole, £l2O. In a few months two more will be left, and the trustees are likely soon to have the whole estate on hand, and before-long the estate will be nothing but a rabbit war- ren. When the trustees found they had made a foolish bargain, they offered me £7OO for my lease, and now; because I will not accept their offer, Mr. Moore has tried to make everything as disagreeable as he can for me. It is Mr. Moore's wish to make me give up the lease if he can, but he cannot. I advertised that I have traps and dog spears placed in the woods, and that I would shoot any dog found hunting on my land, and likely to hurt a hare of mine; yes, even if it were the Prince of Wales's dog." , CLAIM BY A TENANT FOR COMPENSATION.—In a recent appeal to the Sheriff of Elgin by Sir W. Gordon-Cum- ming, Bart., of Altyre, the decision of the arbitrator be- tween the landlord and the outgoing tenant has been upheld. Mr. James Davidson was tenant, under Sir William Gordon-Cumming, of the farm of Auchness and others in the parish of Dallas, at a rent of £333, under a lease for 19 years from Whit-Sunday, 1879, but with breaks available to either party at the expiry of the fifth and tenth years. Notice having been given by Sir William that he wished to terminate the lease at Whit- Sunday, 1884, Mr. Davidson intimated a claim, under the Agricultural Holdings Act of 1883, for £l3O for compensation for unexhausted manures, and for £lOO for damages for an alleged breach of contract as to burning heather. The parties having failed to agree, and the referees named by them having also failed to agree or to name an oversman, an application was made to Court to do so, and Mr. George Gordonnand sur- veyor, Elgin, a gentleman of well-known practical ex- perience, was appointed. The landlord, in, addition to his objections to the claims of the tenant, made a counter-claim for £23 4s. 6d. for repairs to houses, and for £29 15s. for repairs to fences. He also claimed that £3O, the manurial value of straw which was sold, should be deducted. Mr. Gordon awarded on Bth July, £49 16s. 9d. for unexhausted manures, out of a total ex- penditure by the tenant of about £230 to £240 in the course of the years 1881-82-83, and? on the other Viand, he sustained the counter-claims of the landlord to the extent of £l2 12s. for repairs to the houses and £7 7s. for repairs to the fences. He disallowed the claim of the landlord for the straw of the way-going crop. An ap- peal was lodged by the landlord against this award, but the Sheriff has upheld the decision of the arbitrator. HOW FARMERS PERPETUATE ISE POTATO DISEASE.— The leaves and haulm of the potato decay during winter, but these resting spores survive, and are washed by the rains into the soil. When the proper season comes round they burst, expelling a number of moving spores, or germinate in the damp earth, or on any ordinary natural substance on which they chance to rest. . . . It has been proved that they may be dormant for at least three years, and then wake up to their work. _These resting spores are very abundant in the oid exhausted seed potatoes in the autumn, at the time when the crop is lifted. They are equally common in decayed potato refuse. Farmers have often unwittingly done every- thing possible to facilitate the progress of the disease. Many of them, laudably desirous of making the most of everything, have the haulms, decaying tubers, and other refuse of their potato crops removed to their manure heaps, where they rot and become manure. But the little resting spores do not rot; they lie quiet with all their vitality shut up in them till the spring, and when the farmer has his manure spread thick over his potato fields he is sowing broadcast myriads of these little germs, which will yet grow up ip a mischievous crop. If he feeds his stock with unboiled diseased potatoes he is pnly taking another way of preserving the germs. Boiling destroys, however, the vitality of the resting spores. On the other hand, if he allows the decaying haulms to lie about his fields the resting spores will be washed into the soil, and into ditches and drains, and . such moist situations are especially favourable for their preservation and germination. It is thus of first im- portance that the diseased tubers given to cattle should always be thoroughly boiled, and the other refuse of potato fields effectually destroyed by burning. In this way the resting spores are killed. Further, as they have been proved to be able to survive for at least three years, potato crops should never be planted in the same ground unless at intervaLs of four or five years. If the farmer were to adopt these precautions, he would at least have the consciousness that he had done his duty, and that, so far as lay with him, he had taken the steps requisite to prevent disease.—R. Turner, in Good Words. A FLEMISII YEOMAN'S FARM.—" Near Alost, Flanders, we met with one of the smallest farms which will main- tamn a family without other work—it was barely five acres. There wag a small orchard of about a quarter of an acre, in which there were some thriving apple and plum trees. The grass under these was good, and the Only cow 'which the man had was led by the _wife to

, . wheat was cut he began to hack the stubble about four inches deep with the heavy hoe, and as fast as he got a piece done it was sown with turnips, after having some of the contents of the urine tank poured over it, for small as the farm was it had its reservoir for this precious manure: Thus a considerable portion of the wheat stubble was soon covered with young turnips of a quick growing sort, which if sown before the middle of August were fit to be pulled in November, and stored in the cellar for winter use. There was a small patch of cameline, which was sown less for the seed than for the stem, of which' he made brooms in his leisure hours when snow covered the ground. The whole five acres had to be dug in the course of the year, and as much of it as possible trenched, the soil being a stiff loam of a good depth; which was much improved by trenching and stirring. The milk and potatoes, fed the family, with the addition of a little salt pork, for a pig was fed on the refuse of the food given to thedcow and a very little corn, and consequently was not overburdened with fat. Most of the wheat and all the flax were sold, and more than paid the rent, which was not high—about £lO a year. Incessant labour kept the man in good health, and his wife was not idle. They had two or three young children; but, except the wish for another cow;there seemed no great dissatisfaction with their lot, nor any great fears for the future. They had no parish fund to fall back upon nor out-door relief, nor even a union workhouse; but had they come to want by unforeseen accidents they would have found the hand of private charity stretched out to help them." THE APPROACH OF Aurtosx.—A correspondent writes in a contemporary A great change has overtaken the country, for we have, exchanged summer for autumn, and the leave/ are rapidly falling around us. At present there &re few forest trees in our northern counties which compare with thel ash for vigour of green and freshness of colour. In the South, in Kent fpr instance, where I have recently been,l the foliage is less changed than here. The fruit of the ' wild shrubs and the forest trees are nearly at their best, I taken as a whole, and there is a splendid show except. in the horse cbestnuts, which vary much. Acorns, which are abundant and fill their cups well, 'are not quite ripe enough to fall. The " wicken " berry is far gone toward decay, and the " keys " of the sycamore are fully ripe • and falling, making beautiful spiral courses in their descent. The...`: hops " are numerous and striking objects of beauty in the hedgerows. The "haws" are very numerous and, well fed, and hang beautifully on the hedges in their russety brown coats. The berry of the white bean is unusually well fed for our northern climate, and is nearly ripe. The. black, berry is quite at its best and a wonderfully good crop, vast quantities of it having been collected which will save the other fruits. The "old man's beard" on the briar is very numerous. There is a great quantity !of elder berry this season, and there will be abundance for those who care to make it into Wine. Mushrooms are still very abundant. Other and more dangerous fungi are getting plentiful, and as the season advances we shall probably see a great quantity of differ- ent kinds, and it would be as well to exercise caution in collecting them. The crabtree has fruited much better than I had anticipated. As an instance of the ready way in which the willow tribe of trees mul- tiply, I may mention that several withy trees were cut down last spring and some cattle were turned into the field, a damp one, and trod splinters with the bark upon them into the 'ground. Now there are from 80 to 70 young trees, many of them over a foot high, shot up in this way. I was lately over the Wyre, where I saw the greatest collection of starlings that I ever witnessed. Long before sunset they kept arriving in clouds, and I could hear their chattering in the plantation where they found a lodgment nearly half a mile away. We still have the pied and a few of the gray wagtails with us. Our swallows have thinned away very much, and are now mostly, found in favourite places only. A little over a week ago I saw a large swarm of them sheltering on the iron rods of the bridge which spans the Wyre at the Shard, and in the same locality I disturbed a heron in a marl pit. dne of its legs was broken and hanging down; it allowed me to approach very close, and then moved off without alarm. A correspondent at Swinton informs me that he saw there a short time ago a small party of redstarts—probably a brood. This is a rare bird in that locality. One of the family was shot. A pair of cole-tits -were seen in the same locality, also a party of great tits and a pair of yellow wagtails. At SeeWey there is a brood of pied sparrows, two of which have one of the long feathers of the tail quite white and, one of them has a white head; the tail coverts of the latter are also white. In Lancashire wood pigeons ap- pear very plentiful, and rooks are much more numerous than they were a year ago. Yesterday, I saw in Che- shire, near Mobberley, a very, fine wifidover, the only one I have seen for many weeks past. OCCUPYING OWNERSIIIP.—Last week, at the Social Science Congress, in the department for Economy and Trade, Mr. H. W. Freeland in the chair, the papers bear- ing on agriculture were read. Mr. E. J. Watherston read a paper, by Mr. Jesse Collings, M.P., upon the question of peasant proprietary and occupying ownership. The paper pointed/out that many grave social questions were connected with the cultivation of the soil, and there was not a man, woman, or child who was not interested in it. -The history of landowning in England was one of -confiscation, and the small owners and the great mass of the rural population were reduced to the condition of merehirelings. It was the fashion to speak' of the cul- tivation of land not paying, but it would always pay the cultivator to cultivate his own land, for he would have a more permanent interest in it, and would devote more personal labour and attention necessary to the I raising of small articles of food. It did not follow that a man was to gain his own living on a small piece of land, but his income might be largely increased by that means • The land laws of England would not be allowed in any other country in Europe; they had half ruined the tenant farmer, and kept the labourer in semi-serf- dom, and Nemesis seemed to be overtaking the landlord. His remedy was to give pecuniary facilities to the culti- vating classes—tenant farmers and labourers—to acquire proprietary rights in agricultural land. The system had been already adopted in our own country and m Ireland, and it could be defended on the ground that it was for the public good. The State should advance money at the lowest possible interest to the County Boards, which they might expect soon to exist, to be advanced by them to the tenant farmers for the purchase to the extent of, say, four-fifths of the price, the other fifth to be found by the owner himself. The County Board would charge the borrower k per cent, more than the Government charged, which interest was to be a perpetual quit-rent to be paid to them. The extra f per cent, would be invested by the local authority at three per cent. compound in- terest, which in a period of 66 years would extinguish the debt to the State and the quit-rent would belong to the local authority.—that was, the people, for ever. He would limit the farms to be purchased to about 150 or 200 acres each. The local authority should also have power to purchase farms or estates and divide them into holdings of from one acre to 40 or 50, for the benefit of the-labourers, the cost of dividing to be added to the original cost and apportioned to the several holdings. To prevent rack-renting, the owners of the communal farms should not be allowed to sub-let, though they might sell at any time to cultivating owners.—After a discussion, the Chairman said the establishment of the scheme pro- posed by. Mr. Collings would go a long way towards giv- ing the labourer an interest in the soil. Landowners would act really in their own interest and those of the countiry at large in selling off more readily than they did some portion of those immense holdings, all of which they could not cultivate, and which produced those heartburnings which he hoped they might all outlive.

PRESENTATION OF A HIGHLAND PLAID TO MR. GLAD. STONE.—One of the most interesting featuree of the late franchise demonstration at Inverness was the spectacle of the Holm Mills weavers engaged in weaving a plaid to be presented to Mr. Gladstone, the motto they displayed being—

- This plaid we weave for yol, Willie, You'll catch nae calds nor chills By wearing this memento traa the weaver! of Holm Mills. The plaid, which teas begnn to be woven as the precession started, was finished by the time the proceedings were over. It was duly forwarded to Mr. Gladstone, who has just sent the following acknowledgement :—" I beg you to accept my sincere thanks for the beautiful Highland plaid with which you have been so good as to present ma. I can as- sure vou.that I highly appreciate your kindness. Circum- stances connected with the county of Inverness have a spwcial interest for me, and the plaid itself is much ad- mired." Ma. ItussEr.r. Loavnu. me Dzatoortectr.—The American Minister in London delivered his inaugural address on Mon- day evening, as President of the Midland Institude, in the Birmingham Town Hall. Taking democracy as his subject, Mr Lowell sail it was only by the instigation of the wrongs of men that what were called the rights of man became tur- bulent and danger6,us. The sentiment which lay at the root of democracy was nothing new, but it was new that men were more and more gaining a controlling hand in the management of their own affairs, and were learning more how to be worthy of it. The democratic theory was that those constitutions were likely to prove steadiest which had the broadest base, and that the best way of teaching a man how to vote was to give biro the chance of practice. The ballot lathe hands of men was less dangerous to society than a sense of wrong in their heads. Democracy was that form of society, no matter what its political classification, in which every man had a chance, and knew that he had it. Mr George was right in insisting that humanity made by far the largest part of political economy. Some who own gardens pass their lifetime „potatoes, so that the clover did not recur sooner than in without having occasion to plant a fruit tree, and of six years, the flax mil pOtatpes.in_nine. tAs boon as the those who have planted, some hay" ibstantial _ . . . . nave ph.. some have even su._ proof that they were quite ignorant of what they were doing, so clumsily has the task been performed. In most cases we find the trees have been planted too deep, and in others the wrong season has been selected. Of this there is ample evidence in the dead and dying branches. No doubt the roots are also badly treated in the act of transplanting. We consider October the most fitting season to remove all kinds of fruit trees, also bushes, though the latter may be planted any time, with more or less suerPcs, from now till they commence grow- in the swing. But, from reasons we shall give, it will be obvious that October is the best month for transplanting. A novice in tree planting would be scep- tical as to the wisdom of moving a tree in full leaf, whilst the:experienced tree planter finds that his sheet anchor—for so long as a tree is possessed of leaves, so long will it forp roots. A tree that is about to be moved is deprived of a great portion of its roots before it can be released from its present position. The roots are the real mouths of- the plant, the thicker ones acting as channels to conduct the moisture absorbed by the fibres info the stem, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit. Root extension is formed by the action of the descending sap from the leaves, through the branches, and where the first are removed or severed the course of the sap is in- terrupted, and for a time it will exude at the end of every broken root. Ultimately it sets about repair,ing the breach by forming granules all round the wound be- tween the bark and the wood, which gradually extend and become roots. So long as a leaf remains on the tree they will increase in size, and, stimulated by the heat of the soil, they will soon lay hold of it, so that in spring the tree will scarcely exhibit any symptoms of having been interfered with. The November or winter-moved tree , will, as far -as root-making is concerned, remain motionless from the time it is put in till itis incited by increased heat in the spring, when it attempts to de- velope its buds, but suddenly comes to a stand, they, having exhausted the supply of sap that was stored up in the tree, must wait till fresh roots are formed. The supply of descending sap is so very limited that the process goes on very tardily. If we examined the roots we should probably discover that many of those severed have decayed a few inches at the end. The October wound is self-healing; but the winter one is converted into a gangrene. The bark will ere long assume a' wrinkled appearance, and the small shoots will have lost their flexibility. The exist- ence of; the tree depends on the weather in April and the early part of May, and the larger the tree the greater the risk. We might observe here that young trees received from a nursery are always in a better state for removal than any trees in cottage gardens, because the first are ,annually moved. This has a tendency to form an extra number of fibres, which are not so susceptible of injury as thicker roots. In moving all trees it is necessary to excavate,a trench round them, the distance from the stem depending on the size of the tree; those about six feet high should be two feet or a diameter of four feet. With the' assistance of a fork this bulk of soil should be gradually reduced till there is no more than a man caurlift. All the roots must be carefully preserved during the operation. The hole for the reception of the plant should be made sufficiently large to admit of some of the best fresh soil that can be procured tto be placed all round, so as to encourage the roots in their early stage. The necessary width and depth of the hole may be ascertained accurately enough by placing a stick across, :as well as in an upright position. No tree should be placed at a greater depth than it was before, but if any difference is made it should be a little higher, and all the roots should be laid out flat, and no deeper than a foot. In wet localities a hole six inches deep 'would be ample for any tree, and the roots should be 'covered by mounding the soil over them and graduating to the ground level. THE FRONT GARDEN.—NOW that the beauty of the, choicer kinds of Geraniums has passed away they are no more an ornament, and the sooner they are taken up the better. This should be done at a time when the plants are dry. The leaves may be stripped off them, except- ing a few at the point of each: shoot. . They may be potted one, two, or three together, according to their sizes, and if the soil is moderately moist they will not require i any water for some days. From the appearance of the soil n pots that have been filled at this time of the year we feel sure that it is frequently too wet when used. If pie following rule is observed there is -no fear of erring in tljat direction. Take up a handful of soil and press it in"the hand With force, and allow it to fall a distance of one foot On a table or floor. If the fall causes it to separate into its original condition it will be fit for use, but if it only divides into lumps it must be dis- carded. Even hardy border plants do not appreciate such soil about their roots when transferred to pots. THE WlNDOW.—Cottagers would do well to make the acquaintance of the Scarborough Lily (Vallosa Purpurea), one of the best of window plants, which may be seen in flower in a few windows at the present time. No plant can be grown with so little trouble as the Scarborough Lily, for it will thrive for years in the same pot (better than if potted), and we have allowed them to remain till the bulbs and roots increased so as to burst the pot. They require a regular supply of water when growmg, and not so much when at rest, but at no time must the soil appear dust dry on the top. WORKMEN'S GREENHOUSES.—In referring to these last week, by a slight omission we are made to say that the air outside a .greenhouse is purer and sweeter than that inside. All intelligent readers will have already con- cluded from their previous knowledge, and from the context of our remarks, that it should-be the other way about, and all whose olfactory organs have been or are within reasonable distance of a greenhouse full of plants must have arrived at a similar conclusion. It is satis- factory to learn that the yards in which these green- houses are situated are noteworthy for their cleanliness. The owner feeling proud of it and the plants it contains, is ever ready to show them to his friends and fellow- workmen, and it is only natural that he should endea- vour to preserve the place as neat and clean as possible to receive them.

div.head: ROOKERIES.
div.p: ROOKERIES.

The following is extracted from an article in the Man- chester Guardian:—Rennie says: "Young rooks will readily devour their own weight of food in the course of a single day." Basing his calculations upon the esti- mated number of rooks in Lancashire and Cheshire, the editor of a periodical calculates that 702 tons of insects are consumed in the two counties in a single year by rooks, and taking those as a teat for the whole country he shows that the rooks in England annually consume the astounding weight of 14,040 tons of insects of various kinds. With the rooks of Lancashire and Cheshire upon that estimate destroying 13 tons 16 cwts. 13 qrs. of insects per week at this season of the year these birds certainly have a claim to be reckoned amongst our benefactors. The flight of rooks is matter of common remark, and much that is interesting might be written upon it. In the winter they fly great distences every day, and the birds belonging to a number of rookeries roost together. For instance, those at Trafford Park and those at Astley go to Worsley every evening to roost. Claughton, near Garstang, Huntroyde, near Burnley, The Hazles, Prescot, are great rook centres in Lancashire, and one of the largeA of these has been at Park Hall, Char- nock Richard, but the birds have been driven away during the past winter. The following are copies of letters sent to the writer in respect of some of the local rookeries :

With respect to the rookeries in the neighbourhood of Lathom, a correspondent writes :—" As to the rook- eries near here, the oldest is that in the wood standing in Lathom Park, on rising ground on the south side of the house, known by the name of the Temple Wood. As the people say, they have always been there,' and the trees are some of the oldest in the place, being large beeches, some 200 years 'old. No doubt the rooks settled there when the trees were young. The labourers always call it the Crow Wood;' as there have been many trees blown down in the course of the last forty yew; and so nesting ground diminished, the rooks (some of them) migrated to the woods by the Preston Lodge (the one closest to the Parsonage), and there they have as large a colony as at the parent rookery, and the rookeries we have here (Blythe) are off-shoots of the Lathom one too. They came to the trees close to the back of the house— first one or two nests some thirty years ago and as they increased they went to the wood at the end of our grounds some 400 yards away, so that we have two settlements now. The curious thing is that while we have many big trees all round the house they have kept to the back. Only twice do I remember them attempt- ing to build more in front. Once at the garden side one nest appeared, but as soon as it was nearly finished the old rooks came and pulled it to pieces, and this happened several times till the builders gave up attempting to go on. It seemed a law that the colony was not to spread. The other instance was a nest in the big bee& on the lawn, but we had that shot down, and they have never built there again. Every May dozens are shot, but all the same they increase enormously, and I often wonder where he surplus go to. My mother has just told me that she thinks a few nests have been here longer, than I have said—more like fifty years, and perhaps more, as that was the time she first came to liTe here." Miss ffarington, of Worden Hall; Leyland, writing of the rookery there, says :—" The rookery here is a very old one, and in my father's days was much larger than the present one. He kept hounds, and their larder was in the rookery, much to their advantage, and this, I sup- pose reconciled them to having their young killed with cross-bow bullets every Spring. After this, the house had to be rebuilt, all but the stables, &c., and we had to leave it, and, for a year or two they de- serted us. Ido not suppose they liked the lime pits, the woodwork, &c., which went on, but they gradually came, back again, but never so strongly as before. Worse . for them, the tall old trees they had built upon were succumbing to age, and a .great many of them had to. be cut down. There were always some trees that they would not allow nests to, be built Upon. A few years since they had got down to eight or nine nests, but we have now a better show of nests than that, and the rooks are branching out and building new nests here and there in different places in the park, and

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

those new establishments threaten to get larger than the old one. Where they come from I cannot say, but the park always seems full of them, to a greater extent than the nests would warrant. They do some mischief to gamekeepers and farmers no doubt, but the latter are amply repaid by their keeping down grubs and in- sects. They are not molested here, for we like them for old times' sake."

The Duke of Devonshire's keeper at Ifolker says : " We have not had so many rooks for the last few years; late frosts and cold winds spoiled their eggs. I have repeatedly remarked that when we are going to have a storm they go away to some more sheltered place, and i do not return till it s over. Ido not consider that they are enemies ?of farmers ; they destroy insects that do damage, which benefits the farmer. We kill from 20 to 100 dozens each y&r." The head keeper at Tatton says :—'Rooks do some good to the farmers, and they also do a great deal of harm if not closely watched, and of late years they have destroyed a great number of pheasants' eggs. I consider rooks are on the decrease in this neighbourhood." The following are named amongst Rookeries in Lanca- shire. div.head: MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.'
div.p: THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.'

WHAT WE ARE TO PREPARE FOR. Now that October has been entered upon it is only natural to expect that the beautiful weather which has been our lot this year will leave us, and that we shall arrive at the period of cold, damp days and nights. The rapid shortening of the days and the earlier lighting of the lamps show us that we must expect to have to wrap up, to draw near the fire, to shut out the cold. Whilst not forgetting ourselves, we must remember our fowls, for. they need, to be especially looked after at a time when sudden changes are alniost as regular as the day- light. We know how difficult it is to avoid ourselves taking cold, even though we have the power of thinking and the ability in large measure to suit our clothing, our food, and our circumstances to the atmospheric varia- tions.. But in the case of fowls, whose power is limited in all these respects, for they are fed and housed as their owner decides, it is imperative on the owner that he shall prepare beforehand for these variations if he would prevent his fowls suffering thereby. Even then it is not always easy to do this. Changes are rapid. The even- ing may be mild, the morning bitter cold. These are the things that bother the poultry keeper and make him long for a more equable climate. But as the longing will not bring that much-to-be-desired state of affairs, isll that he can do is to make the best of his present con- ditions. That will pay better in the long run than any amount;of grumbling. It is imperative, In the first place, to see that the poultry houses are in proper order. A hot summer like that which we have had is sure to dry whatever materials .the house is made of, and to thus create in- terstices, which will admit both wind and rain when they come. Many of these can be seen if looked for. With that 'object there should be a thorough examina- tion of the roof and walls of each house, and such re- pairs as are necessary made. Some of these places will not be discovered until the weather breaks, for they are not to be seen; but if all that may be apparent are attended to beforehand, there will not be, much to do afterwards. Above all, every wooden house should have a good coat of paint or tar outside, and perman- ent houses also lime washed within. These are matters which will be difficult to do later on, and so long as the weather is good they are best and most easily done. If a wooden house is thought to be thin in its walls, and consequently cold, there are two ways of meeting this great drawback in a cheap manner. One method is to nail on the outside the material known as roofing felt. If this is nailed on horizontally with a slight flap of each •upper piece over the one below it, and then the whole well tarred and slightly dusted with sand, the house will be warm and comfortable and perfectly weather proof. Such a house will last for years if it has a coat of tar laid on once or twice a year. The other method is even a cheaper one. This is to cover the outside or line the inside of the house with thick brown paper. In the former case it should have first a coat of tar below the paper, and then above it another coat or two. But in the latter case the brown paper is put next the wood, and then a good coating of lime wash above. The brown paper is not quite so effective as the felt, but it is a remarkably good substitute. In only too many houses, which are more or less per- fect in other ways, the ventilation is entirely neglected. The houses may be warm, well made, and well ap- pointed, but all will be in vain if care is not taken to have a proper system for the provision of fresh air. In ,too many, houses the position of the perches is right be- tween the window and door, and as these are the only ways in which the current of air can enter and find its • exit, there is little wonder that in cold or windy weather roup and other diseases ensue, or in other houses where there is provided a ventilator in the roof, the entrance for the air is only by the door, or the trap, or the win- dow, and as all these are nearly certain to be below or on a line with the birds, they are exposed always to a draught whilst at roost. The dangers of such a system we have pointed out before, and it is, therefore, un- necessary that we should repeat them in full again, for to every reader they must be obvious. But, for the in- formation of those who do not know how to remedy the matter, we shall show how to avoid them. Doors and windows should always be made to close tightly. We do not mean that they should be made difficult to open, but simply to be closed when they are shut Hanging an old door on to a shed does not do, for when that is done there is generally as much space all around as will admit of a gale of wind. We always prefer the door to open outwards, and if not fitted into a proper door-jam to lap over a little all round. Of windows the same may be said. It is to be remembered that a door and window is of greater importance in a small poultry-house than a dwelling-house, for in the latter there are passages to break the draught, but in the former there are not. The object sh3uld be to fit the door and window so that they will not admit the air. There is less danger from their being wide open than fitting badly. The fowls' trap presents more difficulties, for it can seldom be kept closed at night, and if unpro- tected appears to gather the air from everywhere. The best plan is to have a shed or dust box at the side of the house and to make the trap open into this. The shed is then a protector, and as wind does not easily run round ininksharp corners as would In necessary to get in here, the trap an with safety be left open. Some provision must be made for the circulation of the air. The best we know of is that in which a cham- ber is formed of a portion of the roof, with lower boards at each end, and loosely fitted boards dividing the house from this chamber. All foul air is carried off, and with- out the least draught. Another good way, is to have a few holes or a sliding lattice shutter in the side of the house above the level of the perches, the openings covered inside the house with a box, on the upper side of which is a number of holes. This, with a ventilator in the roof, is nearly as effective. The other part of this subject we must leave over to next week. SEASONABLE HINTS. As we have hinted in our article this week, we need at this time of the year to look ahead a little, and those succeed best who do this. They are prepared for even- tualities., and can meet the necessities of each season as they arise. If sand is used in the poultry houses, a stock of it should be laid in, as it is difficult to get in wet or snowy weather. Or, if fine earth or ashes are used instead, let these be got also as far as possible. Old mortar, lime, or oyster shells had better be got also, for it is a well-known fact that the thing wanted is not always the easiest to get just when it is required. Old mortar is always worth taking, and the pulling down of a really old house is an opportunity for getting a stock of it not to be missed. For shell-forming, and as an aid to digestion, it is invaluable, as also is a stpply of fine gravel.

• Tux Losr WAiP.—The court-martial at Portsmouth, on Monday, found that H.M.S. Wasp was wrecked on Tory Island in consequence of want of due care in navigation, and acquitted the survivors of all blame. Siz more bodies, appare,rtly , those of seamen, have been recovered since Saturday from the wreck. LORD KRNMARS AND IRISH EVICTIONS—The Earl of Keumare, while driving outside Killarney with Colonel Deese, came upon a family wbo bad been evicted from their cabin on his lordship's property three days previously. On ascertaining the condition of affairs, the earl got a hat- chet and broke In the door of the house, bidding the poor people to re•enter their fotmer home. He was not aware of the eviction.

The Roman hot baths of Volterra, discovered in the last century by a Signor Guarnacci, have lately been further explored by Signor Cinci, and the beautiful example of tesselated pavement of coloured glass and marbles has been removed to the Guarnacci Museum. The Danish gunboat Fylla has completed the explora" tion",tof the coast of Greenland, and has returned from Arctic [waters. The gunboat was four months away, and reached 70 deg. north latitude. Several new *odes . of marine fauna are said to have been found by the explorers, and a meteorite weighing 2,0001 b. At the meeting of the French Academy of Sciences this week, a paper by M. Ckiandi' an engineer, who has been engaged in manipulating sulphuret of carbon for 20 years past, was read on the qualities of that- sun" stance as a disinfectant. The author showed that th,e, sulphuret is soluble in water, and stronOT recommendeu its use against cholera and other epidemic diseases. M. Mairet has lately read a paper to the French Acei; demy of Sciences on the association of phosphoric ova with the nutrition and action of the brain. He states that intelleCtilal work retards the general nutrition by modifying the elimination of phosphoric; acid, dirniniee_ ing the proportion of acid in combination with entail' and increasing the earthy phosphates. SEWER VENTILATION.—We are glad to see, saYs soul! Lancet, that the suggestion we made repeatedlY time ago for the benefit of Brighton has been adliPt,V,-. by the Corporation of the city of London, and that LH% Commissioners of Sewers are about to arrange wit af builders of new houses to construct pipes for ventilat- ing the sewers, and to carry them to a level above te! roofs of the houses. When this is done the grounA level openings can be closed, and then the plague " sewer gas will be a thing of the past. HIGH Gams.—lt is sheer wantonness to throw away game because it happens to be a little " high," but is necessary to use permanganate of potash to purifC from the taint, though it is sometimes used successflua if carefully employed? It will generally suffice "" cleanse .the game thoroughly and wipe it quite a7t, with soft cloths, rubbing a little salt into the wr_tee" parts. Game which is simply "high," without beifl putrid, is particularly easy of digestion, and of gres' value toeinvalids.—Lancet. ELECTRICAL ITEMS.—MM. D Toramasi and Radi-euet have brought out a new battery with two carbon e,lec"' trodes. The positive electrode consists of a carbon lunte:/ placed at the bottom of a porcelain vessel and cover with peroxide of lead; the negative electrode cons,ists of a carbon plate containing on its upper surface plaL•l ised coke. The two plates are separated by a sheet 0 parchment paper. The liquid used is a saturated 501 u.; tion of:common salt, Which must not completely cove; the upper plate. The electro-motive force on closed circuit is 0-6 volts.—A victory has been gained by Van Rysselberghe in Belgium by the solution of the problein of transmitting a telegraphic and a telephonic 'messafer • along the same wire at the same time. A trial of this has been made at the Antwerp Universal Exhibition where concerts held in important towns in Belgium wein heard; the transmission being made with ordinal instruments along ordinary telegraph lines and wits earth returns.-2Vature. PHOTOGRAPHING A COAL MINE.—The first attenint ever made to photograph the interior of a coal mine was successfully carried out on August 28 at Kochinoor CO)- liery of ;:the Philadelphia and Reading Company, at Shenandoah, Pennsylvania, under the direction of Mr- • J. T. Brown, the .agent of the Smithsonian Institute. ' The incline is 500 feet in, depth, and the breast photo- ' graphed is 40 feet wide by 60 feet high. The photo- ' grapher:was Mr. G. M. Dretz of Portsville. The work- ' fug was illuminated by the Arnoux electric light. Eigitt exposures were made, occupying from 10 to 30 minute& each, and resulting in five perfect negatives, showing not only the formation of the coal measures but also the practical operation of cutting coal and loading cars. ' The views are intended to conSttute a portion of th_r United States Government exhibit at the coming New Orleans Exposition.—lrtm. AN 'APPROACHING STAR.—OHO of the most beautiful' - of aOtars in the heavens is Arcturus, in the constella:. ' tion-Bootes. In January last the, Astronomer Royal ' communicated to the Royal Astronomical Society' n ' tabulated statement of the results of the observations made at Greenwich during 1883 in applying the meth"of Dr. Huggins for measuring the approach and recce- , sion of the so-called fixed stars in direct line. Neal ' 290 of these observations are thus recorded, 21 of which were devoted to Arcturus, and were made from March 30 to August 24. The result shows that t4is brilliant '• scintillating star is mOVillg rapidly towards us with a velocity of more than 50 miles per second (the mean of the 21 observations is 5018). This amounts to about • 3,000 miles per minute, 180,000 per hour, 4,320,000 miles per day. Will this approach continue, or will the star • presently appear stationary and then recede? If the ' motion is orbital, the latter will occur. There is, how- ' ever, nothing in the rates observed to indicate any such l orbital motion and as the observations extended over five months this has some weight. Still it may be travel- ling'in a mighty orbit of many. years' duration, tho ; bending of which may in time be indicated by a retards- tion of the rate of approach, then by no perceptiblg ' movement either towards or away from us, an this 3 followed by a recession equal to its previous approach. 3 If, on the other hand, the 4,500,000 Of miles per day con' ; tinue, the star must become visibly brighter to posterity, in spite of the enormous magnitude of eosmical tances. Our 81-ton guns drive forth their projectiles ' with a maximum velocity of 1,400 ft. per second. Arc- ; turns is approaching ue with a speed that is 200 greater I than this. It thus moves over a distance equal to that between the earth and the sun in 21 days. Our present ' distance from Arcturus is estimated at 1,622,000 times ' this. Therefore, if the star oontinues to approach us at the same rate as measured last year, it will have com- pleted the whole of its journey towards us in 93,000 years.—Gentleman's Magazine. ' WOMEN AS INVENTORS.—Tho Scientific American, quot- ing from the North American Review a list of inventions recently patented in the United States by women, says : —" The writer has omitted from his list a large number ' of patents which have been granted to women, some of which have proved of considerable value ta the paten- tees. He commences his list with a spinning machine ' capable of running from twelve to forty threads; a ro- tary loom, doing three times the' work of an ordinal"' ' loom; a chain elevator, screw crank for steamships, a ' fire escape; a wool feeder and 'weigher, one of the most' I delicate machines ever invented, and of incalculable , benefit to every wool manufacturer; a portable reser- voir for use in case of fire, a process of burning petro- leum in place of wood and coal for steam generating purposes; an improvement in spark arresters, to be ap- plied to locomotives; a danger signal for street cross- ' ings on railways, a plan for heating cars without fire, a lubricating felt for subduing friction (the last five all bearing upon railroad travel); syllable type, with ad- • justable cases and apparatus; machine for trimming pamphlets, writing machine, signal rocket used in the navy, deep sea telescope, method of deadening sound on elevated railways, smoke burner, bag folding machine, &c. Many improvements in sewing machines have been made by women, as—a device for sewing sails and heavy cloth, quilting attachments, the magic niftier, threading a machine when it is running, an adaptation of maclunes for sewing leather, &c. This last was the invention of a .practical woman machinist, who for many years carried on a large harness manufactory in New York city. The deep sea telescope, invent. by' Mrs. Mather, and improved by her daughter, is a unique and important invention, bringing the bottom of the largest ships to view without the expense of raising them into a dry dock. tly its means wrecks can be in- spected, obstructions to navigation removed, torpedoes successfully sought for, and immense sums annuallv saved to the marine service. A machine which, for is complicated mechanism, and extraordinary ingenuity, has attracted much attention both in this country and Europe, is that for the manufacture of satchel-bottom paper bags. Many men of mechanical genius long di- rected their attention to this problem without success. Miss Maggie Knight, to whose genius this machine is due, it is said, refused $50,000 for it shortly after taking out her patent. Miss Knight has since invented a ma- chine doing the work, the writer says, of thirty persons in folding bags, and herself superintended the erection ,of the machinery at Amherst, Mass."
At Ashton-under-Lyne, on Saturday, a steeplejack named Christopher Delaney fell from a factory chimney and was instantaneously killed.

POISONING A RITER.—At Listowel, en Saturday, five men were charged with poisoning the river Teale. by means of which they succeded in killing a quantity of fish, which they subsequently sold for £8 ss. chree of the accused were each fined £5 7s 61. Tho other two were acquitted. - THE LIQUOR TRAFFIC ON THE NORTH B.—Mr C M Kennedy, C. 8., of the Foreign Office, and Mr C Cecil Trevor, CB., assistant secretary to the Board of Trade' have been appointed British delegates at the International Con- ference about to assemble at the Hael‘e relative to the re- gulation of the liquor traffic in the North Sea. Belgium, Denmark, and France have, in addition to Great Britain,. accepted the invitation of the Netherlands Government. THE GARMOYLE BREACH OF PROMISE cASE.—ALLEGED - SETTLEMENT—It is stated, says the Laudon correspondent - of one of the Dublin papers, that the great breach of promise case of Miss Forteecue against Lord Garmoyle has been settled. It is further stated that the young lady is to have a substantial solatium by the payment of a round sum of £25,000, and that the correspondence, especially certain letters addressed by Lord Cairns to the plaintiff. shall he given up. Lord Gannoyle solemnly assured him that on no • eohsideration would he submit .himself tO Mr.lttileelPs eress-examination.—This story is authoritatively denied. and it is stated that the case will really come into court. SRA CANAL TO ST. PirrimSßltiu3.—A trial was made last week of the navigability of the Ssa Canal to St Petersburg, ass rehearsal of the formal ceremony of opening.vvhich is to take place before the Emperor at a date not yet definitely fixed. Four vessels—the cruiser Africa, commanded by Captain Dubasoff, who blew up the Turkish man-of-war on the Danube •, the Imperial yacht Derjava, the frigate Olaf, and the yacht Tsarevna—were cboaen to attempt the pas- sage from the canal basin into the Neva, in the presence of the Minister of Marine. The Africa, with the deepest draught of 17ft., was unsuccessful, and grounded twice, which caused the adjournment of i Le trial till the following morning, when, after much trouble, she and the other yes- sels passed through the river.

FOREIGN NEWS.

EGYPT AND THE SOUDA.N. MURDER OF COLONEL STEVVART. WADY lIALFA, MONDAY.—It is persistently rumoured here that Colonel Stewart went ashore after his steamer had struck a rock it the Wady Garna, and was murdered by Bedouins. Canto, MONDAY.—Major Kitchener telegraphs from Am- bukol that Colonel Stewart's steamer from Khartoum struck on a rock in the Wady Game Cataract. Colonel Stewart subsequently sent a messenger to Major Kitchener, who has consequently asked for reinforcements from Dongola. 9-30 p.m.—further particulars of the alleged murder of Colonel Stewart are contained in Major Kitchener's telegraphic re- port to the British authorities here, according to which, after the wreck of Colonel Stewatt's steamer near the Fifth Cata- ract, a Sheikh offered to conduct the Colonel and party a- cross the desert to Merawi, but on the way the Sheikh tur- ned traitor, and murdered the whole party. CAIRO, WEDNESDAY.—The report that M. ilerbin, the French Consul at Khartoum, was killed at the same time as Colonel Stewart, is mere surmise, clused by General Gor- don's announced intention of sending the English, Austrian, and French Consuls at Khartoum with Colonel Stewart to Berber. There is no further news regarding the Colonel's fate.

Colonel Stewart was, we are informed, within about a eamel's ride of Merawi when he was assassinated. There is now little doubt (says the Press Association) that the Colonel left his steamer trusting to the good faith of the Bedouin chief to conduct him to Merawi. All Colonel Stewart's party, numbering perhaps over 100, seem to have met the fate of their leader. Colonel Stewart was the eldest son of Mr John Stewart, of Ballygawley, county Antrim, and was the owner of considerable estates in the counties of Down, Tyrone, and Antrim. He was unmarried. WADY LIALFA, SIINDAY.-A. full company of the cornmisariat and transport corps, together with a railway com- pany of Royal Engineers, have arrived here. The plate layers forming part of the latter have gone on to Sarras to work on the railway.--7.30 p m.—Lord Wolseley arrived here at 1-30 p.m. to-day in the Khedive's yacht Ferroz, and received Generals Earle and Wood and their staffs on board. Lord Wolseley is expected to remain here for some little time. Assonew, MONDAY.—On the arrival of the Black Watch yesterday a case of smallpox was discovered amongst the men. The betabon his consequently been placed in quar- antine Three hundred and seventy horses of the Egyptian cavalry started for Wady Haifa to-day by road, for the use ef the 19th Hussars. SUBMISSION OF THE TRIBES. .

DONGOLA, TUESDAY.—GeneraI Gordon has received in- telligence of the Mudir of Dongola's victory at Korti. The news has had the effect of greatly inspiriting the garrison of Khartoum and General Gordon's followers. The Sheikh Mahomed Keir of Sawarah reports that the Mandi. on arriving at Shalt, on the Nile, learnt that the people of Jebel Dair had risen against him, and he imme- diately set out to quell the rebellion. Some Skeikhs from the Sawarab and Hawawoo tribes, dwelling between Shendy and Khartoum, have visited the Middies Vakeel at Ambukol, and tendered the submission of their tribes. numbering 15,000 men. Mahomed Keir recommends El Debbeh as a suitable spot for a depot. He is willing to contract for the hire of camels and the supply of cattle. The Mudir of Dongola is rendering every assistance to the expedition. He despatches spies in all directions. WADY HALFA, TITESDAY.—Lord Wolseley inspected the hospital to-day, and expressed his entire satisfaction with the arrangements made by Brigade-Surgeon Norris, Surgeon- Major Churchill, and Quartermaster Copping. Tue first death here occurred yesterday, when a private of the Staf- fordshire regiment succundbed to enteric fever. There are fitly-nine cases of illness in the hospital, but none are of a serious cha racier.
