- - - - _ • CAIRO, SkTURDAY.—Nubar Pasha replied to-day to the protest of the Consuls against the suspension of the Sinking Fund. His reply at ,tes that this suspension was a measure if absolute necessity in view of the situation of the Egyp- tian Treasury. Lord Northbrook will proceed on his journey up the Nile as far as Assouan. He will be back in Cairo by the 20th inst.
THE FRANCO-CHINESE WAR.—vIcroRY OF THE
FRENCH.

PARIS, SATURDAY.—The-.ll:finiet-e'r of Marine has received the following telegrams from Admiral Conrbet :—" Kelung, Oct. 3. I commenced operations against Kelung on the Ist inst. by the occupation of the height of Saint Element. After a fairly warm engagement during the night of the Ist, the Chinese troops evacuated two works to the west of the height, and we subsequently took possession of them with- out striking a blow. We are now engaged in fortifying them. Our loss is four killed, one missing, five severely and eight slightly wounded. The inhabitants of the country estimate the Chinese less at 80 to 100 killed, and 200 to 300 wounded. Admiral Lespes commenced an attack on Tamsni on the 2nd lost, and will occupy the port, if pos. sible." " Horn-Komi SATITRDAY.—A serious riot occurred here among coolies, originating in the refusal of some boatmen to =lvey cargo to French ships, which led to a general strike. The military were called out to quell disturbance, and in the encounter which ensued several natives were killed or wounded. The populace maltreated the police. The excite- ment has now subsided. Paws, MONDAY.—A telegram from Hong-Kong of to- day's date state that the French have bombarded and rem. pied Tamsui, and that three battalions of Marines are being despatched thence in order to effect a junction with the French troops occupying Kelung. An agreement has been come to between General Campenon and the Budget Com- mittee with regard to the reduction of the Budget of the Ministry of War. The amount of the military estimates is now fixed at 14,000 000 francs, instead of 23,000,000 franca. _ _ .

PARIS, WEDNESDAY —The following telegram has been received here, dated Hanoi, 10 a.m., to-day : A battalion of the Foreign Legion, two companies of infantry, and one sec- tion of mountain artillery, under the command of Colonel Donnier, have gained a brilliant victory on the Loochnan River. The enemy offered an energetic resistance, but, after an engagement lasting six hours, was completely routed. The gunboats /Lehi, Masane,Carabine, and Eclair took part in the enzagement. The French loss amounted to four killed, including one captain. and 20 wounded, one isf whom was a lieutenant. The French continue to ad- vance,
ANOTHER CHINESE REVERSE. LOSS OF 1,000 MEN.

Paws, THURSDAY.—The Minister of Marine has received the following telegram from General Briere de Lisle, dated Hanoi, Wednesday, 7-30 p.m. :—A. body of Chinese regu- lars, in an attempt to take the offensive in the Upper Foto. chnan, were repulsed by Colonel Dounier on tbe 6th lost, with the loss of 1,000 man. We had four killed, inclu- ding Captain Deyna of the Foreign Legion, and 21 woun- ded, among whom were Lieutenant B ttaille, of the Tonquin Sharpsbootert. The gunboats Carabine Massne, La Bache, and Eclair, took part in the battle. The column under the command of General Negrier has again gone up the Phu Lang in order to endeavour to cut off the retreat of the Chinese. _ _
SHANGHAI, THURSDAY, 10-12 A.N. The bombardment of Tamsui continues. The forts have been destroyed. The Chinese troops are strongly entrenched.
THE CHOLERA.

80, MONDAY.—In the city of Naples the cholera is de- creasing. The number of cases reported on Sunday were 49, with 14 deaths; and on Monday 36 cases and 12 deaths. Pews, MONDAY.—The mortality returns published on Saturday report 806 deaths in Paris during the week, as against 922 in the preceding week. This is the lowest death rate that has been registered for some time past. Four deaths occurred on Sunday in the Pyrenees Orientals. MADRID, MoNnay.—On Sunday three cases and two deaths occurred in the province of Alicante. To-day there have been no fresh cases nor deaths in the province of Ali- cante, Lerida. or Tarragona. MADRID, WEDNESDAY.—TO-day's official bulletin reports that during the last 24 hqurs there have been four cases of -cholera and four deaths in the province of Alicante. It is affirmed that no fresh cases of a suspicious character have occurred at Barcelona during the last 24 hours.

- ROME, WEDNESDAY.—To:day's official bulletin reports that 30 cases of cholera and one death have occurred in the city of Naples, besides seven among patients already under treatment. In the remainder of the province of Naples there have been 26 cases and nine deaths, in addition to 10 deaths of persons already ender treatment. COLLIERY EXPLOSION.—SERIOUS LOSS OF LIFE. _ _ _

OLVIITZ, TITURSDAY'—An explosion of firedamp occurred yesterday in the Emma shaft of a mine in Polish Ostrau. About twenty miners are known to.have lost their lives, but the exact number of killed and injured has not yet been as- certained.

div.head: FOURTEEN CHILDREN DROWNED.
div.p: FOURTEEN CHILDREN DROWNED.

ESSEGO (AUSTRIA), MoNnay.—Fourteen children have been drowned in the Drava by the capsizing of a boat in which they were playing. DENMARK.—THE DESTRUCTION OF THE CASTLE OF CHRISTIANBORG. COPENHAGEN, SATURDAY.—The fire at the Royal Castle of Ohrietianborg was not got under control until half-past one o'clock this morning. Important works of Art, includ- ing some by Thorwaldsen, as well as the archives of the Rigs- flag, have been destroyed. The damage is estimated at several million kroner. The Castle Chapel and the Thor- waldsen Museum have been saved, although at one time they were in great danger. The King and the Crown Prince were present at the scene of the fire until midnight. COPENHAGEN, MONDAY.—The Rigsdag was opened to-day with a speech from the throne by the King in person. Owing to the recent fire at the Castle of Obristianborg, the ceremony took plane in the grand hall of the University. THE RUSSIAN BLACK SEA SQUADRON. ST. PETERSBURG, SATMIDAY.—The ceremony of laying the keel of the new Ironclad Katharina 11. took place to- day at Nicolaieff in the presence of the Grand Duke Alexis. The keels of the two new irenclads, Tschesme and Sinope, and of a new floating dry dock, will be laid at Sebastopol on Monday and Tuesday next. SEBASTOPOL, MONDAY —The ceremony of laying the foundation stone of the first dry dock in South Russia took place here to-day, in the presence of the Grand Duke Alexis.
THE FLOOD IN BUENOS LYRES,
Nino TORIC, SUNDAY.—A despatch of yesterday's date,

received here from Buenos Ayres, states that during the re- cent inundations in the province of Buenos Ayres the com- munications with many towns were cut off for 11 days. The damage is enormous. Entire families have been drowned, and many persons are dying of hunger. Sub- scription listshave been opened for the relief of those in dis- tress. THE DUKE OF CONNAUGHT. SIMLL, SiTIOIDLY.—The Duke and Duchess of Con- naught have visited the Khyber Pass, and are now proceed- ing to Cashmere. HURRICANE IN SICILY : GREAT LOSS OF LIFE. ROME, WEDNESD&Y.—A cyclone of extraordinary vio- lence yesterday swept over the city of Catauia, uprooting trees and damaging houses. Twenty persons are stated to have been killed and fifty injured. The severity of the gale was such as to render all assistance impossible. ROME, THURSDAY—Despatches from Catania give har- rowing details of the havoc caused by the cyclone which swept over that city the day before yesterday. Later advices from Catania give the number of those in- jured in the cyclone as 400, and estimate the damage caused at 4,000,000 lire. FRANCE. Paws, WEDNESDAY.—Count Herbert von Bismarck, who has arrived here from London on his way to the Hague, exchanged visits yesterday with M Jules Ferry. A decree is officially published to-day prohibiting the im- portation into France of rags and bedding from Spain. President Grevy has signed a decree grantieg fifty thou- sand francs for distribution among the needy workmen in Lyons. There was only one death from Cholera yesterday in the department Pyrenees-Orientales.

A RAINFORD MAN'S ADVENTURE AT
-WARRINGTON,

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and Mr John Fair. dough, Mr William B Berry, described as a corn miller and dealer, carrying on business at Rainford, was charged on a suinimms with having wilfully obstructed James Tanner, a foreman portsr in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company, at Arpley station, on the 2nd of September, and also with using abusive language on the station, tending to interfere with the comfort of the pas- sengers. Mr Preston, junior, solicitor, Liverpool, appeared for the company, and Mr J 0 Swift, solicitor, St delens, defended.—Mr Preston explained that the defendant got into the wrong portion of a train at Liverpool and came to Warrington instead of going to St Helens, for which station he had booked. At Warrington the porter told him that if he would wait he would put him in the right way to get to St Helens, and Flom after defendant became a ,usive and used bad language. U. challenged the officer to "toe a mark " and fight him, but that person sent for the station master. The defendant then tried to get away from the station and pushed about in the crowd, and in so doing struck a woman on the hand. Mr Preston then read a let- ter from the defendant's solicitor, intimating his intention to commence an action against the company for assault and false imprisonment, the damages being laid at £l2O, and the imprisonment consisting in the defendant having been detained against his will in the station whilst the sta- tion master was sent for. In the letter it was complained that the defendant's clothes were much disarranged, that he was strained and hurt so much that he had been unable to attend to his business, and that he had been detained at Arpley station for a long time.—James Tanner, the porter, bore out the statement of Mr Preston, and said that the defendant clenched his fists and wanted witness to toe a mark. (Laughter.) Witness told him that the company did not put him there to fight passengers. (Renewed laugh- ter).—George Warburton, farmer, Heatley, near Lymm, corroborated, and added that he did not hear any bad lan- guage used by the porters on duty at the station.—Mrs Mary Holcroft, Lymne, spoke to her hand having been struck by the defendant, and Thomas Houlton, brakesman, and James Shaw, porter, gave evidence respecting the con- duct of the defendant —Mr Swift, in his defence, said that the summons had been issued without any informa- tion being sent to him, and he thought that it was not a case in which proceedings would have been taken in the ordinary course of events. He contended that they had been taken to ask tho Bench to convict Berry of some offence or other so that it might prejudice him in the ac:ion he purposed bringing against the company.—The Mayor said that the defendant had been guilty of gross misconduct, the evidence on that point was clear and concise. There appeared to be a doubt, after hearing a contention from Mr Swift, as to whether they had power to convict in the first case, and they would give the defendant the benefit of the doubt. In reference to the second charge there could be no doubt. The defen- dant was the first aggressor, refused to give up his ticket, or state his name and address, and his conduct must have been a nuisance to everyone at the station. He would be fined in the highest penalty of 40s and costs.

div.head: ASHTON.
div.p: ASHTON.

STAR HOTEL BOWLING GREEN.—The closing game came off on Saturday he splendid weather. The green was in good condition, and the bowling proved to be very satisfac- tory. The bowlers generally were evenly drawn, as will be seen by the score :—Captain's side, 61; secretary's side, 68. Afterwards a knife and fork tea was provided, to which ample justice was done. POACHING AT ASIITON.—At the Wigan County Police Court, on Friday, Thomas Hill, of Goose Green, was charged, under a warrant, with using a net for the purpose of taking game on land in the occupation of James Turner, at Ashton, and over which Lord Gerard has the right of shooting.—Messrs Cruppin's gamekeeper said that on the 25th March last he saw defendant and another man draw a net across one of Turner's fields where a hare was sitting. The hare, however, get up and escaped. Witness caught the defendant, who bad a net in his possession.— The bench in- dicted a penalty of 403 and costs, and defendant was also fined 103 and costs for a charge of drunkenness. PARK HOTEL BOWLING CLUB —BOWLING SWEEP —The members of the above club bad a sweep for prizes to close the bowling season on Saturday last. It being a beautiful day, and the green in excellent condition, some good play was shown. After the bowling was over all sat down in the Park Hotel clubroom to an excellent knife-and-fork tea, provided by Mrs M Cuoliffe in hr usual good style. Tea over, the prizes were given to the winners. After the prizes were distributed the captain of the club was called to the chair, and Mr George Lowe to the vice-chair. Songs were given during the evening, and the healtbs of the members of the Park Hetet Bowling Club were heartily drunk. A vote of thanks was given to the chairman and vice-chairman, and to Mrs Cunliffe for her able catering.

div.head: HAYDOCK.
div.p: HAYDOCK.

HAIrDOCIC BRASS 1317.11,--Co—N-cia—T.—The first of a series of concerts in connection with the Haydock Brass Band took place in the Colliery Schools on Monday evening, and was of a very successful character. The want of proper uniform for the members of the band has been long-felt. They have therefore decided to make an effort to raise funds with which to purchase the required clothing, and the gathering on Monday night was the first venture with that object. It was held under the patronage of Mr Joseph Evans, J.P., DL., Mr A L Evans, and Mr C Pilkington, J.P., and Mr Pilkington kinnly presented a ticket of admission to each of the apprentices employed by the firm of Messrs Richard Evans and Company. Altogether there would be an atten- dance Of about 500 persons, who were highly pleased with the proceedings. The vocalists were Miss Lewis (Earles- town), Miss Rose (Newton), Mr P Hastie (Earlestown), Mr W Lythgoe and Mr J Potter (Warrington), and their selec- tions were much appreciated. Mr H J Darman officiated at the pianoforte. During the evening the band, under the able leadership of Mr Mclntyre, excellently rendered the 'Caliph of Bagdad," and selections from "Patience." The programme concluded with the National Anthem.

div.head: CHORAL FUNERAL AT ST. JAMES'S.
div.p: CHORAL FUNERAL AT ST. JAMES'S.

The choir and many of the parishioners of ilaydock were present on Sunday afternoon, Oct. 5, on the occasion of the burial of the remains of Mr T Haze'den, a former member of the choir. The service was choral, and ths hymns sang wee—" 0 Paradise," " For ever with the Lord," and "Rock of Ages." The young man was very much beloved by all who knew him; and what made the circumstances more sad was the fact that only two Sundays ago had the marriage banns been called for the third time of asking between him and one who has been indeed bereft. After the morning ser- vice at St James's and again in the afternoon, the "Dead March" in Saul was played on the organ. The concourse of people who gathered together in the afternoon was unprecedented; in fact, never before have there been so many people present at a funeral here. At the grave the Vicar (the Rev H LI Kear- ney) exhorted the mourners to find comfort in the sure and certain hope that, though taken awaylrom them for a time, their dear brotrier and friend had entered into the land of peace; and that though they had all hoped to have been gathered together for his marriage here on earth, yet in His all wise mercy, for reasons unknown to man, his Heavenly Father had thought it better to take him to Himself out lf this world of sin and sorrow. The Vicar bore testimony to the many good words which on all hands were to be heard in reference to Thomas Hazelden ; whenever there was any good thing to be taken in hand he was always ready to help. The brightness of that funeral spoke of the Christian's hope in a bright future. The music and the flowers contrasted with the fashion of gloom and mourning now fast dying away in all denominations of Christians. The flowers as they bloomed each year seemed to tell of the Resurrection Lift; and the music upon earth seemed to be the foretaste of the Songs of Paradise. Many amongst the crowd were moved to tears by the tender and loving address given at the grave side. This young man had originally worked in Haydock in one of the pits, but had lately been a policeman at Bootle, where the accident happened which caused his death. He was cleaning a window, and missing his footing fell on some iron rails, upon one of which he was impaled. He was at the Bootle Hospital, where with much kindness and attention he was well treated, and all seemed well until he suddenly collapsed, and to the sorrow of his friends he died on Wednesday, October Ist. The card commemorating his death concludes with these words—" Blessed are they which are called unto the Marriage Supper of the Lamb."

DEATH IN A RAILWAY CARRIAGE.—The body of a gentleman who was found in a second-class carriage on the Chatham line at Walworth station, London, on Wrdnesday morning, was identified at midnight as that of Mr David Green, of New York, who was exhibiting some of his in- ventions at the Health Exhibition. He is believed to have died from natural causes.

div.head: ME EXAMINER, SATITRDAY4 OCTOBER 11, 1884.
div.p: ME EXAMINER, SATITRDAY4 OCTOBER 11, 1884.

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL- A monthly meeting of this Council was held In the Town Hall, on Tuesclity evening, the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presiding. There were also present—Aldermen Kemn, Webster, Davies, Chandley, Burgess, Holmes; Councillors Brown, Dixon, Crosfield, Barker, Dakin, Ashton, Fiancomb, Monks, Broadbent, Mackie, Bolton, Burgess, Hutchinson, Marsh, Milner, Pierpoint, Wright, and Tinsley.

abstaining from making the figures public surely the Council tumid understand that they had only one object in view that was not to prejudice the purchases. (Hear, hear.) The MAYO 2 said that although £31,107 was a large amount, when they re-sold the land for what was considered to be a reasonable price, the actual cost to Oh town for that great improvement would only be something like £6,000 or £7,000, which was surely not a very great expenditure for a town of the importance of Warrington. Alderman DAvpm : Let it he well understood that the estimate includes street improvement.
The Tows CLERK: That is so. Tbe minutes of the Streetimprovement Committee were then confirmed.
PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.

Alderman limes moved the confirmation of the minutes of this committee. They contained nothing of special mo- ment except the estimates for the next half year. He thought that they would shortly have a report from the Borough Surveyor showing the Council what might be saved by borrowing Money for paving the streets instead of using so much macadam. Alderman Homes expressed disapprobation of such a course. He did not think that they should ever borrow money for the purpose of paving streets. He hoped that they should never do anything of the sort. The minutes were then confirmed. CEMETERY COMMITTEE.

Mr Bnoww moved, and Mr PIERPOINT seconded the adop- tion of the minutes. Alderman BURGESS asked how it was that the commit- tee were not getting so much money as was the case in the corresponding part of last year. Alderman KEAN : The sanitary improvements of this town are so great under his (Alderman Burgess's) leader- ship, that there is not so many deaths, and consequently we do not get so much money. (Laughter). The MAYOR : I hope you are sa'isaed, Mr Burgess. Alderman BURGESS: Not by any means. The minutes were adopted. SANITARY COMUITTEE : THE "SURVIVAL OF THE FITTEST.
Alderman BURGESS moved, wad CaDtleillOr CROSFIELD seconded, the adoption of the minutes of the Sanitary Com- mittee.

Alderman DAVIES said that in the minutes there was a suggestion that the work of two men should be porformed by one—who was the one to survive? Was it Bloomfield or Bayley? [A Voice: Or either.] It simply said that the work was to be performed by one man. [A VOICE: The survival of the fittest.] Alderman BURGESS said that it appeared that nothing had attracted the attention of the Council except the recommen- dation that "The duties heretofore performed at the Infec- tious Di•eases Hospital by Bloomfield and Bayley, the gar- dener, be in future performed by one man alone, and that his wages be 26e per week, with house, coals, and gas." Mr Sutton, who compiled the resolution, was not present, or he should have asked him to explain bow be made Bloomfield and Bayley into one person—" the gardener." Bloomfield had been employed at the hospital since its opening, and his duties were of a multifarious character. Bayley had charge of the ground as gardener. He was glad Alderman Davies bad raised the question, as it gave him an opeortunity tbat he should not otherwise have had of saying that the duties at the hospital had become very light. In fact he believed he might say that whilst so much was heard of infection in every direction, there was not at that moment one patient in the hospital. In consequence, they bad come to the conclu- sion that the duties hitherto performed by two could be un- dertaken by one. [At this juncture information was handed to the alderman that four patients had that day been ad- mitted.] He had, he explained, been speaking on informa- tion received up to the previous evening. Bloomfield, who had been the longest engaged, had undertaken the extra duties at his usual wage.
The report was appt7eyed. THE PRICE OF CIA.S.
Alderman HoLuEs moved, and Councillor WRIGHT se- conded, the adoption of the report of the Gas Committee. . . . .

Mr BROADBENT remarked that he had been at Wolver- hampton the previous week, and was told that the price of gas was 2s 44 per I,OOJ feet. In reply, he said "Well, you are very well placed here, you have got coal near you ;" but he was told in answer that the coal there was not suitable for gas, and that they had coal from Lancashire. Alderman Houtss had no doubt that there were good rea- sons why gas should be 2s 4d per 1,000 at Wolverhampton, and that there were equally good reasons why it should be 3s at Warrington. They went over the question carefully a few weeks before, and came to the conclusion that 3s per 1,000 feet was as little as they could charge. Alderman BURGESS: It is easily done if you make every- body pay for twice as much as they are consuming. (Laughter.) The report was confirmed. . GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE —THE DESPATCH OF THE MAILS.
The adoption of the minutes of this committee was pro- posed by the MAYOR, and seconded by Alderman WEBsraa

• Mr DIXON asked if anything had been done respecting a matter he mentioned in committee—the placard in the window at the post office respecting the despatch of the mails. The other night, he mentioned, he saw three or four people at the post office desiring to know when the mails would be despatched. . _

Dr MACKIE said that the matter had been entrusted to him and he communicated with the postmaster. They to- gether examined the document that Mr Dixon complained of, and it had certainly been lined and inter-lined in a won- derful manner. The postmaster suggested that they had better wait a week or two, because at present they were re- arranging the district, and there was every prospect of there being an improved service at an early date. (hear, hear.) The minutes were passed. FINANCE COMMITTEE.

Alderman HOLMES moved the adoption of the minutes of this committee, which included the estimates that had been stated in the various committee minutes. He was sorry to say that the call of Is 6d in the £ they would have to make would not quite cover the expenditure. It was undesirable to have such deficiencies, but they thought that it would be a serious thing to add to the rate during the winter. He hoped that the various committees during the waning half year would keep well within the estimates, and then they would be all right. Alderman WausrEu seconded the adoption of the report. . . .

Mr MACKIE and Alderman Devise remarked that it should las known that the various estimates had been dis- cussed in committee before coming before the Council, and the latter, continuing, said that he mast refer to a previous discussion they had had that evening as to the widening of Bridge-street. He thought he was speaking for Mr Monks as well as himself, and for those who wiahed to have infor- mation on the matter, that they were anxious for such im- provement, but they were on the eve of evil times—they might call him pessimist or not, as they liked—and they should be careful not to go further than they could hell) in burdening the taxpayers with heavy rates. Both he and Mr Monks agreed with the improvement, but they were in- deed anxious that they should not exceed what they thought should be the cost. He Was afraid it would far exceed the amount of money that it was thought it would cost. If it did not exceed it he must congratulate the com- mittee and the Conseil on their action. Alderman WEBSTER said that there was an item in the borough rate of £250 for legal and other expenses con- nected with the Ship Canal. He should like to know if that was the whole of the money owing up to the present tims, and if it was, would the Town Clerk tell them what the total expenditure on that account had been. The Tows CLERK said that he thought that was the whole of the amount owing, but he had not the account there and could not exactly tell. He thought it would cover the amount expended in. the last half year.

Alderman KE-AN said that when the question of widening Bridge-street was first mooted in the Council Mr Crosfield was Mayor and said that the thousands of cases of fever and death that had been canoed by the crowding and dilapidated buildings had been quite sufficient to move the Council or the Improvement Committee to action. Mr BROAD/38NT, referring to an allusion to the price pain for street lighting made by Mr Dixon, said that the price had been the same for a considerable time, and he thought the question merited consideration. Alderman HOLMES said that the arrangements entered into for the lightingmf the street had been in force a long time. The subject then dropped and the minutes were passed.

outside the Council who expressed themselves in favour 'of the nuisance against which he was protesting, and which he was very anxious should be removed. Since the proposal he was about to make had become known he had received many spontaneous thanks for his proposed ac- tion, and one gentleman wrote that had be known a few days earlier he could easily have got a few Clod:sand signatures to a petition in favour of the motion He did not propose it with any feeling of hostility towards the Sanitary Committee. He recognised the care and thought that that committee brought to bear upon their duties and their activity, but no one was always right, and even the Sanitary Committee was not infallible. As the Sanitary Committee bad not taken the matter up them- selves he considered it his duty to do so, and to ask upon it the opinion of the Council. In passing, he would say that it was not uncommonly the custom in Warrington to put wet material in dry dust, which custom, though he did not propose to deal with the question of dry dust, he very much deprecated. For that he did not blame the committee. but; thought an intimation of the injuriousness of the practice to the general public might do good. He did not think that there could be any objection to his proposal in the abstract. It needed no argument to prove that if practicable it would be preferable that the nightsoil should be removed at night, as was the case with regard to the removal of refuse from slaughterhouses. He ventured to say that the things that the Sanitary Committee sent about the town were as offen- sive as was the refuse of the slaughterhouses. It was said in the first place that the change was not practicable, and in the second that even if practicable it would involve such additional expense that it was undesirable to make it. He had a letter in his hand from the Town Clerk of Wigan, who wrote—" 'The pail system is in operation in Wigan ; the nightsoil is removfd in the night." He had also had a com- munication from the borough officials of Birmingham, and he was informed that the nightsoil in Birmingham was col- lected in the night, with the exception of a few dry ashes. If he was told the change was impracticable, he could only say that what could be done in Birmingham and Wigan could be done in Warrington also. If there was a difficulty it was one that should be overcome. There was no insuperable difficulty in connection with the removal in the night. .With regard to the cost, be had consulted an official of the Corporation. who looked with disfavour on a large expenditure, and who had perhaps a better knowledge of the working of the de- partment than any other official in Warrington, and having looked over what were the expenses of the collection he did not hesitate to say that the change he proposed could be effected at a cost to the borough not exceeding £3OO a year more than at present, so that about a farthing rate each half-year would cover the cost of what he was sure would be a very great convenience to the town. He doubted, in- deed, whether there need be any additional c.st at all. The pails in Birmingham, he was told, were collected at a cost of about id to ID per pail, according to distance, and the cost of removal in Warrington, according to figures taken from the Town Hall, was 15.61 for every pail removed. What he protested against was the annoyance which oppressed everyone who lived in Warrington, or who walked through its streets, and he hoped the Council would see its way to expressing its desire for the removal of the nui- sance.

Mr PIERPOINT seconded. He was convinced that it would be far better to have the removal by night. His opinion was that as they had got the pail system, the scheme adopted at Birmingham and Wigan would be a good thing, if they could induce the Sanitary Committee to give the matter fair consideration, and, if possible, to give it a trial. It would do away with a great nuisance in the streets.

Mr Duos said that when that subject was brought up before it was stated by the chairman of the Sanitary Com- mittee that the cost would be something like 60 or 70 per cent more than at the present time. He (Mr Dixon) thought they ought not to make any changes before the scheme at present under contemplation was brought to maturity. Mr FRANCOMB opposed the mtion. He believed that eventually they should be able to remove the contents of the pails at night, but he thought the present was not the time to do so—they were not arrived at such a state of per- fection as to be able to do it. There were several things very much against it. There was the great noise it would cause in the night if they had the great vans rattling about in some of their narrow streets. He thought they would get no sleep at all. They were possessed of an old town with some of the most intricate courts man was ever allowed to examine, and he was quite certain if they went to some of those courts and saw the care that was bestowed upon them by the Sanitary Committee they would say that they deserved the greatest credit. There were a great many houses from which the pails had to be brought through the front door, and how would that be done in the night-time, and besides the expense would be very much greater as they would have to have a staff engaged at night. There was no doubt that at present they were in the midst of very great changes, and in a very short time they would know what the Sanitary Committee would propose doing for many years to come, and until they had tested the machin- ery cow at Longford, and until they had tested the scheme mentioned by Councillor Burgess, they could not really tell in what position they should be in the future. He had no doubt that the night removal was done to a very great ex- tent in Birmingham, but they might not have the same dif- ficulties to contend with there that they bad in Warrington; and he contended they were not in a position to face that change as they ought to do. (Hear. hear). Mr WRIGHT also opposed the motion. He thought Coun- cillor Burgess had overlooked the fact that the property owners in Warring!on during the past few years had been put to an enormous expense, and if that scheme was carried out it meant a further expense of many thousands of pounds, because property owners would not be willing to leave their back doors open for any kind of people to prowl about at nights. The expense of carrying the thing out would no much more than Councillor Burgess admitted, and as the Borough Surveyor was well on with a scheme which would do away with the removal by carts altogether, they ought to let the matter stand in abeyance for a short time. Alderman CHAMBLEE regretted that he had to vote against the proposal, but he did not think it desirable for the Coun- cil to press any committee into any course of action against their own consent. The Sanitary Committee were doing their best to remove the evil complained of, and ultimately he was sure the committee would very much improve on their present system. Mr CROSFIELD said he thought Councillor Burgess had treated the subject with moderation, and that he (Mr Cros- field) had no doubt whatever that he was expressing an opinion which was held by a great many people of the town. The collecting carts, there was no doubt whatever. were a nuisance at times. They had been a nuisance to him in the streets, and the public were very apt to condemn a thing of that sort without knowing the difficulties that the committee had to contend with. If the committee could collect those things in the night time the committee would only be too glad to do It, but his opinion was that the diffi- cultit-s connected with night collection were so great that the thing was not practicable. It was certain people would not like to leave open their back doors to have people wan- dering about their premises in the middle of the night, and If they considered the matter impartially he thought they would come to the concluaion that while there were faults on both sides, there were greater faults connected with night work than with day work. He gave Mr Councillor Burgess credit for very good motives in bringing that before the Council, but the Council must trust in the Sanitary Committee dealing with that question in the best way they could. It was almost certain that when the new scheme was brought out by the Borough Surveyor the nuisance of the carts would be very much lessened. (Hear, hear.) •Alderman DAVIES hoped and austed Councillor Burgess would see his way to withdraw his resolution. He ander- stood from the committee that they were now maturing, as it were, a scheme which would most likely eventually em- brace the suggestion of Mr Councillor Burgess, and looking to that circumstance he thought that with all propriety he might appeal in the name of the Council to Councillor Burgess to let his motion stand over for the present. Alderman KEAN supported this suggestion. Mr BURGESS said he did not respond to the suggestion.

Alderman &mins said he gave Councillor Burgess great credit for the way in which he had brought that matter before the Council. He believed that Councillor Burgess thought he was doing a public duty, and every member of that Council who conscientiously thought he was discharg- ing a public duty was entitled to expect the approbation of the Council and its support, so far as they could see with him. It was his misfortune Rot to be able to agree with Councillor Burgess's proposition, nor could he agree with him in the reasons he assigned for asking the Council to accept the proposition. He begun by saying that the Guar- dians had had something to say about the offtnsiveness of the nigh'ssoil removal. The Mayor was a member of the Board of Guardians, and might he ask if it were the fact that they themselves conveyed in an open cart their night soil, which was infinitely more offensively done than any- thing the Corporation did in any part of the borough. With regard to the feeling outside the Council there might be two opinions, and he believed if they asked all those people who discarded sentiment—and there were very few who thought very much about sentiment—they would find that 19 out of every 20 who gave a vote would vote for the continuance of the collection of the night soil in the daytime; and of the gentleman who said he could have got a few thousand sig- natures in favour of that motion, well he (Alderman Burgess) could only say he was exceedingly sanguine. (Hear, hear.) A thousand signatures were not easily got, as the Mayor knew in his own experience. That the committee had considered the question there was no doubt. They had been twelve or fourteen years considering that question. Those wet ashes were a source of great annoyance to them, and if they only knew how to get rid of the evil they would do it very quickly. They would have a placard from the town clerk every day in the week if they thought it would have the desired effect. With regard to Wigan and Birmingham, he had yet to know that Wigan had the pail and tub system. She might be starting on her career of improvement, but be very much doubted whether Wigan as yet knew the differ- ence between a pail and an ashtub. (Laughter.) The town clerk of Wigan had shown wisdom by the conciseness of his letter. With reference to the officials of Birmingham, he should be very glad to hear what they had to say about Warrington—he should be very glad if Councillor Burgess would read the letter or let them know who wrote it. (Coun- cillor Burgess here banded the letter to the alderman) That letter was signed, Alderman Burgess continued, by his old friend Wilkinson. He knew the value of that commu- nication. (Laughter.) He did not think it was right for Councillor Burgess to drag in the borough i .surveyor n the way be did. It was not right for Councillor Burgess to mike it appear that the borough surveyer was reflecting upon the charges that that department brought upon the Corporation. ("No, no," and a member: "It was a slip,")

It might be a slip, and be was willing to accept it as a slip, but it nevertheless was done. He had simply got to say that in his judgment, after 12 or 14 years' experience in that matter,, be looked upon the proposition made that night as utterly impracticable. He then pointed out at some length the difficulties in the way of night collection caused by the large number of houses in the borough with lock-up yards, and the facilities which would be given for stealing and immorality owing to the yard doors being left open at nights. He also asked the town clerk to say whether the Corporation had power to compel people to leave their yard doors open. The TowN CLERK: I do not think you have power to corn- pel them to leave them open. Alderman BURGESS said if they were not satisfi:d with that he wanted to know if they would leave the yards ut- terly unprotected. If not where was the protection to come from. Their present police force would not by any means be sufficient for that purpose. He also referred to the case of manufactories, which they could not expect to be left open at nights. There was more in that proposition, he Said, than met the eve of ordinary observers. It was in- tended for wider purposes. It was not merely the sentimen- tal mover of that resolution and the few co-agitators be had who were swelled into thousands that had not the opportu- nity of signing a memorial. He (Alderman Burgess) was then proceeding to read from an article in "Cornbill Magazine," when Councillor Burgess and some others ob- jected. Mr CROSFIELD thought Alderman Burgess had said quite enough to convince the Council of the foolishness of trying to do that work by night. After the opinion given by the Town Clerk the Council would be of opinion that the scheme was impracticable.

Alderman BURGESS said he should take another opportu- nity of showing that the work done in Warrington within the last 14 years—and that was about the time the Sani- tary Committee was called upon to actually interfere on be- half of the health of the town—was of such a character that they should scarcely find a parallel in any other town. He felt it very hard to be put down by a young fellow like that. (No, no.) The MAYOR said it was only a question of time. Mr CROSFIELD : I can say that the Council is perfectly satisfied with the argument that has been used. Alderman WEBSTER then again asked Councillor Burgess to withdraw his resolution.

Councillor Butioass said he could only understand one reason for their asking him to withdraw it, and that was that they did not want to vote against it. This remark was protested against by several members and was ultimately withdrawn by Councillor Burgess. A discussion of considerable length then took place on two motions to adjourn the debate, one till Friday and the other till Monday. Ultimately a third motion that the debate c.mtinue was carried by a large majority. The debate was then resumed by Alderman BURGESS who read the extract from Cornlaill Magazine.

Dr MACKIE supported the resolution and protested against the feeling that seemed to be entertained by Alder- man Burgess that the Sanitary Committee should never be criticised. He said he believed it was understood when the pail system was first talked about that the collection should ultimately be made at night time. Alder Mali BURGESS here stood up to contradict Dr Mackie and for some time these two gentlemen faced each other, Dr Mackie claiming that he was in possession of the chair and Alderman Burgess asserting a right to corrett Dr M.tckie's statement.

The MAYOR said he thought Alderman Burgess dreadfully out of order. Alderman BURGESS maintained that Dr Mackie should always adhere to facts. Dr MACKIE : I always adhere to facts; I live amongst facts. Alderman BURGESS: You do not.

The MAYOR having read the standing order bearing on the dispute, and Alderman Burgess having been promised the right of correcting any mis-statement at the conclusion of Dr Mackie's speech, Dr MACKIE was allowed to resume, and in the course of his remarks he contended that the difficulties in the way of night collection had been much over-estimated.

Alderman BURGESS then explained that when the pail system was first adopted it was expressly stated that the whole of the collection should be made in the day-time. Dr MACKIE said he would withdraw his statement on Alderman Burg,oss's assurance; he had nr.,t beim in the town at the time, and Alderman Burgess had. Mr BURGESS, in his reply, said he did not think it was right that they should be charged with any hostility to the Sanitary Committee. Alderman DAVIES again asked Councillor Burgess to withdraw his resolution, and the latter again declining to do so, Alderman Davies was walking out of the room, a con- siderable number of councillors having previously left, when
Mr B JEWESS said there were the gentlemen who dare not vote.

• Alderman Devrhs: I should have voted against the reso- lution if you had not remained se long. Mr BURGESS said there would not be a quorum left if Alderman Davies went away. The same thing had been done before, but all he could say was that he would intro- duce the motion at the next Council meeting. There not being a quorum present, the meeting termin- ated.

div.head: REWARDING A fOLICE OFFICER.
div.p: REWARDING A fOLICE OFFICER.

The MAYOR, in moving the confirmation of the Watch Com- mittee minutes, referred to the recommendation that a gratuity of £5O be voted to P.C. Clynes upon his retirement from the police force after 91- years diligent and faithful service. Phatlwas, the Mayor said, an excellent testimonial to give to a police officer after nine years and a half diligent and faith- ful service. It was only right he should explain to the Council that this £5O was not a gratuity given out of any funds of the Corporation; it was given out of the super- annuation fund,for which the officer himself had contributed nearly £5O. From information the committee had got from other sources, they might have made the sum more than £5O, but it was decided that it be £so.—The minutes were confirmed. THE IMPROVEMENTS IN BRIDGE-STREET.

Mr BROADBENT, in moving the confirmation of the minutes of the Street Improvement and Lighting Commit- tee, said that they contained matters of some importance, in regard to which he would give any information that might be desired in his reply. The minutes contained the follow- ing recommendations ;—Recommendation, that the Town Clerk be authorised to offer £725 for Mr Chester's shop in Bridgreetreet, subject to immediate possession being given ; and .13,500 for the property belonging to Mr Fairhurst, in Bridge-street. Recommendation, that the property in Bridge-street, lately belonging to Messrs James Davies, Samuel Woods, Percival, and Baker, be purchased at the price of £8,985 9a 2d, including interest and expenses. Mr BARKER Seconded the confirmation of these minutes. Mr MONKS said he had before expressed his opinion in that Council that in the matter of the improvements in Bridge.street they had entered upon a drifting policy, and they did not know exactly where they were drifting to. He saw that that night they were asked to sanction the pur- chase of property to the extent of £13,210, which was the first instalment of a purchase which was not to be of any very large amount. Ultimately it was to end in a sum not exceeding £3,000 to £5.000 nett. Well he confessed that the more they trod that path the more were the difficulties of seeing how such a nett result was to be obtained, and he would like to ask first of all if this were the whole a the property that was purchased and paid for by that com- mittee. Mr BROADBENT : It is not the whole of the property. Mr MONKS : My question is, has there been any property purchased and paid for that is not included in this. The Tows CLERK : There has been other property. Mr MONKS said that only confirmed his suspicion. He should lice to know by whose authority it bad been pur- chased and by whose authority it had been paid for. It cer- tainly had not been authorised by that council. He thought that they were spending the ratepayers' money in very large sums because those before them were nothing to the property that would have to be taken. He thought that before that Council was committed to such an extent it ought to have a voice as to whether such expense was reasonable and fair and such as the town could afford. He had asked for information in a previous meeting of that Council, and he had been met by the reply that it was not convenient to ex- pose figures, and that a reply would prejudice the purchase of the property. He quite admitted the force of that, but at the same time it did not prevent them from drifting into a very much larger expenditure than any gentleman around that table contemplated, and he for one would prefer to know exactly where they were going even at the risk of ex-1 posing figures that might prejudice the purchase of pro- perty. One of the properties that was to be purchased that night for £3,500, was bought at a very high price some years ago, being run up by the Corporation officials to a price that was considered extremely high, and yet they were going to pay £l,lOO in excess of that price. He did not be- lieve himself that the exposure of figures could make it much worse than that. He had a firm conviction that the property would not be purchased for anything like the amount of money that had been given as the total expendi- ture. There was a good deal of property yet to be bought. Alderman BURGESS : How much? Mr MONKS: I don't know. Alderman BURGESS : Let us know h- w much property there is yet to be bought. The TOWN CLERK: Three lots. Alderman BURGESS,: Let us know something about them; let us not deal with the matter in the dark. Mr MONKS said bethought he had possession of the chair and he did not want any interruption. He bad not said any- thing that was incorrect ; he was simply dealing with figures. So far as that Council was concerned no property had been purchased, but the Street Improvement Committee came that night with a recommendation to purchase cer- tain property totalling op to £13,210, and he thought it was only fair to assume that that was all the property they knew of at present. But they did know there was a very I large amount of property to be purchased in addition to that and before committing themselves too far it was only fair to the Council that they ought to have the fullest details so that they might be able to judge as to its value. Mr Duos was starry that Councillor Monks had not been present at the special meeting which had been called when the Bridge-street property was to be bought. There was a special meeting called, and all the details of the property were given to them. He believed he was right in saying that at the present moment there had not been any money paid above the price then named at that meeting. Alderman BURGESS wanted to know what that large amount of property was that they had to acquire in addition to that which they had before them. Alderman DAVIES: Perhaps it is quite sufficient to say that the amount down on the minutes is not half the amount that it will cost. Alderman BURGESS: That is not enough. If it is so very high we ought not to eatertain it. Alderman DAVIES: I think the proper course will be for the chairman of the Street Improvement Committee to make a statement. Alderman BURGESS: Let us know where we are; if the chairman of the committee replies he will close the debate. Some discussion then took place as to suspending the standing orders in order to allow the chairman of the com- mittee to make a statement without closing the debate. Alderman CHANDLEY moved that the standing orders be suspended, but this proposition was negatived by 16 to eight votes, and ultimately it was agreed that the Town Clerk should make the statement required. The Tows CLERK then said that the information he could give them then was exactly that which he gave when they bad a meeting in that room of a committee of the whole Connell. The prices of the property in Bridge-street with the names of the owners were as follows :—Davies' Trustees, which was one of those included in the purchases mentioned that night; Samuel Woods' property, which was another included in the list that night; Thomas Henry Lyon, which was contracted for but not yet paid for; Baker's two shops, included in the £8,985 Os 2il; Percivals', also included in this amount; Cawley's, contracted for but not yet paid for; Whalley's, purchased andpaid for; Twigs's, purchased and paid for; Leyland's, not yet purchased but under the consideration of the committee ; Hunts', pur- chased and paid for ; Fairhurst's, purchased and paid for; Chester's, purchased but not yet yaid for; Skelton's not yet purchased ' • Duchy, of Lancaster, nofyet purchased. That was the whole of the property, so that there were three pro- perties of those he bad named which were not yet purchased. There were Skelton's, Duchy, of Lancaster, and Ley- land's. There were also two ground rents to be redeemed which were put down at figures (1700) which would be ac- cepted by the owners, and all the purchases were within the estimate that was given, to that Council when they dis- cussed the matter before. (Hear, hear.) The estimated cost depended entirely upon the re-sale of the land. If they sold the land at £3 per square yard, the estimated cost was £11,900. If they sold the land at £4 per yard the estimated cost was £5,827 ; and if they sold the land at £5 per yard it would cost them nothing. Mr MONKS asked what was the gross total for the pur- chase of the property. The Tows CLERK: Including the street making it is 131,107. Dr MACKIE was then proceeding to speak, when Mr BROADBENT objected on the ground that he had spoken already. Dr MAMIE: I simply wanted to put a question.

. . Alderman BURGESS: Dr Mackie has spoken. Dr MACKIE said there was no necesstv for making a speech; he was simply going to congratulate the town clerk upon giving the straightforward and safe statement he had made, and as him if he would supplement it by the assur- ance that there was nothing over and above what he had read out. Alderman BURGESS: You are not concealing anything. (Laughter.) The TOWN CLERK: No. Dr MACKIE said there was nobody supposed the town clerk was concealing anything in that sense. The Town CLERK: Everything has gone as I expected it would go. (Hear, hear.) Mr BRoannErrr, in replying, said he was somewhat sur- prised at the manner and tone of the observations that bad been made that night considering what had gone before. The Council came to a very cordial—he did not know whether it was unanimous or not—resolution that it wee desirable to make the improvements in Bridge-street, and he might also say that the committee whose minutes he had ' moved had nothing whatever to do with any off-hand prophecy as to what this improvement was likely to cost. He might say that the members of the committee were, he thought,less enthusiastic in thematter than many other mem- bers of the Council, but the undertaking necessarily de- volved upon the Street Improvement Committee, and they tried to do in the best way they could what the Council orderad them to do. (Hear, bear.) As to town had told them, there were estimates for that work which were laid before the Council, and in every instance the expenses which they had incurred had been within and not above those estimates. (Hear, hear.) He thought they would give the Street Improvement Committee credit for having done their best in every instance to purchase the property, on as advantageous terms as possible, and they had been most ably seconded in these endeavours by the town clerk. (Hear, hear.) Whenever they thought they were at all likely to give more than the property was worth, or more thaa they could possibly get it for, they again fortified themselves by a valuation from Mr Owen. He believed if there had been more publicity at the earlier stage of those proceedings they should not have got the property at the price they had in many instances been able to obtain it. In

div.head: BATES.
div.p: THE BATES.

Alderman Eforarcs moved an estimate of £3,456 3s 4d for the purposes to which the borough fund is applicable; that the Council order a borough rate to raise that amount; that the contributions be assessed as follows ;—Parish or Town.. ship of Warrington (that part which is within the borough) valuation £130,708, contribution, £3,185 Is lid; Parish or Township of Latchford (that part which is within the borough) valuation £11,124, contribution, £271 Is sd; totals £141,832 and £3,456 3s 4d; and that the overseers be called upon to pay their respective contributions. He said that in March of the current year the amount of call was £4,512, and this time twelve months since it was over £4,000, 80 that there was a considerable reduction. It would be a reduction as far as the borough rate, that would have to be paid by the overseers, was concerned of 2d in the Z. Mr BURGESS seconded the resolutions, which were carried.

On the motion of Alderman IloLmas, seconded by Alder- man CHANDLEY, it was resolved "That the estimate for an Improvement rate as recommended by the Finance Committee, be confirmed, and that the Finance Commit- tee do make an Improvement Rate accordingly at one shil- ling and sixpence in the pound, and be authorised to affix the common seal of the borough thereto."

It was farther resolved oti' the motion of Alderman HOLMES, seconded by Alderman WEBSTER That the esti- mate for a Sewers Rate as recommended by the Finance Committee be confirmed, and that the Finance Committee do make a Sewers Rate accordingly at twopence in the pound, and be authorized to affix the common seal of the borough thereto."

div.head: -REMOVAL OF NIGHT SOIL: ANIMATED DISCUSSION.
div.p: THE -REMOVAL OF NIGHT SOIL: ANIMATED DISCUSSION.

. Mr Sultans moved "That the Council is of opinion that the nightsoil pails should be collected during the night, and recommends the Sanitary Committee to make arrange- ments accordingly." Members of the Council, he said, would have seen remarks in the newspapers that were made at a meeting of the Board of Guardians, in respect to this matter, and also a number of letters in local newspapers urgiag that the course he was about to advocate should be adopted. As a general rule he did not pay much attention to anonymous newspaper correspondence, but sometimes it happened that the general feeling of the community was expressed in that way, and when that was the case it was worthy of attention. From what he knew of the general feeling he did not hesitate to say that it was very doubtful whether they could find half-a-dozen people in Warrington

div.head: SANKEY SMUT, BOARD.
div.p: SANKEY SMUT, BOARD.

An ordinary meetiog of this Board was held in the school room, Greet Sankey, on Tuesday afternoon. There were preseut Messrs Turner (chairman), Houghton, Ridgway, Kerfoot, Cook, and S Sutton (clerk). .

THE ARRANGEMENT WITH THE MANAGERS.-013 the minutes of the previous meeting being read, the CHAIRMAN said he was sorry he bad not been able to be present when the subject of renting the schools from the managers had been dealt with. He thought that £2O per annum for tak- ing the Echo°ls in their present condition was a very high sum. Would the Board have to put the offices behind into decent repair and pay that reutal ?—Mr RIDGWAY thought that had been the undertaking, They looked upon it in the light that there was nothing else they could do but to conform to the terms of the managers.—The CnainmeN said it WAS right they ought to pay A rental, but he thought it ought to be a reasonable rental. The rent they were going to pay was very high indeed.—Mr HOUGHTON said if it were going to be a permanent tenancy the rent would have been high, bet it was only a temporary one, and if they had not paid it the schools would have been stopped.—The CHAIR. TILN : The onus of potting the educational arrangements of Sankey into such a bad state would then have rested with the managers. However, the matter had now been settled. —Mr Iloucterrox then moved the confirmation of the minutes and, Mr RIDGWAY having seconded, they were confirmed.—The CLERK also mentioned that he had written to the Education Department asking for their sanction to the arrangements with the managers. He had received a reply acknowledging the receipt of his letter, and they should probably be hearing further in a day or two. _

THE &floor. APPARATIIS:SOMe conversation took place with regard to the purchase by the Board of the books, slates, dr,c., at present in use at the school, and ultimately the Chairman undertook to eadeavour to make arrange- ments with the managers for their being turned over to the Board. Tate ESTIMATE.—The CLERK submitted a detailed esti- mate of the probable expenditure and income of the Board for the ensuing half year. The nett total of expenditure was estimated to be £lBB 163 9d, to raise which a sixpenny rate would be required.—Mr RIDGWAY moved, and Mr HOUGHTON seconded, that a rate of 6d in the £ be levied, and this proposal was carried. THE Smoot. FEES.—It was decided that the scale of fees at present in use at the school remain unchanged.—This scale is as follows: Infants, 2d per week; first and second standards, 3d; third standard and upwards, 4d. This was all the business of public interest.

div.head: HUYTON.
div.p: HUYTON.

- - - - TEMPERANCE MEETINGS. The first meeting of the season of • tho Church of England Temperance So- ciety was held on Monday evening in the Huy- ton Quarry church schoolroom, which was well filled. The Rev Canon Penrhyn presided. An attractive programme was then introduced of song, read- ings, and a dialogue "The teetotal barber" by members of the fluyton Band of Elope. The Rev J W Tyrer and Mr E B Williams gave addresses and the meeting closed in the usual way.—The usual weekly meeting of the linyton Temperance Association was held in the Huyton Park schoolroom on Tuesday evening. Mr E S Eccles presided and gave an address. Songs were given by Mrs Eccles and Mr H Capper. Miss Capper presided at the pianoforte ; Messrs Perrins, Stoba, and P Capper gave readings. SELLING BEER WITHOUT di LaCENSE.—A the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Captain Willis and Mr C Barnes, Carmelo John Sorge, of Huyton, was summoned for selling intoxicating liquors without a license, at Huyton, on the 30th September.—The defendant, wko was represented by Mr Banks, solicitor, Prescot, pleaded not guilty.—P.C. Myles Burton deposed that be along with P.C. Johnston had visited the Rose and Crown public-house at Huyton OR the date named. They asked for beer and porter, and :were sup- plied by Mrs Sorge. He (witness) afterwards visited the house in company with P.S. Edgar, of Huyton, and they asked the defendant if he was selling on his own account or by whose authority. Sorge replied that he was selling as the servant of Mr Saunders. in whose name the i license had been granted. He added that he had not a written autho- rity to sell, but he was was acting under instructions. Edgar he informed the defendant Sorge that he had not given per- dpmch commit oft nsievevnt ni eyocdinet, btnagotienu—tyl offence.mi idstott submitted no 0: bet tulhlhat toTnt nhtkbheeyet hishrewe penalty,rboi ieueahlanda ablcif at Huyton, gave corroborative evidence.—Mr Banks, for the behalf—P.S. evPoaa• ,nSi ed. aE: opsnrdtoy,i seneawci nrota,:saesenut attatoihoi:ovnrn4ei "tot yydoe for the defendant to sell.—The Bench considered the case and costs —Mr Banks subsequently asked for and obtained a temporary authority for Sorge to sell until next transfer day.
HUYTON LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting of the Huyton-with-Roby Local Board was held at the Local Board offices, Huyton ui Taes-

day, when, under the presidency of Mr Hobell. There were also present Messrs Pinnington, Banner, Parker, Cooper, Brown, Siddeley, Burnyeat, Lsventon, Harrison, Grim- show. Swift (clerk), Worrall (surveyor), and Dr Hall (medical officer). MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—Dr E F Hall read his re- port for the month of August, which stated that there had been a death from dipthei ia at Huyton Quarry, the house being in a very unsanitary condition. He had requested a variety of alterations to be carried out. HIGHWAY AND SANITARY COMMITTEE —A meeting of the Highway, Sanitary, and Lighting Committee was held on tne 30th ultimo, at which Messrs Brundrit and Co.'s tender for the supply of 1,200 tons of macadam, delivered free at anyton Station, was accepted. Letters having been re- ceived asking for additional lamps in Tarnock-read *and Huyton Hey-road, a sub-committee was appointed to report as to the desirability or otherwise of erecting additional lamps in the district and of altering the positions of any of the existing lamps. It was resolved that the footpath from the church to the railway station at Roby be repaired at a cost of £25, in accordance with the surveyor's estimate. It was also carried that the footpath on the west side of Arch- way-road be flagged under the railway bridge. The minutes were passed —The Chairm.m celled attention to the minute relating to the supply of eater to the cottages at Horns Smithies; and after some conversation it w.s moved by Mr Siddeley that notice be giv, n to Lord Derby (owner of the property), to furnish a Bur ply of water to the cottages within two months.—Mr Grimstiaw seconded the motion, which was adopted. _

FIRE EXTINGUISHING APPLIANCES —The Clerk read letters from the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephonic Ex. change Company stating they would connect the Huvton Local Board &Hoes with their "exchange." by which they would be able to hold telephonic communication with the Old Swan fire engine station, the Salvage Corps, or any of the nearly 1000 subscribers for the sum of £2s.—Several members expressed the opinion that the charge was too high, and it was ultimately decided that the Clerk should again write to the Company on the subject. THE ALTERATIONS AT TIIE RAILWAY STATION—Mr Cooper intimated that he had had a letter from the engineer to the railway company stating that the work at the railway station was going to be taken in hand immediately.—Mr Grimshaw : Does that include the cabmen's sheltar P—Mr Cooper: No; he spoke particularly of the paving. FINANCES —At a meeting of the Finance Committee, heid on the 7th inst.. the surveyor reported that the ammnt of outstanding rates was £590.

MOSE LIGHT WANTED.—The Chairman read a letter asking for an additional lamp in Tarbock-ro ad, Huyton, and it was decided to refer the letter to the Highway and Light- ing Committee.—Mr Levington rem-aked that lamps were wanted in many places in the township.—The Cnairrnan said that matter had been previously referred to a sub-com- mittee, and they had better wait until- that sub-committee gave in their report. This was the principal business.
GOLBORN E.

SUDDEN DEATH AT LOWTON.—A. sudden death at Low- ton, on Monday, created considerable rxc tement in the dis- trict. The deceased was I,leanor Taylor, 13 years of age, daughter of Edward Taylor, and was perfectly well on Mon- day night when she retired to bed. About 1 o'clock Mr and Mrs Smith (with whom deceased lived) beard a noise in the girls bedroom and found her complaining of a pain in her side. The usual remedies were at once tried and Dr Dobb summoned. Upon his arrival life was found to be extinct.

FLORAL AND HORTICULTDDAL SHOW AT GOLBORNE.— The Golborne and Lowton Floral and HorticuNtral Society opened their first show in the hall connected with the Leigh Arms Hotel, Golborne, on Saturday evening, and greet praise i 3 due to all concerned for the mignificent display and the excellence of the show. The room was tastefully decorated for the occasion, this department having been en- trusted to Mrs Nicholls and Mr Grainger. A large table ran up the centre of the room, and this contained the fruit, flowers, drc., of which there was a c ipital selection. Round the room vegetables and other produce was exhibited, and amongst this class, as in the fruit department, there were some fine specimens. The judging was entrueted to Mr T Bell (Wigan) and Mr Randall, of Newton-le-Willows. Hun- dreds flocked to the show, and in the evening the show was patronised by members of the leading families of Lowton and Golborne. When the judges had completed their task, the show was opened by Mr W H Arnott, and an adjournment was made to the lun- cheon-room, where an ample spread had ben laid by Mrs Nicholls, whose purveying gave every satisfaction. Those sitting down included Mr Arnott (the vice-president), the judges, the officers, and the committee. Mr Arnott p,itt• sided, Mr T Beswick occupying the vice-chair. The chair- man said he was glad to meet them on that occasion and to see them take such an interest in floral and horticultural produce. A number of toasts followed, including "Success to the Society " and The Judges." At 8 p.m. the prizes were distributed by the vice-president, assisted by Mr Her. wick (treasurer) and Mr Talbot (secretary.) The Golborne brass band occupied a very prominent position at the end of the room, and played several selections during the even- ing. During Saturday anal Sunday evenings upwards of 1,100 persons paid for admisssion, and as a result a substan- tial sum was banded over to the treasurer ft): next year's undertaking, which will be on a larger scale, the committee purposing to hold the show either in a schoolroom or in a large tent erected in a field. PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting of this Committee was:held in the Board Room, Golhorne, on Wednesday afternoon. There were present—Messrs J Fearns (in the chair), TiTaylor, R Yates, W Gattou, r Mitchell, W H Arnett, and C 8 Ben- nie (surveyor). THE WATER CHARGES ON OUTBUILDINGS.—"The Sur- veyor said the question with regard to Mr Jas. Taylor's re- fusal to pay water rent had been left over from last meet- ing. Mr Taylor's objection was that hie farm buildings as well as his house was assessed. Mr Taylor was willing to pay if they only assessed his dwelling-house.—Mr Arnott : Do the other farmers pay ?—The Surveyor: Yes, they pay well enough, and other districts are assessed just the same.—Mr Arnott thought they could not in fairness and justice to the other farmers remit Mr Taylor's charges.-The surveyor said if they made the alteration in that case they would have to make it in all.—The Chairman said he heard that they could not charge for outbuildings.—Mr Taylor Not if the water is not used. He had seen a case in which the superior court had reversed a decision in favour of the local authority.—After a little further discussion Mr Ar- nott moved that Mr Taylor's application for a reduction of water rent be not acceded to.—Mr Garton saconded this pro- posal, which was carried.

FIRE EXTINGUISHING APPARATUS —The Surveyor ssid he had been over to Manchester. and had seen several carts, and he produced an engraving of one which he considered the most suitable, and which would cost £l5. If supplied with hose pipe and other apparatus it would cost about £7O —Mr Yates thought that before they got a cart they ought to have men to use it.—The Chairman : The Com- mittee will have to use it. (Laughter.)—After a short con- versation the further consideration of the subject was left over till the next meeting. SUBSIDENCE OF ROAD : A CURT REPLY.—The Surveyor read a letter which he had on the instruction of the High- way Committee sent to Messrs Evans and Co. claiming £2.0 damages for the subsidence of the road near Golborne Smithies owing to their mining operations. He also read a reply from Mr Glover, on behalf of Messrs Evans and Co., acknowledging the receipt of his communication, and stating that they had handed the papers in that matter to their solicitors, and had instructed them to defend any action which the Committee might commence against them. —Mr Taylor : That is rather curt.—Mr Garton : It doesn't look very nice.—Mr Arnett suggested that legal advice be taken in the matter, and this course was agreed to.

THE CLEANING OF ASRPITS.—A letter was read from the Leigh Rural Sanitary Authority asking the Committee to take measures for emptying the ashpits in the district, and pointing out the hardship in the case of cottagers having notices served upon them to clean their ashpits.—ln the course of a short conversation it was stated that there were scarcely any instances in Golborne in which difficulty had been experienced in getting the ashpits cleaned out, and ultimately it was agreed to write to the sanitary Authority te ask them to point out the cases they referred to. DANGEROUS I'm —Mr Taylor called atteritlan to two dangerous unguarded pits by the side of Ashton-road, and the surveyor was instructed to write to Mr Pardy calling his attention to the same. WATER CONSUNPTION.—The Surveyor in his report stated that the montAy consumption of water equalled 855,000 gallons. This was all the business of interest.

The armor plated hirbette ship Rodney was launched at Chatham on Wednesday, the christening ceremony being performed by the Duchess of Edinburgh, who was acnom- panied by the Duke. CONOREGILTIONAL UNION —The autumnal session of the Congregational Union was resumed on Tuesday at the City ITemple. The Chairman (Dr Parker) delivered his inaugu- lral address, wherein he spoke eloquently of the "larger ministry "to which all good Christians were called. It was reported that the Jubilee Fund had now reached £350,000, of which more than two-thirds was paid. Papers on the moral and social condition of the poor were read by the Revs. G 8 Reaney (Stepney) and Thmsas Green (Ashton). The former considered that poverty prevailed because the poor were under-paid and over-worked, and did not get a fair share of the profit their toil realised. Mr Green thought the duty of the churches was to labour for a change of character, ands chanrm of circumstances would soon follow. After some discussion it was agreed to postpone the debate, and the Union then adjourned.—On Wednesday, after the introauction and welcome of visitors and delegates from other countries, a resolution was submitted and adopted im- pressing upon Congregational ministers and churches the importance of creating by special sermons or meetings a more general and deeper interest in Wiclint teachings and influence. Papers upon the relative obligations of the de- nominational churches and colleges were then read, and here was a short discussion. A favourable report was pre- tsented with regard to the English Congregational Chapel Building Society, which in the last thirty years had mater- ially assisted WEI churches, and now stood in a satisfactory financial position.—On 'Thursday a motion warmly com- mending the scheme of congregational work among English residents and travellers on the continent was carried. A motion proposing that each church should assure t. ULU. of the pastor for the amount of at leaat one year's stipas unanimously adopted without discussion.
