--- By the capsizing of a small open boat near Seascale, on the Cumberland coast, on Thursday, a young married maa named Nicholson and two boys (brothers) named Bell were drowned. Nicholson's body was washed ashore during the day, but the others have not been found. PERILOUS ADVENTURE OF A DRESSMAILER.—At Nantwich Police Court, on Saturday, Wm. Parker, of Chester, described as a gentleman of independent means. was charged with as- saulting Jeannette. Corlette, aged 18, milliner and dress- maker, of Wrexham, whilst travelling on the London and North-Western Railway between Wrenbury and Nantwich. The proseentrix allegZed that in order to avoid the impor- tunities and insult to which he was subjected by the pd.' aoner, she got out of the carriage, and rode some miles on the footboard.—The Bench expressed surprise that only a charge of aggravated assault had been preferred, and Ins- Posed a penalty of £lO and costs.

THE position of the Tory party on the question of the extension of the franchise is getting more and more deplorable. They have shifted their ground so often that at present they neither know where to stand nor how to turn. It is true Mr. JAMES LOWTHER, ex-Secretary for Ireland, has not deserted his pop-gun, which has been all along pointed against the Two Millions of householders in the, counties who are demanding the Franchise. As he said six months ago, he would say to-day—he is "dead against the bill, root and branch,. and every line of it." He hates an extension Of the franchise, and he does not hesitate to say so. He is a Tory of the old type—very stupid it may be, but rather to be preferred to the Tory of the new school who, while still hating the fran- chise, would "make believe "that he loves it. Sir RICHARD CROSS belongs to the latter class; he manages, with the bulk of his party, to wheel round, though he does not by any means do it gracefully. Twelve months have not yet elapsed, as Mr. CHAMBERLAIN pointed out on Tuesdly, since Sir RICHARD, at a Tory meeting held at St. Helens, said there were many things which ought to be undertaken before the reform of the fran- chise, and he was convinced that the whole matter had been started by the Radical caucus, who were trying to force. Mr. GLAD- szorta to take up the question. He would !make it appear now that he is equally con- vinced not only that the demand comes from the people, but that the Tory party are dis- tressfully anxious to confer the franchise upon them. Indeed, as we had occasion to point out the other day, he asserted, in the after-dinner style of oratory which seems to have taken possession of him, that it was "a wilful and deliberate lie to say that the House of Lords had rejected the Franchise Bill." .We referred at the time to this use of " bad language," and we notice that it has attracted the attention of • Lord HARTINGTON. Ad- dressing his constituents, on Saturday, his lordship suggested that Sir RICHARD must have come to the conclusion that it was not likely he would ever again be Home Sec- retary ; and that the strength of his language was, therefore, in inverse ratio to his sense of responsibility. But Lord HARTINGTON Went further; he proceeded to demonstrate the fact that, according to the technicalities of poli- ticians. the House of Lords had rejected the Franchise Bill. It was, he said, "a usual and well-known parliamentary practice to meet an important measure such as this, if you want to defeat it, by a resolution aimed at some one of its provisions, or at some one of its supposed defects, which appears to the Opposition to, be most convenient, and to afford the best subject and object for attack. This is a well-known piece of par- liamentary procedure. It has been used be- fore by both parties, but it has been always understood that the carrying of that adverse resolution, although it did not absolutely and conclusively reject the bill, was equivalent to the rejection of the bill, and was only moved with that object." Perhaps when Sir RICHARD addresses his Warrington suppor- ters next waek he will deal with this point, and proceed to show that Lord HARTINGTON is wrong; or, if he cannot do that, perhaps he will be good enough to apologise for the use of language which, to say the least of it, would not be tolerated in Parliament. But it is Lord SALISBURY who has proved , the greatest of political weather-cocks. So bitter was his hatred of the proposal to extend the franchise to householders in boroughs in 1867, that he resigned office rather than be party to it. Nay, more than that, he de- nounced Mr DISRAELI as "a political adven- turer" for surrendering to the enemy; and jeeringly described how, step by step, Mr. GLADSTONE had compelled the Tory Govern- ment to accept his reform proposals. We are asked now to believe, contrary to the

1 evidence of our own eyes, that this Ethiopian has changed his skin. It was the other day only that Lord GRANVILLE challenged Lord SALISBURY to say that he really desired a further extension of the franchise, and the leader of the Tory party could give no direct answer. When the question was put to him point blank, he was mute. He tells us in his latest utterance that he has full faith in the people; but that it is necessary that the- "franchise and redistribution should be con- sidered both together, and that they should both be placed upon the statute book at the same time." According to his own admission, there is no question of principle involved; it is a matter solely of procedure. Mr. GLAD STONE, with an experience of Parliament extending over half a century, declares that it is a sheer impossibility to get both bills through in one session; and, believing this, • how can Lord SALISBURY honestly ask hini to do that which he regards as, on the face of it, an act of folly? And when there is a' .difference as to mode of procedure, who is to decide—the Minister who is responsible to i'arliament, to the Country, and to the Crown for the conduct of the business of the nation, or the House of Lords responsible to nobody but themselves? What if there should happen to be an extension of the franchise without a redistribution of seats during the present Parliament—and it will not happen txcept as the result of the blind- ness and stupidity of the Peers—is it to be regarded as a terrible thing in itself that Two Millions of men 'should be admitted within the present pale of the constitution? Lord SALISBURY would appear to think so, for with all his "faith in the people" he confesses that this is a contingency Of which he has great dread. It would increase-the prese (34atc anomalies of represcntation, it is said. course it would, but it is since yesterday only that the Tories have been able to perceive any ancinaly ; and there is no anomaly to-day so great as the denial of a vote to Two Mil- lions of men in the counties of the United Kingdom. Let the Lords stand out of the way, and before next year is at an end the statute-book will be adorned both with Franchise and and a Redistribution Bill. But will they make way? That is the question. Lord HARROWBY, speaking at Liverpool on Tues- day, said,—" Every word Mr. GLADsToNE has said about the House of Lords has contained, a veiled threat of what he will do with the House of Lords "—and this after the Pandit MINISTER has gone out of his way again and again to build a golden bridge as a means of escape for the Peers! We will not follow the bad example of Sir RICHARD CRoss, or we might Characterise the statement of Lord HAFt- aowisv as a wilful and deliberate lie." We will say rather that it proceeds from mental and moral obliquity of vision. It shows, too, the temper in which some of the Tory lords are disposed to receive suggestions of com- promise; and we cannot but think it is well that this is so. There will yet perhaps be an opportunity of killing two birds with one stone. It is a case in which it plide goeth before destruction and an haughty spirit be-- fore a fall."

'HE Provisional Committee for the prOmo' tion of a Ship Canal between Manchester and Liverpool have no reason to be discouraged with the reception which has been accorded to their new scheme. On Monday night the people of Manchester showed themselves - enthusiastic ,in the matter. There was a large meeting of ratepayers, with the Ma.yolt; in the chair, at which it was decided, almost unanimously, to contribute the sum of two- pence in the pound—equal to £lB,ooo—to- wards the cost of promoting a new Bill in' Parliament. Alderman lhavtrooD argued, in, seconding the motion, that, if it was right for the Corporation of Liverpool to spend money" in opposing a Ship Canal Bill, it was equalsiT right for the Corporation of Manchester to use the ratepayers' money in supporting it. But, without saying that the Corporation of Manchester are not justified in doing what they propose to do, it seems to us desirable to point out that there is an essential difference' between the two cases, more especially as the ratepayers of Warrington will be appealed to, I ere long, to make a contribution upon similar. 'grounds. if they are willing to tax them- selves to promote the Ship Canal Bill—and we do not doubt that they are—they plight not to do it under such misapprehension as seems to becloud the reasoning of the Manchester Alderman, A Corporation is entrusted with the duty of protecting existing rights; and when any bill, public or private, .is laid before Parliament whicii is calculated to interfere with those rights it would be a bteach of trust not to tahe action at the right time, in the right way, and at the colt of the rate- payers. Eut t4i3 is a widely different thing to that of handing over Corporate funds to promote a private Bill. in Parliament; for it should be borne in mind that the Ship Canal scheme—vast as it is—is still a private Undertaking for commercial purposes. Sup-- pose, for instance, a Tramway Company should be formed for running cars through Warrington. There can be no question that it would be likely to prove a great conveni- ence to the inhabitants . but, if powers were being sought which might trench upon Cor- porate rights, the Corporation would un- doubtedly be, warranted in opposing at the cost of the town. But put the case the other way about: Suppose the Tramway company should„ ask for a contribution from the Municipal funds on the ground ;hat the work would be of public utility, would it not be at once seen and acknowledged that the right to support was not on all fours with the right to oppose? If the rates are, then, to be diverted from the ordinary channels in aid of the Ship 'Canal scheme, let it be done with a clear understanding that it is upon wholly exceptional grounds, and that it can form no precedent for the future. Reverting to the progress which is being made, we may state that on Thursday the Corporation of Salford followed the ex- ample of Manchester in giving their sanction to the levy of a rate-in-aid of twopence in the pound. On the same day, the authorities of Runcorn and Widnes held special meetings 1 to consider the idvi:ability of accepting invi- tations to send deputations to Manchester, with a view to a conference upon such features of the scheme as are likely to affect the interests of these places.. The object of the promoters is to,elirninate the elements of risk and friction- by satisfying, if they can, those who might o,therwise''become oppo- nents of the bill. At Runcorn there was a feeling that, after spending some hundreds of pounds in conneCtion with the. two previous bills, they must be cautiots and economical; and at Widnes, the Chairman of the Local Board pOinted out ,that, if certain streams which feed the Mersey were turned into the Canal, it might'be a question for them hottt far it would interfere' with their use of the estuary. It was resolvtd, however, both at . Runcorn and at Widnes; to send deputations, to Manchester; and thus far as to the neW

OURS is undoubtedly the age of improve- ment, and if we go on as we seem to be doing there will Soon be n 3 such thing as a " waste product" Councillor FoiTER, of St. Helens, appears to have come to a conclusion rather different from that usually arrived at as to the products commonly regarded as " w6te " 'which are sent .UP the tall chimneys of the smoke-smitten borough. Most people— "doctors an' al' "—are under the impression that "a great quantity of chlorine gas coming from chemical wnrks, and a great quantity of sulphuric gas from the copper works and • glass works," would be injurious to health. But Councillor FOSTER has views of his own upon 'the subject, and he accordingly pro- ceeded to catechise Dr. McNtcorx, the Medical Officer of Health, at a meeting of the St. _Helens Health Committee, on Wednesday last. He asked, in the first place, if the doctor remembered any serious epidemic in .the borough in his go years' experience; and, , getting. an answer in .the affirmative, with L, instances to boot, he put a question as to whether the gases from the various works did not tend to "purify the air and, prevent epi- demics occurring?" Dr. McNrcou. now answered in the negative, adding that "good air did not need improving by sulphuric acid Or anything else.;" but then it may be that even the doctor is a littlt behind with his notions. Still. if Couneillor FOSTER is so much ahead of everybody else in matters of this kind, he ought to condescend to en- lighten the world, and not bother a Medical Officer of Health with needless questions. What is it that he has discovered ? and how is he going to apply his knowledge? Is it go- ing to be necessary to set' up a St. Helens every half a dozen miles or so, as a means of encouraging vegetation and preventing bad harvests? Or is this combination of chlo- rine and sulphuric gas more particularly beneficial to man? And if so, could we not have it laid on like ordinary gas, and thus ensure that eVerybody shall live to a patriar- chal age? How would it be to promote a Great Chlorine and Sulphuric Gas Company? With such acconimodating gases at command, there should be no difficulty about " float- ing " Meantime, Councillor FOSTER. must make a further move ; he must come out of his shell, and astonish the natives.

HALTON WESLEYAN BAND or BOPS. The first of a aeries of entertainments was given in the Wesleyan echool- room last evening week. Songs. readings, and recitations were given by the members' and well received by a large congregation. Mr James Looker, occupied the chair. At the close 14 pledges were taken. WIDNES PARISH CHURCH SCHOOLS.—Thamembers of the Church of England Young Men's Mutual Improvement Society and Gymnasium inaugurated the session on Friday evening by a tea meeting, which was well attended. Subse- quently the Rev W Preston, M.A., of Runcorn, delivered a lecture, entitled "Off to America," to a large audience. The Rev J Wright Williams presided. Tax SHOCKING SUICIDE ET HALEWOOD.—Mf Brighouse, county coroner, on Saturday held an inquest at the Derby Arms, Halewood, on the body of James Singleton, aged 31, who committed suicide on Thursday, under circumstances already reported.—After hearing the evidence, the jury re- turned a verdict to the effect .that the deceased committed suicide whilst temporarily, insane. Ruscorter Femme Cittiecn Cnotn Plc-lete.--The annual pic-nic of the Rancorn Parish Church choir took place, when the party were driven to Tatton Park, Knutsford, in a conveyance supplied by Mr Peck. The expenses of the trip were borne by the churchwardens. the vicar, and Miss Barclay. A pleasant day was spent In the grounds and con- servatories of 'Patton Park, and in the evening an excellent tea was partaken of at the Royal Georgeellotel. A NATIONAL Footpath Preservation Society, the offices of which are at 6, Fetter-lane, Fleet street, London, has just been formed It is intended in have branches in various parts of the Kingdom. Several local societies are already in existence,and it is thought that by affiliating with the parent society much good may be done. A determined stand filmed be made in every town and village when a landowner through lenerence or greee eudeevoure to deprive the public of a right .Of way. OUTBREAK OF IDIPIITHERIA AT Hateweeen. -- Consider- able anxiety has been created in Halewood by the outbreak of diphtheria. Within a very' few days no less than five deaths hive occurred, and it has been thought necessary to close the National Schools for a time. In one family alone, that of Mr Nell& no lees than three deaths have occurred, and much sympathy is felt in the villege for the bereaved parents. Every p-ecantion, medical and otherwise, is being taken to prevent the further spread of the disease. WIFE DESERTION AT WIDNES —At Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Wednesday, John Broxton was charged, under a warrant, with deserting his wife and family.—Mr Hartley appeared for the Present Board of Guardians, and' Mr Knowles for the prisoner.—The prisoner had been remanded on the char.e, and he bad since arranged with Mr Hartley to pay the sum owing to the Guardians, and to contribute in • future 8e per week towards the maintenance of his wife and child.—The magistrates made an order accordingly. IMPROVEMENT OF THE MERSEY AND TRWELL NAVIOA- TION.—We are informed that the Board of Directors of the Bridgewater N ivigatien Company have had under their consideration for some time plans for the development of the Mersey and Irwell Navigation, of which navigation they are the proprietors. Their project comprises the deepening, widening, and straightening of the rivers Mersey and Irweit, and the reduction of the number Of locks and weirs from 11 to six. The remaining locks would be increased in size, their length and breadth and depth being doubled, as it is intended to make the navigation sufficiently large to pass vessels of at lesst 10 feet draft. The CoMPenY is in the position of having the necessary parliamentary powers to carry out these works. We understand that the directors have received assurances of the approval of their nelest in- fluential shareholders, who are determined to support them in at once Coking action in this undertaking, a`nd'for which they have more than sufficient uncalled capital at their dis- posal. This actian of the Bridgewater Navigation Company would secure the abatement of floods, and no doubt greatly economise the cost of conveyance. . WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD FINANCES—A. special meeting of Widnes School Boatel was held on Thursday afternoon for the purpose of considering the half-yearly balance sheet. Bruce and damaging his ewhistle.—Ths officer rated that on the previous morning the prisoner was drunk and very noisy in Warrington-road. He took her into custody, and she became very violent. She threw herself to the ground, and kicked the officer in a frantic fashion. She also broke his whistle, and smashed the chain into three pieces.—She was fined in the total sam of 19s Bd, and was ordered to be sum- mooed for the assault. Baocicu4G DEraivir,r AT ,lIONCORN —Before Mr James Handley. at Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, Thos Hot- lingworth, 79 years of age, ,was brought up, on remand, charged with attempting M cammit a rape tapas Mary Ellen Hayes, aged 12 years, on the list October, and wi.h inde- centlY assaulting Eliz tbeth Elayee, aged 9, on Frditv even- ing.—Mr Barton watched the naafi cm the prisoner's behalf. —The prisoner was the caretaker of the cealyard andletke- house in Heath-road, belotigine to Mr Sweetm in. and on the evenings of the days mentioned he committed the offences in the bakehhuse.—lle was committed to the 'Sessions for trial on both charges. Waterloo-road, from Thomas Williamson to Jeeeph Saunders; the Grapes Inn, Halton-road, from Ed- ward Banks to John Ormester ; the Greenwey Vaults, Green- way-read, to Mrs Chadwick from the executors of her late husband; the Angel Inn, Wellingtun-street. from Michael Ryan to John Bunt; _the Albion Inn, Peel-street, from Richard Morgan to Eliztbeth Williamson; the Crown Vaults, Heath-road, Joseph Wilkinson permission to self; and the Lord Rodney, Church-street, train Joseph Dean to Charles Whitfield. WIDNES SCLIOOL BOARD AT WORK —OR Wednesday, at Widnes.Petty Sessions, Mr Q U Denby, clerk to the School Board, prosecuted the following persons for neglecting to send their children regularly to school :—Elizabeth Delaney, John Bums, Archibald Sullivan; Catherine Lancaster, Thomas Smith, Joseph Carr Jelin Emery, Henry Whitfield (two was), Robert Heey, Richard Qiesey, John Mnrphy, C McCafferty, and Patrick Caine. The usual fine of 51 was imposed in each case. Attendance orders were made upon James Fallon, Richard Glassey ; and John Frain, a waif, was sent to St George's Induetrial School, Liverpool. Evidence was given by school attendance officers, Messrs

Davies, Joynsoti, and Ifoare. ATTEMPT TO DEFRAUD THE RAILWAY COMPANY AT WIDNES —At Widnes Petty Sessioerr, on Wednesday, John Murray and Martin Quinn, apparently labourers, were char- ged with travellibg on the Lnnden and North-Western Rail- way without haying paid their fares. Mr Perrand, of the solicitors' department, Lime-street station, Liverpool, prose- cuted. It seemed that on the previous night, the pris- oners alighted from the St Helens trek' and presented to the collector tickets from Whines to Clock Pace. Tney attemp- te,d to rush away, bat the collector stopped them and deman- ded 10.1. Quinn pushed him against the door and behaved otherwise in a violent manner. but the station master arriv- ing on the scene both the priseners were secured. Murray was fined 103, and costs 12e, or 14 days, and Quinn 15s, aud costs 12e, or 21 &ye' hard labour. ROBBERY_ PROM A WIDNES DRAPER:9 SHOP.—TbOrna9 Smith, a middle-aged man, was brought up at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, charged with stealing a pair of stockings, value Is, the property of Mr Birchen, draper, Waterloo-road.—lt appeared that on Monday evening about six o'clock the prisoner asked Mr Sandland, Mr Birchali's manager, the price of some scarfs which were hanging at the door. He did not purchase any, and five minutes after- wards a pair of stockings (produced) were missed. Shortly afterwards P.C.Evans 8911 the prisoner in Waterloo-road and noticing that his pocket was very bulky took him into cus- tody. He found the stockings produced in his pocket, and charged hint with stealing them. Toe prisoner, who was under the influence of drink, said "That's more than know."—Saperintendeut Barker said the prisoner was a drunken idle fellow, who had been three times to gaol this year for sleeping in chemlcel worke.—lr Hall said drunken- ness was no excuse for stealing, and the prisoner was sea- tenced to a month's hard labour. SHOCKING IJE9TITUCION AT WIDNES —Before Captain Willis and Mr C Barnes, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Michael Glynn was charged with deserting his wife and three children. whereby they became chargeable to the Prescot Union.—Mr S H Hartley, clerk to the Prescot Guardians, said that was a very heartless case of desertion. The prisoner systematically neglected to proviee for his wife and children; and was a most drunken, idle ova:send, who spent his wages in drink and left his wife and children starving. They were found by the relieving officer in a most dirty, hungry, and almost naked condition, and they had not even a bed to lie on. When the prisoner's wife made application for relief he said her husband had always spent his wages in drink and had repeatedly left her.—Mr Scannel, relieving officer, deposed that there was not a vestige of food in the house; there was no bed to lie on, and the only blanket in the house was pawned for 91. 'They were half naked when he found them.—The prisoner was committed for two months with hard labour.

CHU &LT! TO A HORSE AT WIDNES—. At Widnes Petty Sessious on Wednesday, Joshua Smith, aged 15 years, was summoned.for working a horse whilet. in an unfit state, and Messrs Davies and Oakes, coal dealers, were summoned for permitting the animal to be worked.—Mr Oakes appeared for the firm and pleaded guilty. Superintendent Barker thereupon withdrew the charge against the bov.—P C Davie deposed that on the morning of the 30th ult he sew Smith in charge of a horse and cart laden with coal. He exam- ined the animal and found a raw wound on the backbetie about the slas of a two shilling piece, and another uuder the saddle. The saddle had cut into the first wound. They were old wounds and had been but some time. The horse was in a poor cendition.—John Green, a carter, stated the wounds were not larger than a threepenny piece.—Mr Oakes admitted thet the boy hal told him that the saddle was making the horse's back sore and he had total him to get a new saddle made. The wounds had healed up three days after the officer saw the home at work, and he asked the Bench if that would have been possible had the wounds been as bad as stated.—As this was the defendants' second offence the Bench imposed a penalty of IL and costs 15e 61 ' to A aims BUTCHER AND His WEIGHTS.—John Bower, pork butcher, Victoria-road, was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday to answer a charge of being in pos- session of a weight which was not according to the Board of Trade standard.—Superintendent Barker said on the 30th September he visited the defenaant's shop, and under the counter found several 561 b weights. Amongst them was the fifty-six produced, which had marked upon it in small figures" 60." It weighed that amount less an ounce. He need not point out that a parson using that weight to buy pigs with could easily count 41bs to himself as profit. Ac- ending to the denomination of the Board of Trade a 601 b weight was illegal. He understood that the deenclint bought large numbers of pigs each week.—P.C. Laing oor- roborated.—Mr J W Knowles, who defended, argued that it was palpable to anyone that the weight was not a fifty-six, and it was not in fact used at all by the defendant, who had purchased it alone with his brother's stok some months ago. He contended that the weight was sel'gel as any other weight, because, as required by Act of Parliament, it was a multiple of a pound.—The Bench after five minutes consul- tation with Mr Lewin, the clerk, fined the defendant lOs and costs and ordered the weight to be forfeited. - - - - -

A- .Boy's QUARREL AT WlDNlX—atephen Cusick, 12 'years of age,-was broaiglit up at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, charged on remand with unlawfully wounding Wm Brady, aged *bent 13, by striking him on the bead with s can.-4t the instance of Supt. Barker' the charge was reduced to one of common aleault.—MrJ W Knowles ap- peared for the prisoner—Froth the evidence of the prose- cutor and a witness named Frederick Hoyle, it appeared that on Saturday afternoon the hove were watching a footbell match in A field off Milton-road. At one point of the game Brady said tit It's a try," when the prisoner asked What do you know about it ? I'll drown you." Ha followed up his words by throwing a quantity of water from a CAE at Brady, who wan thua set upon by the prisoner and his brother, and knocked to the ground and kicked. The pri- soner, wi,h a elle he carried in hie hand, ~truck him on the head, inflicting a wound two inches long penetratieg to the bone—Mr Knowles contended for the defence that it was simply a frivolnen quarrel between boys, ending in a fight, and he called Edward McAnley, who alleged that Brady was the aggressor, and struck Cueick a blew on the mouth with his fist that sent him to the ground.—The Bench, tak- ing into consideration that the prisoner was the son of a widow who had a large family to keep, only imposed a fine of 2e 131 and costs 9s 81, or seven days in default. JUVENILE THIEVES sr WiDeras.—At Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Wednesday. Corbett Gardiner and Daniel Cart- wright, aged respectively 12 and 9 years. were charged with stealing 60Ihs. of creel, the property of the London and Nerth-Weetern Railway Company.—About seven o'clock on Sunday miming P.C. Bowarbani met I he,prisoners comiper, from the Old Marsh carrying the hisket of coals produced. Gardiner stated that they had got the coals from "the heart." —lnspector Carter deposed that the coals were the property of the company.—Gardiner was sentenced to receive six and ' Cartwright four strokes with the• birch-rod. --Alfre I Whalley (16), Michael Ford (13), and Elias Gl4BFieV (16), were charged with haying on the 6th inet, stolen five cape, the p-eperty of Lewis Merkles.—Annie Jones said she lived at 15, Waterloo-read, and manaeed a hat shop for Mr derides there. Between eight and nine o'clock on the even- ing of the 6th hest, she saw Ford and ,another boy standing near the shop and apparently 'watching her. She ordered Ford away and went ineide. In a few ininutee she heard a noise in the doorway, and went there. She miesed five caps, from the spot. The cape produced were her employer's pro- perty.—P.C. Cummings deposed that on the 7th inst. be apprehended the prisoners Ford, and Whalley in a field off , Victertroad. They were wearing the caps produced, and had their old caps in their pdckets. He afterwards tont, Glasse', in custody.—Whelley and Glasiey were each gnel 10e and ceste or 14 days'hard labour, and Furl eme ordered to reCeive six strokes with pe birch-red.

ALLEGED EXTRAORDINARY ROBBERY FROM A

RUNCORN TRAIN. Yesterday, at the Runcorn Police Court, before Mr James Handley, George Bitshell, of Lock-street,. jtuncorn, and Thomas and Elizabeth Oxwortb, husband and wife, of the Holloway, Runcorn, were brought up in custody charged with stealing and receiving. knowing to be stolen, eight £5 no.es,three £lO notes, and four cheqrtes, one for £6, two for £5 and one for £3, the monies of Richard John Jones.—Mr T II Elitchen appealed for the prisonars.—From a statement by Superintendent Leah, and ths evidence of Inspector. Roche, it appeared that Mr Jones is a tradesman at Lien- fairfechen, near Bangor, North %Vales, and on Wednesday morning, the Ist of October, his Nile left home to go to Manchester' to make some purchises. She bad with her a large sum of money in bank notes and chews. At Chester. instead of getting into the Manchester train Mrs Jones entered a 'train for Lime-sheet, Liverpool, and when t)ld of her mistake by a porter she hurriedly alighted. leaving, noes and cheques to the extent of _about £BO behind her. Two men, eupposed to be Bushell and Oxworth, were in tbe compartment. and they alighted at Runcorn. Buis, offering a reward of £lO bad been issued, but nothing was heard of the missiog money until Thursday, when the police at Runcorn ascert.ined that the prisoners had bosra changing bank notes and making somewhat extenave pur- chases. Inspe'tor ROehe went to BusbelPs house and questioned Bushell and Oxworth, but they denied .11 know- ledge of complcity in the matter. Later, at Oxerorth's house, Inspector Roche found a £lO note concealed beneath a wash b tsin, and Oxwerth produced three of the missing th,ques. WIDNES.

A few months ago the Widnes Local Board reduced the price of gas from 3s 31 to 2s 9d per 1,000 cubic feet nett, and simultaneously announced with the view of increasing the consumption of gas amongst householders, that appli- ances for cooking and heating by gas would be hired out at the low rent of is 61 per quarter' and fixed free of charge. At the lut meeting of the Board Messrs H and C Davies and Company, of the Metropolitan Gas Stove Works, Camberwell, London, suggested the desira- bility of holding an exhibition of gas stoves for various purposes, with the additional attraotion of. lectures on the art of lei:ling. The aeggestion was favourably con- I sidered, and the Beard agreed le.previda gee for the occe- sied and to bear the cost of securing a sulteble room. Carr.—Mr F H Gessa,ee, in op 'ming the exhibition, -said he hal hem asked to makes few remarks as cheirman of the Whines Lees! He Was net one of those whe thought the USA of. gee would be put an end to by the introduction of the eleorriclight. The., exhibition was tin itself 'a capital illustration of hoyi new uses arose for golds. They had a striking illustration of this fact when they remembered that the great number of dynamos which Was necessary to produce the electric light were driven by engines propelled by gas. After taferrtog to veriens exhibits, the speaker said the hire per quarter for one of Messrs Davies and Co.'s cooking stoves, capable of cooking for four or dye peonle was only Is Si, and these stoves could be ott kited frorn the Widnes Local Board. The nett price of gas in Wein-s load. as they all keew, been greatly reduced, being 2s 01 per • 1,000 cubic feet for Use in private !noses, which was an exceed- ingly low figure. The object of the exbibition Was to set ,before them the 'economy of cooking by gas; ad he could !meek personally to this fact because for the last Mx or seven years he bad cooked for a very large housshold with it. He bad sometimes 40 or 5b people, in the house and he could cook for all these with a range 5 feet long, 2 feet 6 inehee tom beck to front, and about 2;leet 6 inches ha height. Alongside the stove was a meter, so that he always had a check upon the quantity of gas urea Ho :yes 'bus able to keep a separate :account of the amount of gas used for. cooking pu:pnes,aud he tented there was cot sidersble seviog by gee over the open fireplace with cool. lie bed lived down all Objections that had been raised to caking by es, and he could assure them that he Apoke with the greatest centidence when he . recommended every- body iii Widnes to use gas in preference to the open fire- piece in cooking.. It was also a positive fact that there was also a great saving in the weight of the meat in this pro- Ores of coeking. Messrs Davies, he saw, clainvd. that in their sieves a jeint of meat weighing 101hs only lost 115 in cooking. He (the spetkei ) found that the average cost of cooking plena food for SACA person was from 1/i to 41, aud tbis was certainly more econonficel than using coal. Another advaaago in using gas Was that in a morning there, was rap tire to meke, no ashes to clear awey, and no polish- ing of tbs. grate.. 'the cook *limply took a match in her band and lighted the gas, and in five or ten minutes a very good breakfast for any or... Hoary family could be cooked— that was in may Viet a chop, bacon, cram omellette could be caokee ie ten minutes. As soon as they bad finished cooking they could nut out the tire. He now declared the exhibition open, and Mrs Thwaites, of aeonnt Vernon-road, Liverpool. delivered a lecture on cookery, and in A was stove cooked several kinds of food. Messrs H and C Devise and Co. of Manchester, etiowed a varied assortment of heating and cooking stoves, to suit the requirements of small or large families. Messrs Singers exhibited a sewing machine driven by a 2-inad gas engine, made by Messrs J E El Andrews and Co., engineers. Senn leotattful specimens of Cincinnati new slag ware, m ttle from lion el.g' the tefeees kens blast fu-naces and the waste products of was tare were shown , by Mr E Sydney, London. The steam washer made by Mr John Gremall, of Oxford-street. Matcheefer, who claime4 that they woeld ace implish in two, hours, what was now a hard day'e, weir, were yiewel with interest. Mr lingoes said he hart not aoy rope in the place of that kid, but he showed two bundles he had taken its on the Monday ramming. Next day they found some of the rope produced at the Old Quay yard.—By Mr ft:dgway :Mr Hughes said they could look at his ropes' if they Heed, and did not attempt to conceal anything. The ropes at the Old Quay wharf had been seat there by Mr Hughes —George Green, carter in the employ of the Bridgewater Navigation Company, living at 9, sting- street, stated that on Wednesday, the let lost, he went to Mr Hughes', at Weston Point, for a load of ropes. Tne ropes were tied into 26 bundles. He conveyed them to the Old Quay wharf.—Thomas Pearson, foreman at the Old Quay wharf, said the ropes weighed upwards of 27 cwts. There were no other ropes on the wharf except those sent by Mr Hughes on Thursday, the 2nd inst. Mr Hughes had previously sent loads of rope away.—P.C. Bryan deposed that on the Ist lost he went to Mr Hughes' place and asked him if ha had purchased any ropes since Friday. He said he had 2 Coils. that he purchased on Tuesday and Wednes- day, and added that he had not had any ropes for a long time previously. He told Mr Guest's son, who was wite the constable, to look through all the ropes its the yard, but Mr Guest refused because be had known Mr Hughes for a long time, and had found him a very honest man. About 8 o'clock on the evening of the same day the constable and McMichael went to Mr Hughes' house. The sergeant asked him where his ropes were, and he replied that they were down at the Old Quay, as he was sending them away to Millbank, Manchester. Sirgeant McMichael asked the pri- soner for his book, and he gave it to him.—Sergeant Mca Michael repeated the evidence given by the former witness, and stated that he charged the prisoners. Rewlinson re- plied that he met Roberts near, the Crown public-house with a bag of ropes on his back. Re asked him where the shop was were topes were b night. He (Rawlinson) went with him, and they got 63 for the ropes. Roberts stated that ltawlinson Went with him to the but and aided in getting the ropes. That morning witness had charged Mr Hughes with receiving the stolen goods, and he replied that he did not know they were stolen. Rawlicson, he said, was the man from whom he bought the ropes. He ob- tained Mr Hughes' book, and discovered there were no entries for September, and Only One eniry of 511 lbs for July, and 184 lbs for August—Clara Williams, servant in the employ of Mr Hughes, deposed to the prisoners Rawlinson and Roberts •bringing the ropes to Mr Hughes at a late hour on Saturday night. They said they bad some ropes to sell, and on her asking why they had coroe so late they said they had only just come up by the tide. She told Mr littehes and he weighed the rope, anti the men went a way.—Bv Mt' Ridgway : On Thursday Mt Hughes asked her and Mrs Hughes whether they recollected any rope being brought, and witness told him about buying the rope on Saturday. lie seemed surprised when reminded Of it, and then said that he had just " unbethought " him- self that he had bought the rope.—At the request of Mr Ridgway, Inspector Roche was called, and deposed that on Friday he went to Mr Hughes' house and found Mrs Hughes dressed apparently for going out. She told him she was about to visit the superintendent to tell him the result of a conversation her husband had had with the servant girl. Witness added that Mrs Hughes had all through expressed his willingness to aside% the police.—Nir Ridgway for the de- I fence, said as their worships well knew a marine store dealer who did not keep proper b .oks was liable to a very heavy penalty, and so far as the register produced that day watt concerned, Mr Hughes could only be tined for not tieing as the law required, and as regarded the present charge, their worships must be certain in their own minds that at the time Mr Hughes purchased the rope he had a guilty know- ledge that the goods were stolen. The whole actions of the man from the time that the police tir,t went to him. were those of an innocent man, and he gave the police every as- sistance. It seemed on the face of it improbable that a man should buy goods so recently, and pay a certain price for them, and not actually remember the occurrence, but the Bench must have heard or read of cases where peonle seemed to lose all memory of transactions they had taken part in until some particular event called them to mind, and he asked them most respectfully to think that these ropes weee bought in a hurry on Saturday nieht, and that the whole transaction went completely out of his mind, though he wes pressed on several occasions by several police officers, until it wee brought to bis remembrance by the servant girl. It had been on his part a simple, straightforward transiction, and be had no felonious intent in the matter. He was a man holding an important positicn in Weston, he had been in business many years both in Warrington and at Runcorn, and with one alight exception he had had no charge made against his character. He bad no doubt bests very careless, but not criminally., and he asked the Bench to say that the case had not been proved so far as guilty knowledge was concerned.—After a brief consultation with Mr Handley and the Clerk (Mr Ashton), the Rev E A P Campbell said Mr

LONDON, THURSDAY. , The meetings of the Cabinet on Monday and Tuesday _ • bring forcibly to mind the near apprloach of the opening of what promises to be one of the most momentous sessions of medermtimes. The talk of the day is about a compromise by which the oriels will be avoided in November. There continues to be a strong imprearriou that somehow or other the threatened danger will be averted and the Franchise Bill passed. That is a view which it Is more pleasant than safe to adopt. The policy of the Conservative party at the present jancrure is exceedingly well defined. They do not further oppose the Franchise Bill, which they accept as in- evitable. Bat they want to be in a position either to pals such a bill themselves or so to weaken the Government ma- jority that they will be able to take a prominent part in manipulating the Redistribution scheme. That is Lord Sal- isbury's- plan and intention—to force a dissolutioe and get Parliamentary Reform dealt with in a new House, where in no conceivable circumstances can a Liberal Goeernmeet he so powerful as it is just now. That is the one point round which the fight rallies, and it will be sem that there is no opening here for compromise. Everything will depend upon Lord Salisbury's influence over the majority in the House of Lords. If he can keep them together the Fran- chise'Bill will be thrown out; if he cannot he may be glad enough to accopt any golden bridge the courtesy of the Government may place at his disposal. Accustomed as the public are to the audacity of Lord It Churchill, there is something in its display at Leeds that almost takes away the breath. Speaking on the Franchise gnestion, Lord Rindolpla said the Peers had taken up a clear and intelligible position, and if they retreated from it they would receive and deserve the contempt of their fellow countrymen. Many who react this speech and enjoy the advantage of Lord Randolph'e personal acqualtrtanes will recall frank expreaelons of opinion on the same subject spoken little more than two months ago, that would have made Lord Brabourne's hair stand on end. Opinions pri- vately spoken are, of course, sacred. But it does net need reference to them to indicate one of the most striking In- stances of ratting known in English political history. One Friday afternoon last session' when the Franchise Bit( had al-. ready been thrown out in the Lord, Lord Randolph Churchill, alluding to Lord Elcho's coming motion, besought Mr Gladstone to renew the offer, solemnly pledging the teovern- ment forthwith to bring in the Redistribution 13111. made to Lord Salisbury on the eve of the division and carefully withheld by him from the knowledge of the Peers who were about to vote. "It would be difficult," said Lord Randolph, "to overstate the responsibility of tk.e person who would ' now reject the offer." Six days later he had dined with Lord ealisbury in Arlington-street, had re-entered the see- vice of the Tory party, and is now able to tell the House of Lords that they will deserve the contempt of their fellow countrymen if they do not take that course which once filled him with patriotic consternation. SHOCKING MORDER AT BOLTON.—A brutal murder has been perpetrated at Bclton. On fliday Mr R Dugdale, a traveller for Messrs Austin Brothers, maltsters, Castleford, near walrefield, was in the town, and visited a number of places on busieese, obttining in one instance a large order from a loctl brewer. At half-past nine o'clock at night he was discovered 'Ong dead with his throat cut on a waste piece of land off Bradshaw-gate, one of the principal thoroughfares in the town. Be was lyiag with his arms stretched out over his head, an 014 pocket knife in bis right band, and his coat and vest unbuttoned., The body was quite old, the face was smeared with blood, and the eyes, especially the right, had the appearauce of recent blows, beiog cat and swollen. The knife was held, as statcd, in the rigbt hand, but the wounds must have tem caused by the left it self. inflicted. The left hand, however, was firmly clenched, whilst the right was loose. The wounds in the throat were of a terrible nature, there b2ing one or two stabs in addition Ito a eat a)meietely savoring the windpipe. No money was found upon the deceaf.ei except a few coppers, but a sever- eiga was found on the ground undernsath hint. In his opoucmkeettobtiosoke.aiitt,iaens,enwtierreelyadfieffwerwenotrdwsr,itbinigdityo tspheedlte,cetoasedv;es effect that be bad committed suicide. 'the body was re- moved to the mortuary, where it was shortly afterwards recognis:d. Subsequent inquiries disclosed that daring the cat, be had been in the company of a young man named Kay Howarth, who resides in Boron, but recently returned , front America, and in his presence deceaSed die- -played a cheque for £B. At six o'clock a friend of Mr Ductile asked Howarth to accompany decetmed to the Wheateheaf idoted as be was rather tbe worse foi liquor. Two hours afterwards Howarth told this friend that he bad loft D ugd ale at the B almoral Hotel, which is our the scene of the murder, id not .at the Wheatsheaf. Howarth w„ arrested at his reeidenee early on Saturday morning, and there was discovered in his possession £3B 10s in gold, 113 s in silver, a cheque, and a watch and guard, the property of the murdered man. He gave no explanation for the pos- session of this properly, but stronglir asserted his innocence. During the forenoon the mtagistrates remanded him until Thursday. The deceased, who was a married man and 38 years a age, bore an eicelletit character, and was touch re- spected by the peopl a he called upon in Lancashire and Yorkshire, where he was widely known.

POLICE INTELLIGENCE. • WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SATURDAY —There was BO business. MoNDAT.—Before the M4yor (Alderman Harrison) and

Mr Fairclough. Darxxxxxzes.—The following were dealt with for drun- kenness as under, viz : John Mitchell, fined 5s and costs, or seven days; John Noon, 63rd appearance. fined 10s and costs, or 14 days. BREACHES OF ma PE&CE —John Birk and John James were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Knuts- ford-road, and creating a breach of the peace. It appeared that James insulted the wife of the other defendant and a fight ensued. Bark was dismissed an James was fined 5.1 and costs for being drunk et mil bound over to keep the peace for six months in his own recognisances of £lO for the assanit.—John Troy and John Fallon, youths, were ordered to be bound over to keep the peace for fighting in Horsemarket-street, seven days' imprisonment in default of finding sureties. BAD LANGDAGE..—EBZIbEttI Tilley was ordered to pay the costs of the case for using bad language in General- street. _ _

CARELESSNE99.—JOhn Liddle was summoned for allow- ing his horse and vehicle to stand in Sankey-street without his having proper control over it He was ordered to pay the costs of the case.--James Hickey, for allowing a horse to stray in Folly-lane, was ordered to pay the costs. A LAZY VAGRANT.—George Gerard, was charged with re- fusing to perform his task of work wiiilsc a casual inmate of the vagrant ward of the Warrington Cabin. It was his fifteenth appearance before the Court. He was sent to pri- on for a month with hard labour. . .

&Ham ATTENDANCE —The following were dealt with for not sending their children to school, viz : Elizabeth Abra- hams, lady-help, Tilley-street, fined ss; James Emson, glassmaker, Cartwt lea-street, fined 51 ; Harrop Chadwick, carter, Church-street, fined ss; Samuel Maxldd. forgeman, Winwick-road, fined sn; Michael Flynn. forgeman, Refuge- square, fined ss; John Forster, labourer, Kindere-yard, fined ss; Thomas Dutton, forgeman, Oliver-street, fined ss. The cases were proved by Mr George Riley, School Atten- dance Officer. TUBSDAY.—Before Councillors Monks and Broadbent. _ .
Helsby, John Tully, and Patrick Dolly were brought up in custody on charges of drunken. ness.—They were dismissed with a caution. WRDNESDAY. —Before Alderman Chandley and Mr John

Fairclongh. DRUFSENITESS.—Thomas Rabbitt, last from Walton Gaol, was fined 5s and costs, or seven days, for being drank at the police station tbe same morning. TEUESDAY.—Before Captain Litton. A SUSPICIOUS CHARACTER—John Flynn. in custody on a charge of being drank and disorderly, was remanded on suspicion of stealing a quantity of potatoes the previous day.

div.head: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.
MONDAY.—Before the Rev E A P Campbell and Mr James
Hand ley.

Mrsextuarsors.—Mary O'Neil Was, on the evidence of P.C. Bann, fined 103 and costs for being drunk in Church. street on the 29th ult.—For being helplessly drunk at the same date and place, Elizabeth Santley and Sarah Ann Meakin were each fined 5s and costs. P.C. Bryan proved the cases.—Thomas Gayter and Michael McDonough were charged with committing a breach of the peace at Sutton on the 29th ult. Gayter did not appear, but Mo- Donough was bound over to keep the peace for six months in his own recognisances of £lO. P.C. Egerton proved the case.—Mary Jane Ann Gallagher,who made her 28th appear- ance, was on the evidence of P.S.Walley convicted of sleep- ing in an unoccupied house in Cooper-street on the sth inst. Mr Campbell said the prisoner had been charged with every description of abomination, and sentenced her to two months' hard labour.

div.head: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.

MONDAY—Before Mr H Gaskell, jun. MISCELLANEOUS.—Martin Collins, Michael Burns, Patrick Cooney, John Clarke, John Smith, Michael Davitt, John Byrne, William Burns, Ann Dogherty, and Michael Harvey, were each fined for drunkenness.—Ann MCGeBVPII was charged with comrnittimg a breach of the peace, and she was bound over to be of good behaviour, herself in £lO and one surety of £s.—James Delaney, for begging in Waterloo- road on Saturday night, was sentenced to seven days' hard labour.

WEDNESDAT.—Before Mr H S Hall and Mr H Gaskell, jun. MISCELLANBOOS.—Jobn Blade, Joseph Andrews, Michael Molloy, Sarah Dogherty, Sarah Ann Sant, and Wm. Dwyer were each fined for drunkenness—Charles Rotherham, for being drunk in the Castle Inn on the 30th ult, was fined 103 and costs.—A penalty of 5s and costs was imposed upon Rosanna Finn for a like offence committed in Manchester House Hotel —Patrick Brady and Ellen Kiogh were sum- moned for fighting in Granville-street on the 2nd inst, and were each bound over for their good behaviour for three months.—Luke Kelly was fined 7s 61 and costs, 7s 6d, for being drunk whilst in charge of a donkey and cart in Victoria-road, on the 24th September.—For allowing the chimney of his dwelling-house in Widnes-road to be on fire stt the 26th inst. Robert Taylor was fined Is and costs, 45. Mary Gallagher, for creating a disturbance in Victoria- street, was bound over for her good behaviour for three months—Patrick Knockton was convicted of sleeping in Messrs Hutchinson's chemical works on the previous night, and on the evidence of P.C. Evans, was sentenced to seven days' hard labour.—Jane Dawn was summoned by Mary Moss for threatening to assault her on the 4th October, and she was bound over in her own recognizances of .£l, and one surety of £5. THE THEFT OF BAcoN.—Michael Curran, an elderly man, was charged with having, on Saturday, the 27th ult, stolen s.Hbs of bacon from the shop of Mr Samuel Sadler, provision dealer, Anne-street, West.—Evidence previously reported was given, and the prisoner, who bad spent 10 days is gaol on remand was sentenced to a month's bard labour. AN OYSI'ER DEALER IN TROUBLE.—Edward Broder was brought up under a warrant charged with having, on the 24th April last kept open his refreshment house after hours. —P.C. Evans proved that the defendant's wife sold oysters to several petsons at a shop in Waterloo-road about mid- night of the day in question.—The prisoner said he did not lice in Widnes. The business was his wife's.—Mr Hall said the prisoner was responsible, and fined him 5s and costs, 18e 64.
PRESCOT PETTY SESSIONS. TinterneY.—Before Captain Willis and Mr C Barnes.

_ SCHOOL BOARD CASES.—Fifteen persons were summoned for neglecting to send their children to Bchool, and in each case the Bench made an order for the payment of a fine of ss. BREACHES OF 7HE PEac2.—Henry Stott and Michael Doolan were charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Bond-street, Prescot, on the 27th nit., and they were bound over to keep the peace for three months.— Catherine Doddy and Mary O'Hora were also charged on separate occasions with committing breaches of the peace; and they were bound over to keep the peace for three months.

THEFTS AT WAVERTnEE —Patrick Walsh, of Binns-street. Wavertree, was charged with stealing 150 feet of timber, of the value of £1 10s, the property of Thomas Williams. joiner and builder, Wavertree.—Mr Murphy, of Liverpool, appeared for the prisoner, who was committed to prison for a month, with hard labour. —Four lads, named Owen Costello (16 years of age), John Costello (13), Thos. Craven (13), and Hugh Brian (12), were charged with breaking into and entering St. Mary's School, Wavertree. and stealing therein 348 in copper money from a desk, the property of , John Cooke.—They were committed for trial at the next Liverpool Quarter Sessions. EXTRAORDIKAne Tartpr.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Captain Willis and Mr C Barnes, Edward Cain, a boatman, bailing from the Isle of Man, and a girl named Elizabeth Crelly, residing at Wavertree, were together I charged with stealing a tin box containing ti quantity of wearing apparel and several miscellaneous articles, togetker of the value of .£3, the property of John Kelly, a joiner and builder, 5, Ono-street, Wavertree.—'l° prosecutor stated that the female prisoner was his granddaughter, and had resided at his !muse for about two years past. On Wednes- day, the lit of Octdaer, the male prisoner, who was the girl's stepfather, visited his house, and witness went ont for a short time. When he returned he was told by a neighbour. that the prisoners had left the house, and on making a i search he missed the articles produced. Be then gave n- formation to the police—Other witnesses were called to prove that the box and its contents had been seen in posses- sion of the prisoners, who booked to the Isle of Man.—The female prisoner stated that every aiticle she had taken was her own property, and had been given to her by the prose- cutor —P.6. Townson, stationed at Wavertree, said from infoim ition he received he visited the Liverpool landing stage, and found the box produced on board an Isle of Man ate.inilr. He had only just time to get the box off More the boat sailed. Ile afterwards received the prisoners in custody from the Douglas (Isle of Man) police. They then bad some of the stolen property in their possession.—The prisoners were committed for trial at the next Liverpool -Quarter Sessions.
ST. HELENS BOROUGH POLICE COURT. FRIDAY —Before Dr Gaskell and Mr A Sinclair.

DRUNIENNESS.—The following persons were fined the amounts stated for drunkenress:-58 and ,costs: Edward Seddon and John Taylor, Parr; John Oakes, Patrick Mc- Govan, Martin Mullen, and Thomas Twist, Eccleston.-78 6d and costs: Michael Birch and Joseph Leacbey, Parr; Robert White and Peter Kiernan, Eccleston ; Robert Seddon, Windle ; George Boardman, Burtonwood.-105 and costs: Michael Burns and Michael Kelly, Eccleeton ; Joseph Cart- wright, Windle.—Henry Newton. Ecoleston, was fined 20s and costs for being drunk on licensed premises.—Joseph Million was fined 10s and costs for being drunk while in charge of a horse and cart on the 24th September. MISCELLANEOUS.—Adam Seddon, Sutton, was fined 2s 6d and coats for allowing a mule to stray on the highway.— Ellen Glover and James Marr, Parr, were each fined Is and 65 6d costa for allowing the chimneys of their dwelling- house to be on fire.—John Thompson' Parr, was charged with using profane language on the highway at Parr, and was fined 2s 6d and costs. _ . .

ASSMILTS.—Jane Knowles was summoned fer assaulting Peter Clare. The parties live at Moss Bank-street, Parr.— Complainant stated that on Saturday night last he was sit- ting on his own doorstep when the defendant threw a piece of brick at him, and cut his forehead.—Defendant called a witness, who stated that the complainant and his wife had struck her about the face with a long stick.—Her face bore evidence of having been severely beaten, both eyes being blackened, and her face. covered with black marks —The case was dismiss,d.--Ellen Jacques was charged with as- saulting Margaret Rylance, on the 22nd ult, at Windle.— Complainant stated that defendant came into her house. Complainant told her she could not pay her the small ac- count she owed her, whereupon defendant flew into a pas- sion, seizsd a basin and threw it at her. She also threw her on the floor, and said she would kill her.—Ellen Anders ccr- roborated.—Defendant denied the assault, and said that last witness was lying drunk on the floor, and so coald not tell what was going on.—The Bench bound defendant over to keep the peace for three menthe, herself in £5, and one surety of £5. WEDNESDAr.—Before Mr J C Gamble and Dr Gaskell.

OLD CLIMES TO MEND —Michael Chester, a middle-aged man, was charged with hawking without a certificate on the previous day. It was stated that the prisoner was going from door to door in Elliott-street, Ecclesten, soliciting orders to repair chairs, but he was without a pedlars' certi- ficate, his last certificate having expired a fortnight age.— The prisoner pleaded to be let off this time, stating that he would get a licence immediately.—He was remanded until

the following day. MIIIMICENNZSS.—John Hill, of no settled residence, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Eccleston on the previous evening, and was fined 5s and costs. MownAL—Before Mr H S Hall and Alderman Cosk.

SLEEPING Otrr.—Charles Rourke and Peter McKeegan were charged with sleeping out near a furnace at the works of Mr H Baxter (Mayor), on Sunday morning ; and they were each committed to prison for seven days. DRUNKENNESS.—Bridget Carson, of Gerard's Bridge, w s charged with committing a breach of the peace on Sunday afternoon. She was discharged with a caution.—Mary Jane Williams was fined 5s and costs for being drunk and dis- orderly in Prescot-road, on Saturday night.—Edward Jen- nings, for being drunk in the Hare and Hounds public-house and refusing to leave when requested, was fined 7s 6J and costs.—Robert Crelly and Peter Kearns were each fined 5s and costs for being drunk and disordetly in College-street, windle, on Sunday.—William Chapman, for being drunk at Sutton, on the 30th September, was fined 5s and costs.— A like penalty was imposed on James Leonard, for being drunk at Eccleston, on the 27th September. Dams° WITHOUT RElNS.—Patrick Riley appeared to answer a summons charging him with riding in his cart without reins in New-street, Sutton, on the sth instant.— lie was fined 2s 6d and costs. Scaoot BOARD Casas.—Joseph Grice and Michael Linskey were summoned for neglecting to send their chil- dren to school.—The cases were adjourned te give the chil- dren an opportunity of attending school.

div.head: PRESCOT.
div.p: PRESCOT.

THE DEATH OF A WHISTON Comirti.—On Saturday, Mr Brighouse held an inquest at Whiston Cross on the body of a miner named Joseph Hughes, 52 years of age, who was killed at Carr's Colliery, Whiston, on Thursday, by a fall of roof, when other two men had a narrow escape. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death." The deceased, who lived with his family in Prescot, came from Mostyn only three weeks ago, and it was enly tbe day before his death that he brought his wife and family as well as his furniture to Prescot.

A PRESCOT RUFFIAN DESERVEDLY PUNISHED.--.l3efOre Captain Willis and Mr C Barnes, at the Prescot Petty Ses- sions, on Tuesday, John Burke, a rough looking young fel- low, was charged with committing a breach of the peace; and also with assaulting P.C. Myles Burton.—P.C. Burton deposed that about half-past eight on Saturday night lea he visited Burke's house to serve upon him a summons for com- mitting a breach of the peace. He went into the honso and saw Burke there with four or five companions. Be told Burke he had a summons for him and offered it to him, but he refused to take it. Witness laid it on the tab:e and went out, but was followed by the prisoner, who kicked him and struck him twice on the face with his fist. The prisoner was under the influence of drink.—Supt. Barker said the priso- ner was a perfect ruffian, and had been up ten times pre- viously for assaults on the police and drunkenness. There WAS no pace in the neighbourhood when the man was out of geol.—The Bench sent the prisoner to gaol for three months with bard labour.

NEGLIGENT HIISB4NDS.-At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Captain Willis and Mr C Barnes, James Starkle, of Widnes, was charged with neglecting to maintain his wife and cbild, whereby they became chargeable to the Prescot Union.—Mr S 1 Hartley, clerk to the Board of Guardians, stated that prisoner and his wife were natives of Widnes, but about eighteen months or two years ago they were in America and were married there. They returned to this country, and since December last Starkie had done very little if anything towards the maintainance of his wife and child.—The Bench committed the prisoner to prison for a month.—David Murray, a chemical labourer, was charged with deserting his wife and child on the 27th of August last, and having been previously convicted of a similar offence, he was sentenced to two months' imprisonment with hard labour.—Andrew Moran was brought up for a similar offence. The prisoner's wife and three children were admitted to the workhouse on the 22nd August, 1883, and from that time no to a week ago nothing was heard of the prisoner. One of the children died on the 13th January last, but the wife and two children had since been chargeable to the Union.—He was coaamitteed for three months with hard labour.

PRE9COT HIGHWAY BOARD—The monthly meeting of the Prescot Highway Board was held on Tuesday forenoon, when there were present Mr W L Evans (chairman), Cap- tain Willis, Messrs Lowe, Newton, W Goldsworth (stir- veyor), and H Cross (clerk).—The minutes of the last meet- ing were read and confirmed.—The Expenditure : The Sur- veyor's statement of expenditure for the five weeks from August 28th to October 2nd, was as follows: Bold £l7 3s 4d, Knowsley £l2 15s 4d, Rainhill £l2 lie 6d, Whiston £lB Is, team labour £2l us sd. new materials £55 5s 9d, Inciden- tale £2, total £139 8s 4d —Claim for Compensation: The ' Clerk read a letter from Mr W Tyrer, solicitor, with regard to the claim against the Board for damages by Mr Joseph Frith, of Whiston, to his crops, done from time to time through the bursting of and overflow from a pipe belonging to the Board and the Sanitary Authority. He understood that the claim bad been submitted on more than one occa- sion, but the Board had been unable to fix an amount for the acceptance or refusal of Mr Frith. For their guidance he (Mr Tyrer) bad obtained from his client particulars of actual loss, amounting to £3l ss. In addition to that pe- cuniary loss, Mr Frith lost one of his children through a sickness (fron, which the whole family suffered) attributable to the smell arising from the sewage which escaped from the pipe referred to. He and his family were moreover for a long time deprived of the use of their farmyard ard there- by put to much inconvenience and annoyance. He would be glad to know what was being done in the matter.—ln the course of a discussion the Chairman remarked that the Board had never admitted any liability in the matter, but Mr Frith bad sustained some loss.—The Clerk Intimated that Mr Frith had no legal claim against the Board.—lt was nltimately decided that the matter be referred to the Rural Sanitary Anthority.—Calls : The Clerk submitted the fol- lowing calls upon the overseers of the different townships for the next half year: Bold £265, Knowsley £3lB, Rain- hill £250, Whiston £368. This was the only business of interest.

PRFSCOT RURAL SANITARY AIITHORITY.—A meeting of this Authority was held at Whieton Workhouse, on Thurs- day forenoon, when there were present—Messrs J Leather. barrow (in the chair), W A Meadows, W Newsome, W Tyrer, E Syder, and S H Hartley (clerk.) The minutes of the last meeting were read and confirmed—The Sewerage of Eccleston: The Clerk stated that he had had several letters from the Local Government Board with reference to the sewerage scheme for Eccleston, alluding to the report drawn up by Mr Goldsworth (surveyor), and which had been fre- quently considered at previous meetings. The Local Go- vernment Board wrote on the let October that it would be contrary to the practice of the Board to direct one of their engineering inspector's to visit the locality for the purpose of advising the Rural Sanitary Authority as to the particu- lar part or parts of the scheme for the proposed works, , which should at once be proceeded with. That was a ques- tion which the Authority must themselves determine, and , when they had done so and had submitted a definite appli- cation for sanction to a loan for carrying out the works, the Board would probably direct one of their inspectors to hold a local inquiry on the subject. On the 13th September the Local Government Board for- warded a copy of a petition received from Messrs Peek and Winch, of London, owners of the Eccleston Park Estate, with reference to the sewerage of Ecclesteu township, and asked to be furnished with any observation! the Rural '-anitary Authority might make on the matter. The peti- tioners were described as Francis Peek and William Richard Pinch. of 4, Pencburch-street, Londen, tea merchants' owners of a freehold estate comprising abont 45 acres, called Eccleston Park Estate, between Prescot and St Helens. No system of drainage at present existed, but there was an open ditch stagnant with sewage until rain washed it away. The ditch was undoubtedly a public nuisance, and owing to the absence of a proper system of drainage parties declined to purchase. The petitioners had been in correspondence with the Rural Sanitary Authority on the matter, and they com- plained that the Authority had made default in providing the district with sufficient sewers. The petitioners therefore prayed that due inquiry might be directed and made, and further, that an order might be mule limiting the time for
