div.p: 114 E EXAMINER SATURDAY. OCTOBER 11. 1884

the performance of the duty by such Rural Sanitary Antbo- rity.—The Clerk stated that the fit at duty of the Authority was to say whether or not they would adopt Mr Golds- worth's report for the sewerage of Ecclestote—Mr Meadows asked what the local committee thought about the matter.— Mr Newsome replied that they would do nothing in the matter. They considered the owners should do it, and that was the opinion of the inhabitants —The Clerk said the matfer had been taken out of the hands of the local commit- tee ao far back as len' when the Authority passed a reso- lution that Mr tioldsworth should make a report. It was now for them to decide whether th9y would adopt the report. —Mr Meadows expressed the opinion that it would be a very hard thing if the whole of the ratepayers bad to pay for the drainage of Eccleston Park. —The Clerk : Do ,00 agree as to the principle of Mr Goldsvrorth's report ?—Mr Tyrer : Yes, as regards the principle of his renort.—The Clerk suggested that the Local Government Board be asked to sanction the borrowing of £5,000 in such periods and in such sums as the Authority might determine.—Mr Tyrer said there was no doubt the whole of Eccleston would require draining in accordance with Mr Goldsworth's schtmae, but it did not require doing all at once. It might be done piecemeal.—The Chairman ultimately moved that an application be made to the Local Government Board for sanction to borrow £5,000 for works of sewerage in Eccleston township, to be borrowed from time to time in each sums as the Authority might determine. —Mr Tyrer seconded the motion, which was carried.— Claim Against the Rural Sanitary Authority: The Clerk read a letter from Mr W Tyrer, solicitor, on behalf of Joseph Frith, farmer. Whiston, who claimed compensation for damage done to his land by the bursting of and subsequent overflow from a pipe belonging to the Rural Sanitary Authority and the Prescot Highway Board.—lt was stated that the matter had been discussed at the meeting of the Highway Board on the previous Tuesday, and Mr Hartley (clerk) was instructed to state that the Authority had no system of sewers in the Wbiston town- ship, and they failed to see their liability. The Health of the District: The Medical officer of Health reported that during the month of September the only c•ses of infectious disease bad been at Halewood where a slight outbreak of diptheria had occurred. There had been three deaths, but they all occurred in one house, and he suspec- ted the water bad been the cease from a sanitary analysis he had made: He had requested Mr Twist to forward a sample to Dr C Brown for his report upon it. A case of fever had been imported into Prescot from their district, but he had been unable to trace the origin of it. The Surveyor's report stated that in Eccleston, from Seddon's-brow to Por- tico the houses were indifferently supplied with water, the local wells being either dry or in all probability contamina- ted from the surroundings. There were about 21 cottages and three larger houses. It was decided that notices should be served upon the owners of the property to get a supply of water for the property.—This was all the business of interest.
Wood, Jos Wood, Brieley, Armstrong, Fitton, Thompson, Ripley, Nield, and Parkinson, forwards. LANCASHIRE CHALLENGE CIJP.

GOLBOIINE V. LYTHAM—These clubs met at Golborne on Saturday afternoon to decide their tie in the first round of the competition for the Laucishire Football Association Challenge Cup. There was a goodly number of spectators. A very exciting and evenly fought contest resulted in a victory for Golborne by two goals to one.

RAHLESTOWN V. RIECHEST ll.—The meeting of Earles- town and Ribchester in the first round of the Lancashire Cup competition on Saturday afternoon, on the ground of the former at Wargrave Moss evoked great interest through- out the district; and as the weather was beautifully fine there was a very large attendance. Both clubs turned out their best elevens, and they appeared on the field shortly after three o'clock. The visitors' captain won the toss for the choice of ground and in the first half chose to play uphill, with the sun in the eyes of the home team. At 3-25 Dagnall kicked off tor Earlestown; and a visit was at once paid to the visitors' quarters, Callender returning the ball with a powerful kick. Ten minutes from the commencement Ellison secured a goal for Earlestown amid cheers. Im- mediately the play was resumed the Earlestonians showed some clever passing and dodging. Sims and Ogden ran the ball down the field, and the former centering it beautifully Ellison tried to score, but the goalkeeper knocked the ball back. Rich rushed up, however, and in two minutes from the last score added a second goal; which brought forth cheers from the spectators. Ribchester again started the leather, and the play for five minutes was of • a very even character; and Halsall five minutes later notched the first goal for his side. The subsequent play was in favour of the home team, who severely pressed their opponents. Dagnall neatly scored a third'goal, and Rich scored a fourth, while five minutes before half-time Dagnall, by a good " screw " shot, was cheered in adding a fifth goal. At half-time ends were changed with the score at five goals to one in favour of Earlestown. After the resumption of the game three minutes had only elapsed when Ellison cleverly notched a sixth goal, and five minutes later Rich sent the leather through for the seventh time. The play for the next ten minutes was of a more even character, and some diversion was occasioned by a sudden rush upon the Earlestown goal, and the leather being passed to the centre from the left wing, Halsall again sent it under the Earlestown bar. Soon after, in a scrimmage, Duxbury landed the leather iust under the bar and made the eighth goal. No sooner had the game been resumed than the home team again ran the leather into their opponents' quarters and Sims sent in a capital shot which the goalkeeper fisted back, but Duxbury rushing up again shot the ball through the uprights. Though but five minutes remained for play it was sufficient for Earlestown to make a tenth goal, Ellison scoring after a nice pass by Sims. The score remained un- altered when time was called, and Earlestown thus won by ten goals to two. The teams were: Earlestown—James Appleton, goal; R Green and J Green, backs; R Bowker, J Duxbury, and J Whalley (captain), half-backs; W Rich and James Ellison, right wing; A W Dagnall, centre ; J Sims and J Ogden, left wing. Ribchester—B Walton. goal; T Callender and II Winckley,backs ; R Holden and J / Barton, half-backs: T Addisen and J Hallsall, right wing; ' L Fletcher and J Magerison, centre; T Walton and E Leem- ing, left wing. The umpires were; Messrs P Hestia (Ear- lestown) and T Martin (Ribchester), and Mr Joseph Cottam (of Blackburn) officiated as referee. NOTES BY THE WAY. ; The Earlestown club fairly recovered its lost prestige on , Saturday afternoon, when the team met Ribchester in the I Lancashire Cup Competition. The poor display of the Barlestonians in the previous two or three matches gave , rise to a very doubtful belief in their ability to pull off the cup tie, out the result of the contest exceeded the most , sanguine expectations. To beat Ribchester by ten goals to ; two in a cup tie is. indeed, a splendid performance. Every , member of the team worked with his fellow-players "like clockwork," while the "shooting" at goal was more ac- Curate and "deadly" than the Earlestoniana ever showed on . a previous occasion. The local lads had the advantage at ; every point and in every respect, and their score of ten goals t is the highest they ever attained in a single match. Their object should now be to attempt to beat that record. Another Lancashire cup tie was also decided in the die- , trict on Saturday. This was the Golborne v. Lytham , match, and was played on the ground of the former. The , general expectations of a bard and even contest between the two teams were fully realised. The excitement at one part ' Of the game reached a high pitch, and a serious dispute was threatened. However, the match was played out to the , end, and the result was a hard-won victory for Golborne by I two goals IO one. . _ . .

Tge Lytham club have since sent in a protest to the Lan- cashire Associttion on the ground that the Golborne club did not inform them previous to the match that they played on a publio ground. One of the rules of the Association is to the effect that if only one of the two clubs in any tie has a private ground the match must be played on that ground irrespective of which club has the choice of ground. Got- borne, it would appear, neglected to so inform their oppo- nents; hence the protest. This is the first point of the kind which has arisen for decision by the Association. At a meet- ing of the Association on Thursday evening It was decided that the tie should be played over again at Lytham. The second team of the Earlestown club journeyed to Manchester and met the second team of the Newton Heath Club. It is stated that several members of the first team were assisting the latter who won a good game by two goals to one.

The visit of the Earlestown Wanderers to Ashton to meet the " Stars " who are both " rising " by name and " rising " by play in football quarters, was an event of some interest to Ashton footballers. It was expected, at least in Earles- town, that the Wanderers would secure an easy victory, but the Stars made a good stand. They did not let their Earles- town visitors have matters all their own way, and scored two goals while the Wanderers notched four. The Ashton team showed that they possessed a good knowledge of the Association game and at times played very smartly. The Earlestown Rovers were beaten by St Thomas's (St Helens) to the extent of five goals to four; the match being played at St Helens. The Haydock St James's club secured a double victory on Saturday, over their opponents. The first team of the "Saint's" journeyed to Liverpool and met the Anfleld on their own ground, and a capital game resulted in a win for the Haydock men by four goals to one. The 2nd eleven of the same club visited Leigh and succeeded in defeating the Leigh Plank-lane team, after an even game, by two goals to one. In Rugby circles the Vulcan (first fifteen) gave the Sutton representatives a thrashing. This is to be partly accounted for by the fact that the Suttonites turned up with only eleven men, and were thus four men short. It is ques- tionable, however, if the four had been present, if the Vul- canites could have been prevented winning, for they. were in rare "fettle "and appeared capable of doing just what they liked with their opponents. 'Lle score at the I close of the allotted time was Vulcan, three goals, eight 'tries; Sutton, nil. The second teams met at Sutton and the Vulcan lot again won by one goal and five minor points, to seven minor points. The St Helens Club came into prominence on Saturday, when the first team secured a splendid victory over Blun- dellsands representatives. The St Helens team met the first team of the Blundellsands Club on the ground of the latter, and comment is needless when it is stated that the scores were :—St Helens, four goals, five tries, and three touch- downs; Blundellsands, three touchdowns. The Warrington, Golborne, Ormskirk, and Wallasey Clubs having joined the Liverpool and District Associatian, the committee recently met to draw the clubs named to take part in the first round of the cup competition. The result was as follows :—Wallasey v. Warrington ; Colborne v. Ormskirk. The first named in each instance has the choice of ground, and the ties have to be played off on or before November Bth. The results of other matches interesting to footballers in this district were the defeat of Bootle by Darwen in the Lan- cashire cap ties by nine goals to one ; the victory of Liver- pool Stanley over Southport by four goals to two; the de- feat of Birkenhead by the Liverpool Ramblers by one goal to none ; the thrashing administered to Everton (the Liver- pool cup holders) by the Crewe Alexandra, who won a one- sided game by eight goals to two ; and the victory of the Liverpool Cambrian over the Liverpool St Peter's by three goals to none. The Warrington Association Club had their second fix- ture on Saturday, and were again beaten, but this tiara not as badly as in their previous match. The Chester St Os- wald's were responsible for five goals to the Warrington team one. The Warrington men are a new club, and have a few promising men, and with plenty of practice they will no doubt, develop into good players. The Rugbyltes made a draw with Failsworth (first), and the Warrington (second) at home secured a victory by two tries to one, Dumbell and Appleton being well to the front. The second round of the Scottish Challenge Cup was played off on Saturday afternoon, with the following results: —Queen's Park v Thistle, four goals to one; Glasgow Rangers v 3rd Lanark Volunteers, two goals each—a draw; Arthurlie v Abercern, the former won by one to nil; Vale of Leven v Central County, the former winning by 14 gals to nil; Pollockshields Athletic v Cowlairs, the former win- ning by two goals to one; Kilmarnock Athletic a Maybole, the first-named club winning by four goals to one; Nor- thern v G-ranton, Northern winning by three goals to one ; Dumbarton Athletic at King's Park, the former winning by three goals to two ; Arbroath v Abercorn, Arbroath winning by seven goals to one ; Ayr v Cumnock. the former winning by five goals to nil; St Mirren v Johnstone, the former winning by three goals to nil; Wishaw Swifts v Airdriehill, the first-named club winning by eight goals to two; Queen of the South- Wanderers a sth Kirkcudbright Volunteers, the former win- ning by four goals to three; Thornliebank v Port Glasgow Athletic, the first-named club winning by one goal to nil ; Battlefield Possilpark, the former winning by three goals to one ; Cambuslang v Airdrieonians, two goals each— & draw.

_ On Saturday, at Derby, the Midland beat the Long Eaton Rangers by four goals to one; at Nottingham, Notts de- feated Sheffield by six to two ; Halliwell beat Aston Unity by five to two; at Birmingham, Bolton Wanderers beat Aston Villa by two to ens; at Wolverhampton the Wanderers defeated Birmingham Excelsior by two to none; at Nottingham, Notts Forest beat Bolton Association by five goals to one; at Birmingham. St George's and Stafford- road (Wolverhampton), played a drawn game, one goal each.; at Sheffield, Heeley beat Rotherham by three to one; and Wednesday defeated Meaborough by five to one; at Barnes, Old Westminaters beat Barnes by five to one.
A fire broke out on Wednesday morning at Messrs. Rum- nev and Co.'s mill, Stebbins Lane, Ramabottom, whereby thunage was done to the amount of about £2,000.

THE REFORM AGITATION. LORD HARTINGTON IN ROSSENDALE, On Saturday the full strength of Liberalism in Rossen- dale was put forth in support of the Government in their resistance to the Conservative Peers. Many thousands of working men who are at present deprived of the franchise assembled at various places in the valley and marched thence in procession to Riwtenstall, where a meeting second only in importance and interest to the great Liberal gather- ing at the Pomona Gardens was held. The day was fine, and holiday was held in nearly the whole ef the district represented at the meeting. The men of Rawtenstall were, of course, present in great force, and they were joined by large processions from Haslingden. Stacksteads, Bacup, Lumb, Water, Waterfoot, and other places. In the lama.' "vale" there ate' it is said, at least 60,000 inhabitants, of whom not more than 3,000 possess the franchise. When the Franchise Bill is passed there will be, on a moderate computation, at least nine or ten thousand added to the number of voters. On the flags carried by the proceesionists the prevailing sentiment was expressed in unmistakable terms. "Justice to the Two Millions" and'" We will have the vote" were frequently repeated. A large axe, on which was painted "By this sign we conquer," was borne by a man en horseback. The reform struggle of sixty years ago was recalled by the presence of a number of men some of whom had actually been present at Peterloo. They car- ried a banner inscribed with the words, "When we were young the Tories ruled." Following these veterans came a number of plump, hearty, fresh-looking lads, on whose ensign was written, " When we were young the Liberals ruled." The "TOry loaf" and the "Liberal loaf" , were also displayed, and it should be needless to say that the former was a very diminutive loaf indeed, whilst the latter might have served a Brobdiugnagian for breakfast. There was not much of hostility to the Peers displayed. The most signficant symbol of that feeling was a black flag which bore the inscription "In memoriam. Sacred to the memory of the House of Lords." This, however, was not taken seriously by the crowd, which moon fell to laughing at the appearance of a number of men with "big heads" such as will be plentiful on the stage during the pantomime season. The one who occupied the front of the carriage was very well got up as Lord Sallibory "bound in the chains of self-interest." Another performer, who might have been dispensed with, wore the sort of disguise which another pub- lic character, who has been known to many generations as Bottom the Weaver, assumed for a time at the court of Theseus. Others were got up to represent the Prime Minister and Mr Bright. A large number of women took part in the procession. The principal meeting was held in a marquee capable of holding 10,000 people, and it was crowded to excess. The usual Liberal songs were sung whilst the crowd awaited the arrival of the chair- man, and it was noticeable that they were sung in a man- ner which showed great aptitude for music on the part of large numbers of those present. Lord Hartington on en- tering the marquee with Mr E Ashworth, Sir J Lee, Mr Gratton, Sir U Kay-Shuttleworth, and other gentlemen, was received with enthusiastic and prolonged cheering. His Lordship's speech was of the moderate but firm style that has distinguished him since he, then a young member of the House, discharged the deity of moving the famous resolu- tion which overthrew the Cabinet of Lord Derby in 1859.. He protested against the demand of the Conservatives that the Franchise Bill should be hung up until they could be satisfied with regard to the scheme of redistribution. Lord Salisbury's proposals, he said, were utterly destqute of the elements of compromise. The Government would "wel- come the possibility of a reasonable agreement which should be honourable to both sides," but in the meantime it was their duty to maintain an unbroken front. Lord Hartington refused to enter into minute calculations as to the possible effect of the Redistribution Bill on the fortunes of one party or the other. As showing the futility of such calculations, he called attention to the fact that whilst in 1874 the Conservatives nearly swept the whole re- presentation ot Lancashire, in 1880, with precisely the same constituencies, the Liberals gained four of the country and at least ten of the borough seats. With this result be- fore their eyes, it was not worth while to stop to discuss the opinions of election agents as to party prospects. Lord Har- tington Brooke for nearly an hour, and was throughout warmly applauded. Mr Grafton was listened to throughout with close attention, but the more "advanced" portion of the vast audience broke out into clamours of delight when Mr Peter itylands came forward. The hon. member was ad- vised to "(live it 'em hot ;" but he refused to proceed forth- with to the demolition of the Peers, and convinced the as- sembly that there were "constitutional means" already in existence whereby the resistence of the Tory majority might be overcome. A resolution declaring the firm intention of the meeting to support the Government was carried without one audible or visible dissentient, and the assembly disper- sed well satisfied with themselves and their leaders. CONSERVATIVE DEMONSTRATION IN MID- CHESHIRE.

The Conservatives of Mid-Cheshire spent a very plea sant afternoon in Tatton Park, on Saturday. Their noble host and former member, Lord Egerton of Tatton, threw open his beautiful gardens, and in other ways made suit- able provision for the amusement of his guests. There were, it is true, no fireworks promised, but refreshments were provided in tents in the park, and a brass band from Manchester was in attendance. Lord Harrowby and Sir R A Cross were expected, but neither gentleman was able to be present. The gathering round the platform when the speak- ing began was by no means large. In fact it is questionable If at any time the audience numbered more than a couple of thousand, and, as a considerable number had journeyed from Manchester by special train, the number of electors from the district must have been very small. Lord Eg-r- -ton presided over the meeting, and he was supported on the platform by Sir H Holland, M P, Mr P E Warburton, M P, the Hon Alan de Tatton Egerton, MP, Mr W H Houlds- worth, M P, Sir R Brooke, the Hon Jocelin Amherst, Sir Philip Mainwaring, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Colonel France- Hayhurst, Major Townshend, Major Hill, Mr J Brooks, the Conservative candidate for the division, and a large num- ber of other gentlemen.—The Secretary (Mr L Bentley), announced that letters had been received from Sir R A Cross, the Farl of Harrowbv, Lord Delamere, Lord Stanley of Alderley, Sir Philip Egerton, Mr W C Brooks, M 13, and others.

lord EGERTON received a hearty greeting on rising to open the proceedings. He said they had met to protest against two things. First of all they were met to protest against any interference with the constitutional and inde- pendent action of the House of Lords—(applause); and, in the second place, they were met to urge the Government to bring in a complete scheme of reform, and also to say that the House of Lords was justified in the attitude it had taken in refusing to deal with the franchise—agreeing as it did with a wide extension of the franchise—without a complete scheme of redistribution. (Applause.) He believed that if they did not make a stand now they would never be able to make one under more favourable condicions. On the one side they had a policy of force and franchise, and on the other a policy of reason and redistribution. (Applaese.) Mr. Piers Egerton Warburton, M.P., clawed the following resolution :—" That tais meeting, while approving of the extension of the household franchise to the coun- ties, heartily endorses the constitutional action of the House of Lords in refusing to pace the Franchise Bill until a complete and fair Redistrilan- tion Bill is laid before the House of Commons and the country." When they asked a Liberal bow it was they did not dissolve and appeal to the country, they were told that it could not be done because they wished first of all to pass. this Reform Bill, a measure which they said was one of the first measures in their programme when they came into office. If that was 80 why had they delayed it till now ? Surely after waiting three or four years they could have waited another month or two until they could have brought in a fair Redistribution Bill which would have been accepted by the House of Lords, and thus have saved all this com- motion. (Applause.) The fact was that all this excitement about reform had been got up by the Government to hide their disasters and the failure of all their other measures. (Applause.) Sir Henry Holland, M.P. seconded the resolution, and said the cry that the peers were against the people had been raised. The peers could not be against the people until the voice of the people had been well and clearly expressed. When that voice had been clearly expressed they would find that the peers had always yielded to it ; but the opinion of the people could only be ascertained by a dissolution and general election. (Applause.) The Hon Alan de Tatton Egerton, M.P.. supported the resolution. He said they were told by the Prime Minister, in his speech on the third reading of the Franchise Bill, that there might be a quarrel between the House of Lords and the House of Commons. It took two people to quarrel, and he was quite certain that the House of Lords was not quarrellin4 with anyone. (Applause.) Mr W 11 Honldsworth, M.P., also spoke in support of the resolution. It had been argued with a certain amount of plausibility that the House of Lords had no right to inter- fere in the matter. He agreed, however, with Lord Salis- bury that this was the matter of all others that the House of Lords should interfere with, because it was a matter that affected the members of the House of Commons, and the members of the House of Commons ought not to try their own case. (Applause.) After some remarks from Mr J Brooks, the resolution was carried with a few dissentients, and a vote of thanks hav- ing been accorded to Lord Egerton, the proceedings termin- ated.

A large gathering was held on Saturday at Edgeworth, near Bolton, in support of the Franchise Bill, and to in- augurate the establishment of a new Liberal Association for the district. About 4,000 persons were present.—MrJ IC Cross, M.P., Under-Secretary of State for India, referring to the franchise agitation, emphatically denied the statement made by the Conservative speakers that the question of the fran- chise did not agitate the public mind previous to the general election. They heard now that the Conservatives were anxious to give the people the franchise; but when Sir Richard Cross, in Scotland, called it a wretched bill, and anther member said that it was a miserable abortion, could they think that the bulk of the Tory party wished to see such a miserable thing passed into law? Lord Salisbury described the House of Lords as a vacuum brake, and he could not have better described it. What was a vacuum but emptiness, and what was a brake but obstruction, which sometimes meant damage. One of the most important demonstrations yet held to condemn the action of the House of Lords in reference to the Franchise Bill was made by the Liberals of the Eastern Division of the West Riding on Saturday. The weather was very fine, and everything favoured the imposing gathering of which Woodhouse Moor was the scene. The detachments from the different districts who intended to take part in the procession assembled by the side of the Leeds Town Halt.

The line of the procession was brilliant, the numerous ban- ners and flags making a streak of bright colour which the brilliant sunshine helped to make very stribYing. There were 10.000 persons in the procession, and its progress through crowded streets was watched! with great interest. Upon the Moor three large- platforms accommodated the speakers and their supporters, and in front of these the de- monstrationists were drawn up as they reached the spot. The other spectqators pressed around tham, extending up the slope in front and far back upon the level ground be- yond. When the speaking commenced it was estimated that not fewer than 80,000 persons were present. The prin- cipal speakers were Mr W E Forster, MP, Mr Jelin Mor- ley, MP, Sir JRamedeo, MP, Sir A Fairbsirn, MP. Mr J Barran, M P, Mr Herbert Gladstone, M P, the Hon. Itobt. MilneS, and Mr Frank Lockwood, Cr C. Speaking at Sunderland, Sir Purer Herschel), the Solicitor-General, said that in the North they bad for years, been convinced of the necessity for the Franchise Bill and of its justice: The Government were he added; thoroughly in earnest in the matter, and the more speedily the people mad. their voices known ow the question the sooner the measure would pass into law.

An open-air demonstration of Liberals were heidat Ash- ton-under-Lyne on Saturday arternoon. Mr Jacob Bright, M.P., Mr Leaks, M.P., and Mr Summers, M.P., spoke in sup- port of resolutions approving of the Franchise Bill as a good measure in itself, and condemning the Lords for throwing out the bill, which had for its object the extension of popular representation and declared the time had come when the power of the hereditary House to nullify acts of the re- presentative Chamber shouhd. be taken away. A Liberal demonstration in support of the Franchise Bill was held on Saturday afternoon at Buckley, in the heart of the mining district of Flintshire• A procession was formed, consisting of about 1,000 persons, preceded and followed by bands of music. The meeting was addressed by Mr John Robertson and Sir Robert Cunliffe, Bart. Resolutions con- demning the action of the House of Lords in rejecting the Franchise Bill were passed. A Liberal meeting at Chester-le-Street was addressed by Lord Durham, and one at Jarrow by Mr Alderman Storey, M.P.,and others were held at South Shields, Ashton-wader- Lyne, Bathgate, Buckley, Leicester, Nottingham, Montrose, Peebles, Prudhoe, and mazy other places. On the side of the Opposition Lord Lonsdale threw open Lowther Park, where the speakers included Mr William. Lowther. M P, Earl Cadogan, Mr Cavendish Bentinck, MT, antl Mr James Lowther, M.P. Sir Harding. Giffard ad- dressed his constituents at Launceston upon the great ques- tion of the day. At Okehampton„in North Devon, the chief speaker was Sir Massey Lopes, MP. At Wistow, the %,ark of Sir Henry Raiford. near Leicester, Lord Bury, Lord Bury, Lord Newatk, and Mr Pell, MT, were present: A letter from the Duke of Rutland was read at a franchise demonstration at Wistow, Leicestershire, on Saturday. In this the Duke said: Mr Gladstone and Mr Bright are wrong when they say we are opposed to the Franchise Bill. We I are not; but, beyond this, individually,! have a strong wish to see it passed, and the labourer enfranchised, because I am convinced we should then obtain protection; the in- dustry of the country would again rise from its ashes, and the working man, insead of being deprived of his wages by foreign competition, would again find remunerative employ- meat.

A demonstration in favour of the Franchise Bill was held on Monday evening in the Stretford Town Hall, under the presidency of Mr Reuben Spencer. Mr Leake, M.P., who was the principal speaker, expressed the opinion that the Lords would, under the influence of the Queen and the pres- sure of the people, give way and pass the Franchise Bill. Resolutions expressing confidence in the Government and urging them to press forward the Franchise Bill, and of con- fidence in Messrs Lake and Agnew, were unanimously passed. Mr B Armitage and Mr Arthur Arnold delivered their annual addresses to their constituents on Monday evening, at the Town Hall, Salford. The Mayor (Alderman Makin- sou) presided. Mr William Mather moved a resolution ap- pealing to the Prime Minister not to consent to any com- promise with the House of Lords that would postpone the passing of the measure in its present form beyond the ensu- ing session. Mr Frank S Phillips seconded the motion, which passed with only one dissentient. . .

Mr dhamberlain srls present at a crowded meeting at Hanley on Wednesday night. Replying to a resolution welcoming him and assuring Mr Gladstone and' Her Majesty's Government, through him, of its unabated con- fidence and support, the right hon. gentleman said that the Tories had lighted a flame throughout the length and breadth of the land which would never be quenched until two "mil- lions of capable citizens had received the final sanction of the law to the rights which are now unjustly withheld from them." If the controversy was much prolonged he thought there wonld be other abuses besides a restricted franchise which would be cast into the crucible to be purified as by are before the treat which had been engendered was suffered to cool down. He argued, from the evidence of recent meetings, that the in• dustrial classes of the country supported the Government in this matter of the franchise almost to a man. He did not believe that the Tories would be able to divert public opinion by Saturday meetings, " cakes and ale," fireworks, and juggling ; and though great landowners were better en- gaged in opening their parks to the public Haan enclosing commons, the attempts to get working-men to sell their birthright for a mess of pottage would prove a dismal fail- ure. As to the Franchise Bill, he said that the tardy con- version of the Tories proved that they were not sincere. Lord Salisbury's proposals were so arrogant that they pointed not to compromise but to a surrender of the Liberal party. Those who knew Mr Gladstone knew that having put his hand to the plough he would not turn aside. Mr B Armitage M.P., and Mr Arthur Arnold M.P., ad- dressed a crowded and enthusiastic meeting of their con- stituents du Wednesday evening, in the Cobden Hall, Broughton. Mr Jesse Bryant occupied the chair. A reso- lution was pasaed calling upon the Government not to con- sent to any compromise on the franchise question which will postpone the passing of the measure in its present form be- yond the autumn session. A resolution in favour of the abolition of the House of Lords was proposed by, Mr JOseph Kay, who rose for the purpose in the body of the hall, and was carried unanimously and with load cheers. Lord Randolph Churchill, addressing a Conservative meeting at Carlisle on Wednesday evening, said that Lord Hartington in his speech at Rawtenstall had "chucked up the sponge" by justifying the action of the House of Lords. The Peers were willing to extend the franchise if a guaran- tee was given of an intention to remove the frightful elec- toral anomalies which were known to exist, and on a dis- tinct indication being given of the character and outlines of the redistribution scheme. The noble Lord was of opinion that the present Parliament was "played out, worthless, and effete," and that its dissolution would witness Mr Glad- stone's retirement from public life. On Wednesday evening the Earl of Harrowby addressed a meeting of the Liverpool Working-rnen'S Conservative Association upon the position taken by the House of Lords with reference to the Franchise Bill. He contended that despite the clamour which was being made against the House of Lords, he bad no fear for its future existence, and he claimed for it that, in having the courage to say "No" to the demands of the Government when it was absolutely necessary that "No" should be said,it had deserved well of the country. The House of Lords was not to be forced by any threat to pass the Franchise Bill without a Redistribu- tion Bill, which latter, he considered, it was impossible the Government could pass next year. It is understood that after the debate on the Address at the opening of Parliament the Government will ask the House of Lords to adjourn while the Franchise Bill is pass- ing through the House of Commons. The first adjourn- ment will be fora fortnight or three weeks._

Sir William Harcourt addressed a crowded meeting of his constituents at Derby on Thursday night, and was enthusi- astically cheered. He accused Lord Salisbury of rejecting the Franchise Bill, not because he wanted a Redistribution Bill with it, but because he distrusted the people, and knew well that the more there were admitted to the vote, the more reforms could be carried. He denied the right of the House of Lords to say when a dissolution should take place.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT PRESCOT.
div.p: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT PRESCOT.

A meeting of Conservatives resident in Prescat and dis- trict was held in the Assembly-rooms, Prescot, on Tuesday evening. There was a large attendance. Mr W L Evans presided, and there were also present Messrs E Whitley, M.P., W Pilkington, HP. D A Willis, J Edwards• Moss, J Birchall, C Collins, J D Banks, T A Evans, A F Erans, F Green. H. Cross, Lockwood, E Draper, H Owen, J Black- wick, S Green, W Halsall, J Smith, C Collins, Jas Custin, Dr Gorst, Dr Hall, and Dr Packer.

The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, said the object of their meeting was to give their cordial support to the House of Lords in the course they had recently taken with regard to the Franchise Bill. (Applause.) Mr Edward Whitley, M.P., who was received with cheers, moved—" That this meeting most cordially approves of the action of the House of Lords in delaying the passing of the Representation of the People Bill until the Government scheme for the redistribution of seats is before Parliament and the country." Mr Whitley said he had always felt as a Lancashire man, that if there was anybody in the consti- tuency of this country who recognised and detected the mis- takes and fallacies it was the constituency of the great county of Lancashire. (Hear, hear.) He felt that the great object which those who lead political parties in this country should have in view was to impress upon the mass of their adherents to do unto others as they would be done by themselves. He could not help feeling that the days in which they lived were in some respects a critical time. They were told that they had arrived at a crisis in their national history. (Hear. hear.) If he believed any of their time honoured parts of their constitution were really assailed he should feel great anxiety in regard to the future of their country. He believed that the real essentials of the greatness of the country depended upon the mainten- ance of the time-honoured institutions of Queen, Lords and Commons. (Applause.) It was now the evident object of the Liberal and Radical party to disparage the persons and the work of the members of the House of Lords. It had been said that the Conservative party disregarded the mas- ses of the people. Ile should be unworthy, as a represen- tative of the working classes, if he believed for one moment that the course the Conservative party took was hostile to the working-men of the country. Mr Gladstone said that the object of the franchise bill was to enfranchise two mil- lions of their fellow-countrymen. He believed he spoke the convictions of the Conservative party when he said that they gladly hailed such strength to the constitution as the admission of two millions of their fellow-countrymen. (Applause.) But they should bear in mind that in an extension of the franchise all interests. classes, and trades should be represented —(hear, hear) —for it was only right and just that every interest in a great industrial community like this should be fairly represented; and therefore he believed that it was essential in any extension of the franchise that every I trade, every business, and every locality should be fairly ' respresented. (Hear' hear.) When the franchise bill went to the House of Lords it had been condemned in its present shape by the Conservative members of the House of Com- mons. The House of Lords was not antagonistic to the in- terest of the people of the country. The House of Lords took the view of the Conservative members of the House of ' Commons, and believed that a redistribution bill to be ma- nipulated by Mr Chamberlain would be most dangerous te the interests of the country. (Applause.) The motion was seconded by Mr J Edwards-Moss, and carried unanimously, as was also the following resolution, on the motion of Mr James Croston, seconded by Mr J Birchen :—" That the course of political events, at home land abroad,since the commencement of the late session of Parliament, unite accounts for, and fully justifies, the con- tinually increasing confidence which Conservatives have in I the Marquis of Salisbury and Sir Stafford Northcote, the leaders of the party." _ .
A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the meet- ing.

div.head: FOOTTIALL
div.p: FOOTTIALL

".* Secretaries of Foo`ball Oluos are requested to note that reports of matchee played on Saturday must be sent to the bead office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

I EARLESTOWN ALBIONS V. WHITE STARS played on the ground of the former, and resulted in a victory for the Albions by eight goals to two. HATDOCE ST. JAMES'S (2ND TEAM) V. PLANE LANE, LEIGH (IST TRAM.)—Played on the ground of the latter, on Saturday, and resulted in a win for the visitors by two goals to one. ANFIELD V. HAYDOCE ST. JAMES'S.—This match was played on the ground of the former' on Saturday, and re- sulted in a victory for St James's by four goals and two dis- puted to one. , RUNCORN (2d Team) • OUGHTRINGTON. Played at Oughtrington on Saturday, when the Runcorn second fif- teen won a espied game by one try (Janion) and two minor points, to Oughtrington one ninor point. LONGFORD EXCELSIOR V. WARRINGTON RANGERS.— This match was played on the ground of the former, on Saturday, and resulted in a victory for the Excelsior by one goal (dropped off the field by Daniels), one try (obtained by Daniels),and nine minor points, to five minor points.Speak- man and Hackett also played very well for Longford. RUNCORN RECREATION • ST HELENS (2nd Team.) The Runcorn Recreation paid a visit to St Helens to play off their fixture with St Helens 2nd, who were assisted by Valentine, Gregson, Hankinson, and Robinson, of the St Helens Recreation. The Recreation's captain won the toss, and the ball was set in motion by the St Helens captain, and play was kept up in the home twenty-frve until close on half-time, when Whinyates made a grand run from half- way flag and secured a try for the Recreation, which W Riley converted into a neat goal. Half-time now being called, the ball was again set rolling by the Recreation's captain. Play ensued in neutral ground for a short time, and by a smart rush the Recreation obtained a touch-in- goal. Soon after the ball was kicked out, Valentine got pos- session and ran in a try for St Helens; no goal was the re- sult. After being returned Valentine soon obtained another try, but failed to add the major point. After St Helens ob- tained a dead ball time was called, leaving the Recreation, after a pleasant game, winners by a goal and a touch-in-goal to St Helens two tries, a disputed try, and a clead ball. Roncoux • WERNETH.—These old opponents faced each other on Saturday, when representative teame were planed on the field. Armstrong started the ball, and from the reply by Hugh Hughes a general forward rush was made up LO the Werneth goal-line. Page here fought his way over, no goal being kicked. After Spence had dropped out, Dean and Andrews initiated a line dribble, in which the whole front rank joined, when Andrews grounded the ball behind the posts, W Hughes placing a goal from the try. Restart- ing from centre, the Werneth forwards made a raid into the home quarter, from which Speakman and Hughes by quick exchanges, soon assumed the aggressive, and during central play Wright made a most determined effort to force a pas- sage. Changing ends the ball soon got into the front ranks, where Andrews tackled Brielev. Broady here made a capi- tal run up to the goal-line, where a sharp struggle ensued. Directly afterwards Hugh Hughes was rewarded for sterling play by a try, as the result of a series of exchanges between Wright and Speakman. Its value was not, however, increa- sed. The visitors now awakened and made a raid into the home quarter, when Runcorn were compelled to save. Splendid exchanges by Broady, Speakman, and Andrews, which created much excitement, were the means of again putting the Werneth lines in danger, but a claim for a try was overruled, a capital contest ending in favour of Run- corn by one goal and two tries, to Werneth one touchdown. Teams i—Rrincorn : W Hughes, back; H Hughes (cap- tain), Broady, and Speakman, threequarter-backs W Wright and Andrews, half-backs; Lightburn, Clarke, Lewis, Cex, Maestri, Dean, Barns, Page, and Gatley, forwards. Werneth Futon, back; Myers, Mills, and Greenfield, threequarter-backs ; Spence mid Oreewood, half-backs J

The Duke of Cambridge inspected the forts and garrison of Queenstown Harbour on Tuesday, and subsequently re- turned to Cork, his departure being marked by the firing of a royal salute from the guardship Revenge and forts.—On Wednesday morning the Duke of Cambridge left Cork for England, yid. Dublin, and was cheered on his departure by a number of civilians assembled at the railway station. FATAL ACCIDENT INMANCHESTER..—Two men, named Raw- linson and Russell, were on Wednesday afternoon seriously injured by the fall of a crane which is being employed in the erection of offices in Hunt's Bank, for the use of the Lanca- shire and Yorkshire Rtilway Company. A heavy piece of stone was being raised at the time the crane gave way. Rus- sell died during the evening at the Royal Infirmary to which both men were taken.

BAPTIST UNION.—Tbe autumnal session of the Baptist Union commenced at Bradford on Tuesday, there being nearly one thousand delegates present. The proceedings throughout the day were entirely devoted to the considera- tion of the work of the Baptist Missionary Society. Reso- lutions were passed approving the action of the committee in extending the operations of the society in China and on the Congo, and pledging the Union to raise additional funds for this purpose. In the afternoon the Rev Dr Landells, of ,Edinburgh, preached to four thousand persons in St. George's Hall, and in the evening Mr Isaac Holden, M.P , presided over an enthusiastic miseionary meeting in the same hall.

EXTRAARDINARt LIBEL CASE.—Mr Sam Taylor, barrister, on whose application a summons was recently issued against Mr Edward Brooke, of Manchester and Conway, for publish- ing a libel concerning Mr Wm. Agnew, M.P., whom he ac- cused of having expedited the death of the late Mr Sam Mendel by putting an execution into bin house and remov- ing all the furniture with the exception of the bed upon which Mr Mendel was lying, on Wednesday applied to the stipendiary magistrate of the city of Manchester for a sum- mons against Mr Brooke for libelling Mr Wm. Lockett Agnew in a letter to the Manchester newspapers, and in this letter Mr Brooke withdrew what he had said about Mr W Agnew. M.P., but asserted that the proceedings against Mr Mendel were taken by "a Mr Agnew." Mr Taylor said he would be able to show upon the hearing of the summons that Mr Wm. Lockett Agnew was the gentleman referred to as "a Mr Agnew," and he added that there was no founda- tion whatever for the statement of Mr Brooke, the fact being that Mr Agnew's family had always treated Mr Mendel with kindness and generosity. Mr Headlam acceded to the ap- plication, and fixed Friday for the hearing of the case, that being the day upon which the summons issued on behalf of Mr Wm. Agnew is returnable.
GENERAL NEWS.

Lord Portarfington is said to have soM three of his an dykes for £30,400. M. Gladstone has promised to cut'-tho first sod of the Wirral Railways next Wednesday. The- number of visitors to the Health Exhibition has now reacked three and a quarter millions. Passenger traffic was commenced on the Inner Circle UndergroNnd Railway, London, on Monday. About 1,000 children were absent on Monday from thee Aberdeen Board echooltr through a measle epidemic. At a meeting of the Royal East Berke Agricultural An sociatien, held on Tuesday night, Mr Walter, M.P., intima- ted his intention of not again offering himself awa candidate. for Berkshire. A warrant as bean issued against John P. Smarli onna.- ger of the Dudley, Sedgley, and Wolverhampton Tramways, who is alleged to have absconded with a large amount of [her eompany's money. Mr Edward Brooke, of Paho Hall, Conway, who libelled Mr Agnew, has written stating that be finclobe con- fused Mr Agnew with another person. He bitterly regrets the injury he haw done. LIVERPOOL CANAL MyETERY.—A lock had to be drled en Saturday, and in the mud at the bottom the poor girl's, rag- ged raiment was found. Unfortunately, this discovery affords no clue to thomanner in which the deceased met her fate.

Dormu EximrnoN.—A double- execution took place 111 Newgate Prison on ltheday, the eniprits being Thomas Henry Orrock, the murderer of Pollee-constable Cole at Dalton, and Thomas Harris, who was convicted of the murder of his wife at Kilburn. Berry, of Bradford, was the executioner. There were twenty runners on Tuesday for the Cesar witch Stakes, which were won by J' Hammond 's St- Gatien, Lord Rosebery's Polemic being second. and Mt Lefevres Archiduc third. Wood was the successful jockey: Wall briaging in Polemic, while Archiduc was ridden by 1r Archer.

THE COUNTESS AND HER CATS—Some excitement wall' caused in the streets of Dover on Saturday night through the eccentric behaviour of the Countess de is Torre. she Pro- menaded the streets accompanied by a number of her pots, and solreat was the mob that followed her that she repeat' edly had to take refuge in the shops. Emma ACCIDEN7L —An accident occurred at Ports- mouth on Tuesday afternoon, resulting in the partial der traction of a bridge, over which passengers cross the rail- way, a short distance from the town railway Station. It is supposed that the train was backed by mistake into a siding, and, coming into contact with the bridge, carried the end away.

LOS, OF A STIAMEN AND CREW.—A • Lloyd's telegram from Foochowfoo, dated Tuesday, 5 p.m., states that the British steamer Miramar, from Yokohama for Hong Kong, foundered at sea, and all hands were lost except two Chinese. The Miramar was a steamer of 1,190 tons gross. built at Port Glasgow in 1880, and owned by Messrs Rae- , burn and Verel, of Glasgow. FATAL RIOT.—TWENTY•TWO PERSONS KILLED.—A eerie us affray has occured at Salines, on the Mexican frontier. Senor Santos. the Alcalde of the town, having made him- self obnoxious to the people, they mobbed the Court-house- The police offered a stout resistence, but the mob over-Pow- ering them, seized the Court-house and killed the Alcalde. The Chief of the police and 20 other persons were also killed. DWELLINGS OF THE Pooa.—The Bishop of Peterborough, in his opening address at the Diocesan Conference, at Leices- ter on Tuesday, said he was thankful for the deep intereat which had been aroused in the dwellings of the poor, for it was impossible that human beings could live in abodes 5t only for beasts. and conduct themselves like Christians. Legislation could not improve them en masse, They re- quired individual Christian efforts. AOCIDENT AT A SHOOTING GALLERY.—A quarry mane named John Jones, living at Bethesda, North Wales, was shot through the head on Saturday night by a farm labenrer named Isaac Hughes, and died hal a few minutes. The pair were on friendly terms, and the discharge of the weapon, which happened in a shooting gallery during a slight struggle between Hughes and the proprietress, is bee lieved to have been purely accidental. In the meantime be is in custody. Two. LIVES LOST OVER A BITNCH OF GRA.PES.—Reeentli a boy climbed a tree near San Felice. at Bologna, to steal a bunch of grapes. The owner caught sight ef him, but the frightened boy was only ieduced to come down by a gentle- man whe happened to be shooting near the spot. Scarcely bad he touched the ground when the owner dealt him a blow on the head with a spade, killing him on the spot. The gentleman thereupon fired at the murderer, inflicting a mor- tal wpund. Mns. BRYANT, who has the honour of being the first lady to obtain the degree of Doctor of Science in connection witia the London University (the only university whose degrees are open to women), was on Saturday formally presehted with the hood and gown of that degree, at the North London Collegiate School for Girls, Camden-road, of which college Mrs Bryant was originally a pupil. After the ceremony a large number of the students celebrated the occasion by a fanny dress ball. MILL FIRE.—DAMAGES, .220 000.—On Saturday a fire was discovered in the mill of Messrs Pethoan and Sons, cotter' spinners and manufacturers, Cawdor.street, Moses Gate, near Bolton. Two firemen, James Entwistle, Thynee-street, and Wm. Dawson, Lorne-street, were injured, the first through a stone window-sill falling upon his arensi and the latter by a portion of the spinning-room wall catching him in its fall. The damage is estimated at from £15,000 to £20,000, which is covered by insurance. About fifty workpeople are thrown out of employment. LORD SALISBER‘'S MOVEMENTS.—Lord Salisbury left Blythswood on Saturday for St. Mary's Tower, near Dun- keld, to remain for a few days the guest of Lord John Man- ners. At several stations cheers mingled with groans were given for the noble marquis. Lord Salisbury declined to receive an address at Perth on the ground that railway sta- tions were unsuitable for the purpose, and he has also inti- mated that he will be unage to accede to the request of the Aberdeen Conservatives that he should deliver an address• during his stay in the neighbourhood. SHOOTING & FARMER'S Doo.—At the Bolton County Court, on Wednesday. a Horwich farmer recovered five guineas from Henry Blackwell, a gamekeeper, who had shot the plaintiff's collie dog whilst it was in pursuit of a hare on land over which his employer, Mr Ainsworth. had game rights. The judge held that defendant's plea of having shot the dog to save the hare's life would have held good if the hare had been in danger, but he considered it very improbable that a collie coald catch a hare in a direct chase. POISONINCi CASE.—Mary Ann Eliza Biker, 16 years of age, in the service of Mr Browning, a stockbroker, was on Tuesday charged at the Greenwich Police Court with having administered a quantity of sulphate of copper to her mistress with inteht to murder her. Dr Duped, of Westminster Hospital, gave in evidence the results of his analysis, which proved the existence of a quantity of sulphate of copper in the sample of liquor labelled as having been given to Mns Browning. The case was further remanded.— On Wednesday Baker was committed for trial by the Green- wich police magistrate. OVER NIAGARA IN A RUBBER BALL—Mr Oliver Wor- maid, a fresco painter, of Buffalo, has announced bis inten- tion of going over the falls in a "rubber ball " for a purse of 51,000. as soon as the necessary arrangements are corn- plated. The ball is to he 15ft. in diameter, and is to be made of rubber three-quarters of an inch thick, covered with closely-braided tarred rope. Compressed air is to be in. jested into the ball, which will be hermetically sealed, and Mr Wormald says he can live in it for ten minutes if neces- sary. Mr Wormaid is about 35 years old, and was born in London. It is considered probable he will die at. Niagara. MEETING OF PARLIAMENT.—LIBERAL CIRCHLARS.--. "10, Downing-street, Oct. 3, 1884.—Sir,—Her Majesty has bees pleased to appoint Thursday, Oct. 23, for the meeting of Parliament, and it is intended to proceed at tbe earliest mement with important and pressing business. I trust it may suit your convenience to be present. —I have the hon- our to be, sir, your most faithful servant, WE Goansoona." —Lord Granville has issued the following circular to his supporters in the House of Lords :—" 18, Carlton House Terrace, Oct. 4, 1884.—My Lord,—The meeting of Perna. ment having been fixed for the 23rd inst., I beg leave on behalf of her Majesty's Government to express my hope that it may be convenient to you to attend on that day. Your lordship's presence will be especially important when the Franchise Bill is brought to the House of Lords.—l-have the honour to be your lordship's humble and obedient ser- vant, Grrearyntae." LIVERPOOL UNIVERSITY, COLLEGE —Lord Derby presided on Saturday at the opening of the new session of Univer- sity College, Liverpool. Among others present were Mr Sarreuel Smith, M.P., and Mr J A Pictoo, M.P. Special in- terest attached to the occasion as this is the jubilee year of, the Liverpool School of Medicine' which is connected with University College as a medical fazulty.—Professor. Mac- Cunn, M.A., delivered an address in which he indicated the work the college had before it, illustrating his remarks from the experience of Scotch naiversities.—Lord Derby, who delivered the prizes, said other engagements and other occupations, which they all knew had kept him away from Liverpool and from Lancashire, had compelled him during the last year or twcevery much to neglect those other duties which otherwise it was his pleasure to discharge. The col- lege was opened in January, 1382, and its progress since , that date had beep steady, rapid, and continuous. The last important event was the amalgamation ol the medical school with the College. The medical school, which had behind it 'an honourable record of hali a century of useful and valu- able service, had consented to begin a new existence as the medical faculty of the College. There was no reason to doubt that the College hal received and was receiving the support of the Liverpool public to a degree fully equal to what its founders first expected, and that it was doing steadily and well the work for which it was formed. He had heard with peculiar interest what Professor MacCunn had told them about the Scotch. Universities. They all knew that Scotclamen got on in all parts of the world. He agreed with what the-lecturer said about the value of a de- gree. It was perfectly true that the degree was only a stamp, but after all it was the stamp and the printing upon it which made all the difference between a bank note oS £lOOO and a rag of paper worth some fraction of a farthing- No doubt it was possible that the limit for degrees might be carried too far, that they might become the sole intecest. and not merely a subsidiary object. There was a good deal of talk a few years ago about the endowment of research in the Universities, and somebody suggested that the words ought lobe turned round, as a good deal said about the en- dowment of research meant the reeearch of endowment. Lord Derby than proceeded to deliver the prizes, and votes si thanks followed.

WIT AND HUMOUR.

Why ought slander to be made chief of detectives F—Be- cause it is impossible to escape it. The following is the copy of a bill posted on the wall of a country village :—"A lecture on total abstinence will be delivered in the open air, and a collection will be made at the door to defray expenses." "I beg your pardon, madam," said a gentleman, raising , his hat politely to a richly-dressed woman In the street, ' "but your face is strangely familiar to me. lam sure that I have met you before.' " Yea, Misther Jones," replied the richly-dressed woman, "it's meeelf that knows ye. O'm 7?_FF C 9911 . . Scene—School during examination ' a crowd of parents and friends are present. Teacher, wholes a fiery nose, and great self-importance: "What is a bouquet ?" Boy, inno- cently :"A bunch of flowers." Teacher, benignly: "Right. What, then, are nosegays ?" Boy, with meaning: "Brandy blossoms." Collapse of teacher. Amanita INDEED !—The late Combs de'Hanssonville, French Academician and Senator, won a great reputation for courage in 1870, daring the siege of Paris, when he patriotically mounted guard upon the ramparts. He never ducked his head or threw himself prostrate when shot or shell whistled by or exploded near. "Amazing !" his com- rades used to say. "110 w wonderfully cool!" The fact was, the count was stone-deaf! "ROW do you live? " asked the Police Judge of a pan arraigned for loitering. "At present lam living on Hope, Judge," was the reply, which was a fact. Hope was his wife, and she supported the family by taking in washing. "See here, my friend; that dog of yours killed three sheep of mine last night, and I want to know what you propose to do about it? "Arc you sure it was my dog?" "Yes." "Well, I hardly know what to do. I think I had better sell him. You don't want to buy a good dog, do you?" THE NEW Burrorr.—" Yes, they are excellent boots," said the bootmaker to the young-lady purchaser; "they will wear like iron." "Do you think the buttons are sewed en securely?" she asked. " They are; the boots are sup- plied with 'the old mail's wedding' button, a new inven- tion." "Why is it called' the old maid's wedding' button ?" " Because it never comes off." Jim Webster, a hard-looking Coloured man, was brought before a justice In Austin for stealing some money from the house of Colonel Jones, one of the most respectable citizens. Said the judge very impressive to Jim, "Didn't you know that no good can conic from stolen money—that there is a eaten on it?" " Boss," answered Jim, "I didn't know fiolonel Jones stole dat money. I aline rspected him ob bein' an hones' man. White folks am gettin to be mighty 'onreliable nowadays!" A country lad, sent to the squire's with a message, sat down to regale himself on a round of beef which the cook imprudently put before him. After he had proceeded to help himself many times over with great deliberateness, the cook said sarcastically, a Well, my little man, are you going to finish it?" 'Well, ma'am, I think I could—leesarely !" answered the boy, in all seriousness. The late King of Prussia once sent to an aide-de-camp, Colonel Malichowski9 who was brave but poor, a small port- folio bound like a book, in which were deposited. fave hundred crowns. Some time afterwards he met the officer, and said to him," Well, how did you like the new work I sent you ?" "Excessively, sire," replied the colonel. 01 read it with such interest that I await the second volume with impa- tience." The king smiled, and when the officer's birthday arrived, he presented him with another portfolio, similar in every respect to the first, bat with the words engraved on it—" This work is complete in two volumes?' PRESERVING AN ANCIENT CASTLE. A truly singular method of preserving historical ruins has been discovered in Ireland. On the Case Hill, near Belfast, there was a short time ago an ancient castle. In order to protect its ruins from the ravages of time and of passing Vandals, some local antiquarians determined to surround: it with a wall, and employed a contractor to execute the work. The wall was finished in due course; but, when the antiquarians came to admire the castle it was gone. The contractor had used the ruins for building material, and not a stone of the castle Temained A member of Parliament who owned rather extensive estates and possessed considerable personal celebrity was spending a few days at the residence of a noble friend. There were several interesting and accomplished young ladies in the family, to whom the honourable member, as in duty bound, showed every attention. Just as he was about to take his leave, his hostess proceeded to consult him upon a matter which, she alleged, was causing her no little anxiety. 4' It is reported," said she, "that you are to marry my daughter Louise. And what shall we do? What can we say about it?" "Oh," quietly responded the considerate M.P., "just say she refused me!" Itsraonucrrows.—An adventurous clothier from London opened a branch establishment in Glasgow, and advertised that he would fit any resident in the town with a suit of clothes for thirty shillings. He soon had a customer in the shape of a twenty-two stone tradesman, who desired to be measured for a thirty-shilling suit. The shopman demurred when he saw how many acres there were to cover. Thinking, however, that it would serve as an advertisement, he made the clothes on condition that the customer would introduce ' some of his friends. The latter undertook to do so; and, after the suit had been delivered, he walked into the shop with his brother and an acquaintance, both of whom wanted ' a suit. One was a twenty-four stone man and the other a ' twenty-fiver. PLatrreadox PHILOSOPHY.— De pusson what doan' talk nothin' but slang, doan' think nothin' but slang. Dar ain't no apple so sweet as de one we accident'ly tia's in de grass. All de eddication in de worP • won't make some men wise. All de co'n in de crib won't I fatten de stump-suckin' hose. Er deg has got more sense " den de epen'thritt, fur ef a dog hab got or bigger piece o' meat den he ken eat, 'stead o' throwin it erway, he buries it, knowin' dat arter erwhile, he will be hungry again. What Cr glorious thing it is fur de labourin' man dat de Sabiour didn't come era rich man 'ca'se if He had, tickets on de sal- vation road would cost so much now dater po' man couldn't touch one wider ten foot pole. Bless yer, da' wouldn't let him hang eroun' de dep6t ter see de train start.

div.head: EARLESTOWN.
div.p: EARLESTOWN.

EARLESTOWN TEMPERANCE TONTINE SOCIETY.—On Tuesday evening an entertainment in connectiou with the Earlestewn Tontine Society was held in the Welcome Cof- fee Palace. There was a good attendance, and Mr John Crampton (president) occupied the chair. A programme of songs, readings, dm., was capitally gone through by Messrs Henry Warburton, George Warburton, jun., T Gorse, Wm. Sefton, and others. Mr 'f Gorse presided at the pianoforte. NEWTON CRICKET AND BOWLING CLUB. The mem- bers of this club held their annual dinner on Saturday. About 30 sat down to an excellent repast at the Pied Bull Hotel, provided by Mr H J Bond. After dinner Mr Thomas Stone, president of the club, occupied the chair, and Mr J Ball the vice-cbair. The loyal toasts were proposed and duly honoured. The Chairman proposed the toast of "Suc- cess to the club," which was responded to by Mr W Dud- geon. The proceedings during the evening were enlivened by songs, &a. The secretary's repert showed that the first eleven had played during the season 15 matches, won 3, lost 5, drawn 6. and tied 1. The second eleven had played 6 matches, having won 4, lost 1, and drawn 3. THE Ray. H. E. SMITH AT BuirroNwoon.—The annual harvest festival at Burtonwood Church, on Sunday last, was brought into prominence by the extraordinary action of the Vicar of Earlestown (the Rev T R Matthews). During the early' part of the week placards in Earlestown announced that the preacher • would be the Rev H E Smith (late curate of St. John's Chnrch,Rarleitown), and this would appearto have given offence to the vicar, for the Rev H Wilson, vicar of Buttonwood, afterwards received a note from Mr Matthews in which 'were the words—"l am sur- prised to fled from a circular which has been put into my hand that the Rev H E Smith is announced to preach at Your church on Sunday next. You need not be surprised if I write to the Bishop with reference to the same." In the course of a subsequent conversation, the Rev H Wilson stated that while not wishing to embitter the unhappy con- troversy which was going on, he must say that he was not aware that Mr Smith had done anything to merit the censure of the Bishop, and he therefore hoped Mr Smith would fulfil his engagement. He, also intimated that, several days previous to the receipt of the letter from Mr Matthews, he informed the latter that Mr Smith was going to preach, and therefore Mr Matthews could not be greatly surprised when be saw the printed announcement. This incident created some little excitement among the parishioners of Earlestown. On Sunday, when the harvest thanksgiving services were held, the church atsßurtonwood was crowded both morning and afternoon. The Rev H E Smith was the preacher on each occasion, and the rev gentleman's remarks were listened to very attentively. The sacred edifice had been very taste- fully. decorated for the occasion by the scholars of, the Sunday school under the superintendence of the vicar's family. At the afternoon service the lessons for the day were read .by Mr M Birkhead, of Earlestown, and the Rev H E Smith preaohed an excellent sermon from the 16th veree of the 72nd Psalm. At the close of each service a collection was made in aid of the choir fund, and a goodly sum was realised.

THE EARLESTOVVN CHURCH SCANDAL. DEPUTATION TO THE BISHOP. The scandalous state of affairs in the parish of St John the Baptist, Earlestown, has again been brought prominently before the public during the present week. The committee appointed by the parishioners to make arrangements for the erection of an iron church, in which the scattered flock might hold divine services, have taken an important step towards that end, and though it may not have had a very cheering result for the parishioners it appears to have given every satisfaction. A short time ago the following letter was for- warded to the Lord Bishop of Liverpool :—" 34, Bank. street, Earlestown.—To the Right Reverend J. C. Ryle, D.D.—Right Reverend and Dear Sir.—The committee ap- pointed by the parishioners and late members of St John the Baptist Church request me to write and ask your Lordship whether we could calculate on your Lordship granting a license to our proposed New Church, and if so whether it would come under the jurisdiction of the Rev. T. R. Mat- thews the vicar of Earlestown. If the Vicar must be connected in any way with the above-named proposed Church or Mission Church, I am sorry to say that we shall be under the painful necessity of severing our caeneo:ion I with our dear old Church, and be driven to establish A r branch of the Reformed Free Church.—l am, your Lord- ship's obedient servant, Wm. A. MAWDSLEY." In reply to this communication his Lordship wrote as follows :—" The Palace, 19, Abercromby-square, Liverpool, October 3, 1884. —Sir,—l acknowledge receipt of your letter. I shall feel obliged if you will call on me at my office, 53, Lord-street, on Tuesday next at 12 o'clock.—Yours faithfully, J. C., Liverpool." In accordance with this request, a deputation consisting of Messrs Nevitt, Birkhead, Burchall, and Mawdsley visited Liverpool, and had an interview with the Bishop. They were received in a very friendly manner, and throughout the conversation they were treated with cour- tesy and respect. The deputation briefly stated the unfor- tunate position in which they were placed, and the Bishop expressed his fullest oympathy for them in the d.ncalty they were labouring under. lie was, be /mid, heartily sorry that such a state of things should exists It was a great pity that Mr Matthews could not egret with his parishioners. He (the Bishop) had visited their church, had seen what congregations they '-,ad, and had heard the hearty manner in which tin services were rendered, and he considered it a thottsand pities that a congregation such as they had should be scattered to the winds. When people were once, driven from church it took a great deal to bring then back again. He advised them to go on with their temporary church, but whatcver they did in providing themselves with a place of worship they must not go to any great expense, as, he said, Mr Matthews (the vicar) would not live for ever, and he hoped they would all live to see some Important changes in the law regarding the Church. He was, however, perfectly helpless to assist them as regarded licensing another church in Earlestown, as this could not be done without the vicar's consent.—The deputation then thanked the Bishop for his kindncse and withdrew. With reference to the proposed purchase of a plot of land in Earle-street, adjoining the Co-operative Stores, it may be stated that no definite answer has yet been received from the London and North-Western Railway Company, who are the owners of the land.

LIBERALISM AT EARLESTOWN, LECTVRE ON "FRIENDS OR FOES ?" Under the title of "'the People's question—friends or foes," Mr Alfred Crilly, of Liverpool, secretary of the Finan- cial Reform Association, delivered a public lecture in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, Earlestown, on Wednesday evening. Theaddress was given under the auspices of the Earlsetown and District Liberal Club, and there was a fairly good attendance, including Messrs P Hall, ii Waywell, Butter, B Corlett, C A Luff man, J Davies, T Howard (sec- retary of the club), J Clarke, T Chambers, M Birkhead, W Gilmour, C A Owen, and others. At the commencement of the proceedings Mr T Howard (secretary) stepped forward and said that from some cause he could not explain Mr Pilkiogton had not turned up. He left Earlestown at five o'clock that afternoon on his way to Eluyton, promising to return in time for that meeting, but he had not done so. In his absence Mr Lialman bad kindly promised to preside. (Applause.) Mr C A Luff man then took the chair, and in introducing the lecturer he said he should think those were the friends of the people who were helping them in the accomplishment of their honourable desires. He thought their honourable &sires were to be cheaply fed, properly housed, well edu- cated, and to partake in the government of their country. For his own part• he could not see that the Conservatives had ever acted towards seeking the accomplishment of those objects, and they all knew that the whole course of Censer- votive policy during the last few years had been to place restrictions on food in every way they could. (Applause.) Mr A Crilly was warmly received. He said the abstract question as to who were the friends and foes of the people offered a very wide scope indeed for an answer. He thought the simple answer to the question was, that those who had fought for popular rights through varying generations, and were fighting to-day, were the friends of the people; and that those who opposed those rights and accomplishments were the foes of the people. <Hear, hear.) In classifying the latter he found himself in front of the great and first offender, the House of Lords. (Applause.) There never RSB a tight that the people demanded through their repre- sentatives in the House of Commons which the House of Lords had not ,to the bitter end opposed. The House of Lords opposed the emancipation of the Jews, the emancipation of the Roman Catholics, the abolition of purchase in the army, and quite. within recent memory it opposed the Compensation for Disturbance (Ire- land) Bill. He believed that but for that single act there would have been peace and contentment in Ireland. Follow- ing that came the agitation for the Land Act, but the House of Lords opposed that. Lords and landlords held land to be sacred, and their rights must not be touched no matter who might starve or die, and se the Lords so emasculated that Land Act as to leave it still open to agitation—a cause of bickering and dispute. Remarking that in all their actions the Lords were dead against the people from beginning to mad, Mr Crilly went on to allude to the Cattle Disease Act, and said that the Lords ever sacri- ficed the poor man in order to help the wealthy. Proceeding to speak of the land question, he said that while the people of the country were being driven across the ocean seeking for land it was absolutely monstrous that the few owners of the land in England should be allowed to remain in comfortable possession of it when its redistribu- tion under fair conditions would supply food and happiness to so many fellow-countrymen. (Applause.) He maintained that the land tax had been evaded by the tar downers, and said it was about time they had a change in those matters. (Applause.) They wanted to know why those who did not belong to the people's house should have a voice in its go- vernment, by what title they possessed a more potent voice in the affairs of the nation than the Monarch had, and if they could invariably and at all times oppose the popular will and the good of the people, and the country at large? (Applause). Coming to the Tory party he would ask were they the friends of the people, or were they their foes ? What act of benificence had they ever originated ? Not one. (Hear, hear.) They never had the power of reversing any act of Reform passed, but they had opposed every act of Reform suggested as they were opposing at present the enfranchisement of two millions of people. They opposed that not because they said it would not be good for the people but they wanted to so manipulate matters as to land themselves in the posi- tion of being governors of the land. There was no reality in the present contention of the Tories; they admitted that enfranchisement was good and desirable, and that the peo- ple practically wanted it, but they ran a herring across the path in the shape of redistribution, which was inevitable and

thousand pounds out of the pockets- of the people. The course for the people of the country' to take was, he thought, clear and distinct. There was a Go- vernment in power that offered liberty to two millions of their fellow-countrymen. • The House of Lords through Lord Salisbury said they bad not rejected it, but had they granted it P (" No," and applause.) No, certainly not. Tuere never was a more flimsy basis for a political party to stand upon than that upon which the Tory party stood at the present time, and ipver a stronger foundation than that upon which the Liberal party was appealing to the country for support to carry out its behests. (Loud applause.) Mr P Hall was then called upon to move the following resolution That this meeting of the inhabitants of Earlestown records its emphatic potest against the conduct of the "louse of Lords in unjustifiably stopping Mal Bill for giving the rights of freedom to two millions of their fellow. citizens still held in political serfdom; declares its convic- tioa that the hereditary system in our legislature is bad in principle, ivholly mischievous in practice, and ought to be at once abolished; trusts that the government will take such measures as may be necessary to ensure the passing of the Franchise Bill in the' present Par- liament, and earnestly assures Mr Gladstone and his cabinet of the heartiest support in any steps they may deem it ne- ,l cessary to take for the attainment of the object." He (Mr Hall) thought they in Earlestown were not taking too/strong a course in passing a resolution like the one be had just read. They ought not to be behind hand at the present time in supporting Mr Gladstone's Government as much as laid in their power, and the Liberal party as represented at the Liberal club were wishful to keep the action of the House of Lords before the working ,classes of the country. It was very important that they should do all they could to strengthen the hands of the Government, for the House of Lords deserved all they were receiving at the present time. (Applause.) , Mr M Birlrhead, in seconding the motion, said he could endorse everything the lecturer had said so far as his expe- rience went. He, however, did not condemn all the Tories, for he believed there were some good private men amongst them, but they had. never been in the van when anything was to be done for the benefit of the masses. (Applause.) ' With reference to the House of Lords he was a little bit conservative and should not like to see them driven out, of the country altogether if they could make any use of them at all. (Laughter.) He thought all working-men would cordially agree with the resolution., (Applause.) The resolution was then carried with acclamation.—Mr Thomas Howard afterwards moved a hearty vote of thanks , to the Lecturer for his excellent address, and Mr John Clarke seconded the motion, which was passed —A similar compliment was paid to the Chairman on the motion of Mr Crillv, secondcd by Mr W Gilmour, and the meeting then concluded.
