Sir,—lf it affiuids Mr Hampson any gratification to sup- pogo that I "have deceived myself, or have been deceived by others," in reference to the " return " recently pub- lished by you, he is quite welcome to any pleasure he may go obtain. I may say, however, that while I receive most valuable and leyal help from my assistants. I am not in the habit of leaving matters of ibis kind, or indeed any items of importance, for others to do, bat instead, I take the re- sponsibility and m inaaement of them myself. 1 7,:n0t0 that my return is correct, and I knom also that try party believe me, and there the matter must end so far as lan concerned.—l am, air, your obedient servant, H. ROBERTS, Liberal Agent.

REPLY TO "A VILLAGERS" REPLY. A Villager" in his reply (?) to my notice of Mr ' )Loberts's letter SedM3 disposed to make merry at my logic. Pathapo he is justified in this; when I was young enough to go to school logietformed no portion of a poor lad's edu- cation. Therefore lam apt to look at questions in a plain straightforward fashion. To" chop logic" I hym no am- bition ; I leave it to youths like my friends "A Villager" and Mr Roberts. And should they call upon me to "show cause, or qealification, to pronounce upon the question " of edneatioo, why, then, I should very likely retreat, confess- ing my ignorance. I have beard Christians boast that the followers of Christ yore mostly poor fiMermen unlearned in the arts of sophistry. If "A Villager" will pardon me I may fst.tte that my reading has convinced me that it was only when the early fathers commenced to dabble in logic that the moat complex of all Tensions had its origin. lam quite aware that so complicated a theory as the Trinity is could not be argued out a posteriori to the premise. But what of that? All you h,sva Cod° is to quote the whole of your opponent's remarks, answer none of them, and yon at once provo your power in argument. Now my standpoint is a vary simple one. I have Christianity before ins divided and sub-divided into innumerable sects, each claiming to have all that is necessary for man's salvation. I see these sects, as it were, at one another's throats, the church espe- cially striving all it possibly can to grind beneath its heel whatever it thinks .avours of schism and heresy, and claim- ing to be the sole privileged preaching party. With the Itomien church I have nothing to do; it is out of considera- tion, and although it has within its ranks such able men as Cardinals Newman and Manning, those only can enter its pale who are willing to leave independence behind. The Diseenters are all so consumed with pride, and ambition, that what between chapels in debt and hoz tars to get them cut, their congregations are sick and weary of the everlast- ing grind. This is one phase. Allow me to further sketch Christianity to "A Villager" as it appears to me, and I beg it to be understood that lam neither &nesting nor scoffing—simply obeying the Archbishop of York, who at Carlisle, " exhorted the workino-men to cry aloud, and spare not their clergyman who was their licensed friend, the man of leisure, to attend to

these things." I look at these men of leisure," and what do I See? What is the fruit of all this leisure? of their university education? Why, a Tollemachei Tollecneche, Rector of South Wytham, writes the following letter to the village schoolmaster: "South Wytham Rectory, Sep- teinber 17, 1884. All the villagers desirous of coming to shy house, approach it in a b coming and respectful manner through the back way and to the kitchen door. There is not a farmer in the place who ever has had, or would have the impertinence to do otherwise. I desire that in future yea *ill do the like." I fled the Rev E Thigh writing to the Rock stating that tho Church of England clergy are slaves to an antiquated rubric, that its service is a "jumble of vain repetition." I find another Christian paper asserting t• that our ministers as a body do not really believe the hideous dogma many of them probes." I, in fact, find on all sides a decided admission that Christianity so far leas been a failure. Mr G Harwood, in a paper read before the Cbuich Congress, eaid, "It made one sink with despair to reflect that during this century the influence of the Church of England, in so far as it had publicly manifested itself, had for the most part been nearly always on the wrong side; on the side of privilege against right, on the side of ignorance against knowledge." Now,laek, if this is the case, Las not the churh been a cane instead of a blessing? If the church has taken sides with "restriction against free- Jam been on the side of the few against the many," am I not justified in pointing this out as the fruit? Nay, I moat put ain a strong:r light still. These Ctristians at their Congresses must be charged with duplicity and with a de- liberate desire to humbug the people. The Archbishop of York in one of his epeeches stated that the "mighty army has started to its feel, no longer with supplicatioos, but with demands; it finds us unprepared." Now let us see how it prepares itself to meet the wants of this "mighty army." The Bishop of Bedford read a paper on "Over- crowding of the poor," but I read "Interest in the paper war not sustained, and by the time the papers had been read the audience had dwindled down to very thin proportions." Here these Christians stand, exposed to the scorn of every working-man. Had these papers been concerned with the eastward position, or on the necessity of building new churches, or sending out mission- aries, the audience would not have dwindled to very thin proportions. Oh, no ; but inasmuch as it was a question of the poor it was no concern of theirs. This is not " de- clemation and abuse ;" out of your own mouths are ye judged. Before "A Villager" charges Atheists with being swin- dlers, be must have some facts. Our police courts seem to have the most business with the ministers of various de- ' nominations, and it is only since the light of free-thought Jas been permitted to shine forth, since infidelity became snore common, that the superetitious age of John Wesley has been pushed into the limbo of absurdities. The more free-thought pushes itself among the people, and the sooner it will he impossible for such et inments as the following to be made. I again turn to the Church Congress. The Rev G 0 Haydon said "Toe landlords," Christians bear in mind "had not yet realized that it was their duty to findsufficient• dwellings for the people occupied in tilling on their lands. In his own perish, of 36 schwa miles, he did not know of more than half-a-doz-u cottages Which had even 'two bed- rooms. The landlords were non-residents, and when he asked them to perform their duties, they threatened to with. hold the sums they had been accustomed to give in charity because he was so troublesome." This, sir, is not the fruit of Atheism; it is after eigtheen hundred years of Chris- tianity. And now these men who have preached dogmas they did not believe are heard crying Gut that they— Have healed no wound, would it but fester more, Bound up no eorrow in another's life. Offered no kindness and no hope. Beaded no sickening cry, quenched no despair; Ceded to death no tear. to we no -igh ; O'er desolation breathed no pained prayer. (Mobile 6ch, 1884. CAP rAIN cuT rLE. THE ThillY DEMONSTRATIONS. Sir,—Along with a few more Bade, I determined, on Saturday last, to take part in the political demonstration to he held in Tatton Park, the seat of Lord Egerton. We have the word of Hatfield's Lord that a little healthy exercise will do the people good, and although my Lord of Salisbury was good enough to sneer at " legislation by picnic," it yet , seemed to me very good when attended by so glorious an opportunity as offered itself of seeing all the natural beau- tee within the walks of Tattoo Park. Lauded at Knots- ; lord, I almost seemed to be born again—the air had so much ' a Torifying ieflui nee. The surroundings of Knntsford make it difficult to imagine that for a moment anything like Liberal notions could exist, yet before I left I found it would be a mistake to think so. Wending cur way through a splendid avenue of beeches, acd occasionally meeting a True blue, half seas over, we at . length Came to this "mighty" gathering of politicians. ! Sir, we have been told that "demonstration should be met by demonstration." These Tory leaders reckoned without their masters; the people refuse to be hood-winked. All through the country their meetings have been failures. Cheap railway tic: ets, illuminations, fireworks, turning their ancestral halls into show-palaces--all these attractions have failed to tempt workingmen to follow out the advice given by Sir Michael Hicks-Beach to his tenantry in Wilt- shire —"If: they were to do any good in the world, it would not be merely by getting the Parliamentary franchise; it would not he by attempting to take from other people what belonged to them, bat by etch of them doing their best in the position God had placed them—doing their duty, not merely tswards themselves, but first and foremost, to those among whom they lived." This duty of eelf-ebnegation has been preached from pulpit and Tory platform long enough; the people now demand a share in the election of representatives, knowing; full well, that whe- ther thPy will or no, they must have more than their share in paying the piper. Arrived at the platform erected to hold our pastors and masters, I was not at all surprised to find its occupants far out-numbering the amlieoce. I have not had any experience at guessing at the numbers composing a meeting, but at the time the chief speeches were neing delivered,l should think not more than five hundred listeners were present; this too, after the great outlay in posting the walls of Man• cheater, Warrington, aod the surrourding villages. But something of far more importance than this was noticeable ; nearly every oae I spoke to turned out to be a Radical, and though seeking information, all were fain to confess that they had turned in the wrong direction for that most desir- able article. Women were tkere in great nuntbere, and this in itself was cheering, clearly proving that the gentle sex are becoming alive to the areal necessity existing for their taking, a pirt in petition matters. Respecting the speeches. little can be said. Cries ef shame were elicited when Sir Henry Holland told how this "must Liberal Government had passed two of the most stringent coercive measures that history record.gl, measures that at one time kept seven hun- dred of Iraands hes' sons within the prison walls." It was with great d'fficulty I kept myself trova aeking how many Coneervetives vcted aerainet the paesing of these stringent coercive hills? N ay, 1 knew it meet he within the recollec- tion of neerly all oo the% platform that the Tories were most abortive in their clamour, that the hoed of iron moot he brought to bear upon these poor Irish men who were only just waking up to a sense of their conetryis NVlOqgq; that indeed the only party who opposed these detestable measures

LYNISI LOCAL BOARD.

r A meeting of this body was held at the office, Lymm, 1 on Thursday evening, under the presidency of Mr Cameron. 1 There were also present Messrs Rogers, Appleton, Forster, 1 Gibbon, Callendar, Thomason, Woolley, Ridgway (clerk), and Dr Fox (medical officer of health). DEFECTIVE WATER SIIPPLI.—The following report of Mr Mort, nuisance inspector, was read :—" I beg to call your attention te the want of a proper water supply to two cot- tages situate in Pepper-street, the property of trustees of the late Dr Bennett, and occupied by Mr John Moston and another. Also want of proper water supply to 18 cottages and two villas, situate in Pepper-street, the property of Mrs Mary Holt, and in the occupation of self and others. These properties have hitherto obtained their water supply from the open well in Pepper-street, but that source of supply is now cat off in consequence of the said well running dry, and the various occupiers are now ander the necessity of obtaining their drinking water from pumps, &c., about the , village, or from such other sources as the charity of neigh- hours may permit. I may say that the mains of the Water Company pass in close proximity to the above properties, from which a supply could easily be laid on."— A long discussion ensued, and finally Mr Rogers pro- posed, and Mr Callendar seconded a resolution to the effect that the owners of the property be requested to provide a proper water supply.—Mr Thomason moved as an amend- ment that the owners of the property be not required to pro- vide the cottages and houses with water until the legality of the Board hod been decided as to the water being taken from a well, the suggestion having been made that the water might have been taken into a neighbouring sewer.—The amendment did net attain a seconder, and the original reso- lution was then passed. INSANITARY BUILDINGS.—Dr. Fox, medical officer of health, submitted the following report;—" It will be within 'the recollection of the Board that in a recent report atten- tion was drawn to a block of buildings known as the Rookery. Their general insanitary condition has long been a scandal and a source of peril to the district. A committee met on the ground and such alterations were suggested as would alone make the property conformable to the require- ments of the statute. The owner refuses to execute the necessary work, and the nuisance connected with this block of tenanted houses is being intensified every day. I should be wanting in my duty to the Board and to the community if I did net, as their medical officer of health, call the moot serious attention to what must be the result of non-com- pliance with the directions of the local authority. I wish to intimate to the Board in the most emphatic manner pos- sible that the houses are an ever present outsttnding menace to the health of the tewn. Destitute of proper means of ventilation, entirely without adequate privy ac- commodation, ashes and other domestic refuse standing at their very doors, I regard them as entirely unfit for human habitation, and I call upon the Board to deal with them accordingly. The repeated outbreaks of fever in the town leave the Board no option but to enfore the most re- pressive measures in regard to all insanitary conditions ; and I advisedly and under a due sense of responsibility in- dicate the Rookery as the worst property in Lvmrn, and such as the Board are bound to declare unfit to, human habitation.—Another lengthy di-cussion followed, and it was decided, on the motion of Mr Rogers, seconded by Mr Woolley, that notices be served upon the owner to abate the nuisance by making various specified alterations and pro- visions. THE FEVER EPIDEMIC.—A conversational discussion took place regarding the advisability of requesting that the day and Sunday schools in the vilitge should be closed, and Dr Fox said that be did not know of any extension of the epi- demic that made it a necessity. He did not call upon the Board to do it, but urged nothing against it. There was no doubt, be said, that whenever there were complaints of this kind in a neighbourhood people who at any time were un- willing to Fend their children to school took advantage of it, and said thd they were jastified in keeping them away.— It was resolved to make a request that all day and Sunday schools be for the present closed for cleansing and disin- fecting. This was all the business.

div.p: were the Radicals, Mr Bradlanala himself in the absence of Mr Parnell moving their resection. This being the case, 1 c -mid only wonder as to whom the cries of shirae applied. Afghanistan. South Africa, all these stock subjects were trot- ted out, but it was quite evident the Tory portion of the audience had not met to listen to politics, and while a most feeble representative of the Warburton family boasted that "he as a member of Parliament knew the House of Commons had no dispute with the House of Lords, therefore there was no di-mute only what existed in the imagination of Mr Gladstone," there was a general stampede towards the gar- dens. Looking amongst the audience, and through the oc- cupants of the platform, I was curious to see how large or bow small a contingent Warrington had contributed to- wards this splendid demonstration Would you believe it, sir? With the exception of the solitary "Neutral " I saw not one; yea, after looking again I espied a certain most "Christian brewer," who aspires at some distant day to re- pres:nt this town of ours. I wonder if he made a speech. I didn't stay or I might have heard the celebrated and stereotyped one, "It vsu'll be true to me, I'll be true to yon ; you know I always was your friend." I think this might be taken generally as a text by our Tory friends. To pose on the platform as the friends of the people, and in actual life to carry not the promptings of a selfish nature, has been the rule in Tory rural life. Of this I had ample evidence en Saturday last at Knutsford. Leaving Tattoo Park and strolling into the village ale- house I ventured to air a few Radisal notions, not without some misgivings as to their acceptance, but the Tory element was altogether wanting. A numerous company of farm labourers were present, who, when asked had they been pre- sent at the demcnstration ? immediately answered " No, they had been at work all day; it wasn't for such like as them to got) dernonetrations ;" besides, "they didn't want to go, for yond lot would do them no good." Well. I asked, have you got a vote ? No, but we soon shall have." From this I got to the wage question. How much a week were thr y getting? "Oh. various sums." The man I was speaking to had been working at a thrashing machine, and he said he and his mates had received two shillings for that day, but he knew men that were working regular for eighteenpence a day. Was he married? 'Yes, and he had one child, and was expecting another." Now, here was a room full of Englishmen England's peasantry, the class of men who are told to be Englishmen, for the position in which it has pleased God to place them: young men, actually preparing to meet the strife of life on nine shillings and twelve shillings a week, and the pickings to be obtained from richer men's tibias: the class of men to whom all these demonstratinns have special reference, but to whom all ac- tive participation is denied. In another room I found a company seemingly composed of the Manchesterclerk and the village shopkeeper class,deep in the study of politics, and chiefly Tory. Here the discus- sion soon became "hot." One of the chief disputants soon left, not being able to stand such Radical talk. But the cud- gels were soon taken up by one who seemed to understand trade questions—Gladstane was driving trade out of the country, but when reminded ef the time when trade in- creased by leaps and bounds," he laid the blame on trade unionism—strikes were ruining the country. '4 Well," I said, " strikes have not ruined these agricultural labourers, who are working for nine shillings per week." " No," my opponent said, ' but they hive enabled Joseph Arch to ride about the country with a pony and carriage.' "Ah," I said "you know very little of this subject, it seems to me. I have had eorce experience in strikes, and ao far as It goes it has proved to me that the Tory in the towns is as benighted as the country Tory. The first is so anxious to Stand by and conserve old fashioned ways of working, that if he has his own way, which he won't have, our trade will soon wing its way to other countries, and the latter has been reared to feel, and express such deep veneration for the vil- lage squire and his satellite the conceited parson, that no wonder be dare not breathe without asking permission." The outcome of it all was that at parting a general hand- shaking ensued, and a strongly expressed wish that some one would come amongst them who knew a bit about the other side. Sir, there cannot be a doubt about it, our country cousins are held tight in the grasp of these country tyrants, that the energies of Refcrmers should be turned towards the rural districts. There is scarcely a day passes but the Press gives forth some instance of a bigoted parson or landowner refus- ing to have a Dissenter or Liberal for tenant or neighbour. I heard a labourina. man assert on Saturday that he was a Tory and an upholder of Lord Egerton because he could get better pickings from the owner of a large estate than he could from a man in a small was. I assert, and am not in fear of contradiction, that there is not a Tory working-man in existence who, if pressed with argument, but will allow his aims are of a personal and selfish character. Anything of a national character and likely to benefit us as a nation they are entirely oblivious of. They seem to be utterly un- aware that their action makes it possible for the country magistrate to inflict heavy fines on children for gathering blackberries, as at Great Berkhampstead ; that, as in Suffolk, where the labourers vote for.the enclosure of a heath they gain nothing by it, the heath being divided between the rector and the small proprietors, the poor getting nothing at all. In Lancashire at this moment we have a village in which 30 acres of waste land are being quietly filched from the people who have not the power to resist. • My country, if a wretch should e'er arise Out of thy countless sons who would curtail Thy freedom, dim thy Wory—while he lives May all earties people curse him—for of all Hest thou second the blessing; and it one Waist who would not arm for liberty. Be be. too, cursed living; and when dead • Let him be burial downwards, with his face Looting to hell; and o'er his coward grave The hare sku.lc, in her form.
CLIFFORD DIX.

MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. A great town's meeting of ratepayers and owne-s of pro- perty in Manchester, called by the Miyor (Mr P Goid- echmidt) in pursuance of a requisition, and held under the provisions of the Borough Funds Act, took place on Mon- day in the Manchester Town Nall, to consider the proposal that the Corporation should subscribe £lB,OOO to the fund for promoting the bill next session. The hall was densely crowded, and many persons were unable to get in. Mr Daniel Adamson, chairman of the Provisional Committee, WAS greeted with loud cheers, and the greatest enthusiasm for the scheme was displayed throughout. He proposed that the Curporatioa be empowered to promote, in .mnjunction with others, a bill in Parliament far incorporating a com- pany, and empowering such company to construct a canal from the river Mersey to the city of Mincliester navigable for ocean steamers and ships of large barthen, an 1 to con- tribute out of the city rate to the cost of such promotion a sum not exceeding 21 in the pound upon the annual rate- able value. He explained that no amendment could be moved, the meeting having simply to vote for and against.— Ald. J J Harwood seconded.—Mr Ramabottom, amidst a storm of opposition, challenged Mr Harwood to show who would reap the benefit of the construction of the canal.— The resolution was carried by an overwhelming majority, only about 20 persons voting ag Grist it.—Thereupon Mr W A Lynde demanded a poll—Toe proposl was received with a storm of hisses and cries of "Shame."—When order had been restored, the Town Clerk (Sir Joseph Heron) explained that Mr Lynde had made hie demand as solicitor in that district to the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany. (Groans and renewed cries of Shame.")—The Mayor intimated that unless the demand was withdrawn the poll would take place in a few days.—The meeting then closed.

Mr Lynde has since written to the Town Clerk of Man- chester stating that, having entered a protest against public funds being used for private enterprise in connection with the Ship Canal. the London and North-Western Railway Compmv will not put the city to the expense of a poll. Mr Lyncie therefore withdraws the demand bra poll.

a deputation to wait upon the Rector to ask him to meet, them and endeavour to arrive at an understand- ing as to what was to be done when Mr. Rowley had finished, his engagement. That deputation did not succeed in gaining an audienee with the Rector, and nothing more was done until yesterday week, when the members of the choir held a special meeting in the vestry, and for the second time a deputation was I appointed. Three of the members were appointed to form the deputation, and at once proceeded to the Rectory, when, it is stated, they were again unsuc- cessful, being informed that the Rector could not see them. The deputation returned to the meeting, and it was then decided that in consequence of the two refusals of the Rector to confer with the choir and to givo them an understanding as to what was to be done regarding the position of organist, they should not again resume their duties until such time as the Rector himself approached them. A resolution, bearing date the 4th of October, 1884, was drawn up and passed. It was ad- dressed to the Rector and was worded as follows: —"The members regret that the Rector has not met the two deputatioas from the choir which have waited upon him in the hope of coming to some Batts factory explanation as to the misunderstandings which. unfortunately have arisen between themselves, the Rector, and Wardens, and taking into considera- tion the existing circumstances they reluctantly feel compelled to decline taking part in the services of the church until such time as the Rector and War- dens meet the choir with a view to coming to a mutual understanding." It is urged on benalf of the choir that they have in no way wished to dic- tate, but have simply desired to gain information which they complain has been withheld from them. They were naturally desirous t 3 learn who was to succeed Mr R3wley, and what arrangements were being made to that end, and think that it was a matter in which they should have been consulted, being, as they ate, so nearly interested. It is claimed that the choir has a member who has proved himself competent to take charge of the services— at least until a permanent organist satisfactory to all parties was appointed—and the members feel grieved at having been treated as nonentities. It is probable that if the deputations had been met the matter might have been smoothed over and a very unpleasant state of affairs avoided. As it is, the choir express willingness to resume duties if an understanding be come to as to what is to be done regarding the vacancy. _

It is stated that it is the expressed wish of the Rector to form a new choir, composed in a great measure of the members of the one now "on strike," but with one or two exceptions of members who are apparently objectionable, to him. On the other hand the choir are fully determined that they will not resume duty unless an arrangement is made by which one and all can resume their accustomed positions in the .church. On making inquiries last evening we learned that the position of affairs remains unchanged, except that tin W. S. Woods, of Church- street, Warrington, who has been holding the position of organist at Grappenhall Parish Church, has been appointed by the Rector and Wardens to fill the vacancy caused by Mr. Rowley's resignation.

Some weeks ago we narrated at some length a romantic story in which the principal characters were a West Indian sugar planter from St. Lucia and a fustian cutter of War- rington. It wilt be remembered that the former, a coloured gentleman named Lawrence. married the latter, who was I then a young girl named Ellen Higgins, some years aeo, I and that in so doing he g.eatly offended his fether, who figures as the "stern parent" throughout the whole history. Ths husband was in tine induced to re-visit his island home, and for some time kept up a correspondence with his wife. At length, however, this ceased—the letters, it is supposed, having been interzeated by the father—and as years rolled by, the wife, believing that he was dead; con- tracted a marriages with a man named Molyneux, by whom I I she has had two children. Recently the first husband re- I I appeared under circumstances recorded at the time and k took bec wiih him to St. Lucia his only surviving child, a daughter about sixteen years of age. The wife, knowing that her second marriage was not legal, refused to live with M ilyneux. in spite of his entreaties to renew the intimacy. Having apparently concluded that his hitherto supposed wife could not be induced to again share his home, Molynenx has taken peeseesion of the household goods, leaving the woman with the two children, and under these circumstances she, on Tuesday morning, applied to the Warrington Borough Meets:rates for advice. The gentlemen on the Bench were Messrs Monks and Broadbent. The ordinary business of the Court having been concluded Mrs Lawrence stepped for- ward, and The Chief Constable said that the applicant was the wife of a person named Lawrence, a coloured man' an account of a romance about whom they might have read in the newts- papers. It appeared that he had been away for something like twelve or fourteen years, and the woman, believing without a doubt that he was dead, took ,to herself another man. She lived with this second husband--a man named alolyneaux—until the first husband again turned up a few weeks ago. Toe very mu nent Mrs Lawrence saw her lawful bueband, she went away from the man she was then living with and to whom she had previously thought she wee legally married. She had resolutely declined to again live with Molyneaux, who had been " waiting and watching " and sending for her ever since Lawrence went away. He had also been paying the rent of the house. On the previous thy, however, he cleared the hones ef everything, and the woman was now maintaining the children that ske had had by the second husband. She had been to see the relieving officer, an.l no doubt the Case would be reported to Mr Sut- ton, and the children that she bad born by the second hus- band would be properly affiliated. He was wishful to help the applicant. She bad been to the Heinen Catholic priest, and had no doubt got a good scolding, but for conscience sake she would not live with this second man again know- ing that the first husband Was alive. He thought it was their duty as far as they could to assist her. He had been led to understand that the man had taken the furniture that she had when he married her. Tne Applicant said that she only had a bad, which she paid for with her daughter's money, but she worked, and so did her daughter. Mr Menke : She has a remedy against him for the bed, but nothing beyond that. The Clerk said that a married woman could now acqaire property which belonged to her, and in that case she would have a remedy in the County Court. The Chief Consteble said that he had warned Molyneaux not to take anything that did not belong to him. As for the children, the authorities had offered to take them into 1 the Workhouse, nut the mother had too much pride about her to let them go.

Mr Monks: Whet about the first hush end ? The Clerk: fie has gone back ; he came for his daughter. The Chief Constehle : I believe the daughter has made her mother C promise that if she will get rid of the second man they will recognise her from abroad, but that may be a yeer or two. Mr Broadbent: The daughter is the child of the first hus- band. Ties difficulty is how the mother will maintain her- self in the meanwhile. •

The Chief Constable said that he had an interview with Molyneaux And bad tried to appeal to his better feelings, but without avail. they bad had the daughter before them —she was then an apprentic to Mr Platt—and she was a fine- looking girl. She had a little of her father's spirit in her and had gone back with him. Mr Broadbent: The only question that the Bench can consider is that about the bed.

The Clerk ; I suppose she can maintain herself. Mr Shearer, relieving officer, who was in umrt, explained that it was not a custom of the Board of Guardians to take children into the House without the mothers.

Mr Monks thought that if she were to write to the first husband and explain the circumstances she might receive such assistance an would render that unnecessary. The Chief Constable: That would take about six months. Mr Broadbent Is not this man Molyneaux bound to maintain the children
The Clerk: Under a bastardy order, he might. Mr Breadb,mt : It is not fair that he should desert them.
Mr Monks: It would be for her to summons him.

The Chief Constable: Yet she went away from him. If he had any manhood about him he would contribute to the maintenance of his children. fie said that he would only do wlut the law compels him to do. He wants her and wants to live with her. She says that she wi'l not when she knows that her first husband is alive.
Mr Broadbent said that it was some hardship on the se- cond man as he thought that he was legally marrying the woman. There was a knot for the clerk to unravel.
The Clerk said thit there were many such knots to untie. Mr Monks: I was under the impression that the first hus- band would assist her.
The Chief-Constable : I will not lose sight of your sug- gestion. Mr Broadbent • Haw can she be maintained within the next six months?
Applicant : I am with my mother at present and work at fustian cuttin r. There are two children.

The Chief-Constable: She had three children by Law- rence and two died. If I were in your place (to applicant) I should go to the Workhouse. Mr Breadbent : Why should she if she can maintain her- self by fustian cutting? The Chic:lf-Constable said that the Workhouse authorities might do something to make Molyneux contribute to the maintenance of the children.
Mr Monks said thtit it might prejudice her future pros- pects if she did so.

- - The Chief Conattble : She has a little pride about her. Mr Monks : lan very glad to hear it. 1 think her first husband will thiak.none the worse of her for it. The Chief Constable : How would it be if eh e applied for free eurtunonses to affiliate the children.

The Clerk : I suopose the question is whether you will order free summons.' After a short discussion the Mavistrates decided to grant a free summons for the affiliation of the children and tio ap- plicant then left the court.

On Thursday a special meeting of the Widnes Local Board was held at Alford° Chambers for the purple° of con- sidering a communication respecting the Ship Canal. Mr F H Gossage presided, and there were present Dr O'Keeffe, Messrs Pankhurst, Handley, Wright, Midwood, Dutton, Gasket], Houghton, Martley, Johnson, Webster, Sadler, and J T Allen (clerk), and W Higginson (surveyor ).—The Clerk read a letter from Messrs Grundy, Kershaw, and Co., soli' niters to the Provisional Committee of the Ship Canal scheme, which stated that the premoters proposed to again apply for powers to construct a ship canal to Manchester, and that in order to avoid the difficulties suggested by the opponents to their bill last session, the promoters proposed to continue the canal along the Cheshire shore to a point near Esetham. The Provisional Committee would be glad to meet representatives of the Widnes Local Board to lay be- fore them and discuss the new proposals, and ascertain the views of the Board with reference to them, and no doubt before the parliamentary notices were completed and plans deposited, the promoters might be enabled to make provi- sion for the accommodation of the Board's district, which could not otherwise be provided for.—The Chairman said he bad seen a plan of the proposed canal, and he described its course along the Cheshire side of the river Mersey from Runcorn. It would take along the foreshore through the first arch of Runcorn Bridge, past "No man's land," the Duke's Dock, Weston Point, across the river Weaver, and through the Marshes to Eastham. The promoters would apply for powers to absorb all the water courses of the Mersey above Widnes, as well as the waters from the river Weaver. If all the fresh water was taken out of the Mersey in that way they in Widnes would be in a worse position than they were when it was proposed to use the estuary. What would happen to the estuary of the Mersey when all this fresh water was ab- sorbed they could not tell, and until that was explained they c)uld de nothing. It was also impossible to say what the effect of pouring into the river at a point near Eastern all the water of the Mereey and the Weaver woeld be upon the lower reaches of the river. He did not pretend to he an engineer, bat it appeared to him it would mean the almost total annihilation of the estuary. He thought the promoters would show them some scheme by which the Widnes trailers could take advantage of the canal, or if they could lay some scheme before the promoters, he thought they were so anxious to obtain the traffic of Wid- nes, or some portion of it, that they would do a great deal rather than cause the Board to fight them to the end. They had always found them very reasonable, and ready to con- cede the claims of Widnes, and therefore he did think the Board should hesitate for one moment.—Mr Wright moved that a committee censieting of the Chairman, Messrs Hand- ley, Midwood, and Carey, together with the Clerk and Sur- veyor, should deal with the subj mt.—Mr Houghton eecanded the motion, which was unanimously carried.
"STRIKE" OF THE CHOIR OF nu
WARRINGTON PARISH CFIURCFI.

Worshippers at Warrington Parish Church on Sun- day were somewhat surprised that the usual choir did not put in an appearance, the duties being under- taken by the Sexton, and Master and Assistant. , master of the schools, the Rector's Warden, and two youths who are connected in some capacity with the schools, while the position of organist was occupied by a gentleman from Stockport. From inquiries we learn that the choir, which is a voluntary one, have declined to continuo their duties, in cons,quence of some misunderstanding with the Rector, the Rev W QuPkett, it being alleged on the part of the members of the choir that they have not been treated in a fair and proper manner. The facts of the dispute appear to be as follows. About three months ago the then organist, Mr Rowley, who is held in considerable esteem by the choir, sent in a notice of resignation of that position in consequence of not being able to pro- cure an increase of salary to which it was thought he was entitled. The choir then determined to move in the matter, for the simple reason that they and the organist had worked so well together for the space of about five years. In fact, the choir was attached to the organist and he was attached to the choir, who were sorry to learn that he had decided to resign. ' The choir at once held a meeting and determined to approach the Rector and Wardens with a view to ar- range the matter and induce Mr Rowley to retain his position. They therefore—about two months ago— met the Rector's Warden in the vestry of the church, and laid their views before him, stating that they were wishful that Mr Rowley should remain as organist; though at the same time they had no desire to appear dictatorial in any way. The , Rector's Warden, it is said.left the meeting with the distinct understanding that he should represent to the Rector and his co-Warden, who were not pro- sent at the meeting, what the choir had said and what their wishes were. Nothiag, however, re- sulted through the meeting being held, but about a, fortnight before the notice of resigna- tion given by Mr Rowley terminated, the choir, at the invitation of the Rector, went to the R-3atory to see him. When they arrived there they found that the Rector desired to consult them about the holding of a special service at which the " Messiah " was to be performed, and to inform them that he had arranged with the secretary of the Musical Society to secure the assistance of the members. The choir considered that the Rider should have consulted them in the first instance, knowing that the organist would in the meantime have vacated his position. They did not consider that they had been properly treated, and consequently refused to lend their assistance to the plan proposed. Afterwards the choir appointed ,

At Manchester, yesterday, after a lengthy hearing of the libel case, the defendant Brooke was committed for trial at the Minchester Ass:ars, Mr G W Agnew being bound over to prosecute.

A Durban telegram of Friday evening says the Transvaal Executive Council has resolved to withdraw the proclama- tion pl icing the territory of the chief Montsioa under the protection of the Republic. An inquest was held on Friday, in London, on Alexander Williamson, labourer. The evidence showed that he died frcm apoplexy, inducA by exciting himself in reading a re- port of the execution of Orrock and Harris at Newgate. THE WRECK OF THH WASP— Rear-Admiral Lethbridge has received a telegram from the chief officer of the coast- guard stationed at Sheephaven station, saying that bodies are washing on the shore. One appears to be that of an officer.

At Manehestgr, on Friday, the eleven persons arrested on Thursday in a tav,rn for betting, were brought before the magistrates. Mrs Pigott, the landlady, was fined £lO, and her two sons .C 25 eic J. Toe other sucummees were with- drawn.

COLLISION AT Slila.—During a strong gale on Friday the schooner Elizi, with coals from Porthcawl, to Penztnce, struck the Doombtr on entering Padstow harbour, and will probtbly become a total wreck. The crew were saved by a lifeboat.

The London Gazette states that the Queen has granted letters patent for the annexation to the Cape of Good Hope of certain British possessions in the Transkei. known as Teinbuland Emigrant, Temhuland Geakaland, and Boom- vanaland.

The Prince and Princess of Wake, accompanied by Prince Albert Victor and Princese9 Loa se Victoria and Maud, left Abergeldie on Friday afternoon, driving to Balloter in clos-d cirri iges. The weather was very stormy, with sr.ow on the hills. They left in the Queen's messenger train at five minutes past three. 'Fine 'Frnsr Sow.—The first fall of snow this season took place in North Wales on Thursday night. On Friday morning the Berwyn Mountains were cappNl with snow for several miles along the range. Snow commenced falling in Derbyshire on Friday morning, the snowflakes being unusu- ally large. A fall of snow took place at Walsall, accumu- lating to a depth of three inches. ARREST OF A DEFAULTING WORKHOUSE GOVERNOR.— A cablegram was received on Friday from the New Zealand police stating that Mr Anderson, the ex-Governor of the Liverpool Workhouse, who absconded several months ago, leaving defalcitious to the amount of about £l,OOO, had been wrested there under the warrant taken out by the parish authorities when he absconded. Anderson will be brought to Liverpool by the next mail, and taken before the stipen- diary on a charge of embezzlement.

div.head: SOUDAN EXPEDITION.
div.p: THE SOUDAN EXPEDITION.
Canto, FRIDAY.— According to official telegrams from Soutkim it is not anticipAted at present that the enemy will return in great numbers.

WADY IiALFA, THURSDAY, 7-20 P.M.—Lord WOlSeley will to morrow proceed to Sarras in order to inspect the railway extension there. A c.tble is being laid to the telegraph office on the other side of the Nile. It will greatly facili- tate the despitch of messages. . _

A Central News telogram, dated Cairo, Friday, states:— Owing to the strain on the transport it is believed that the Camel Corps will not leave Cairo for three weeks, and that Lord 'Noiselev will not advance from Wady Haifa until near the end of November. THE REPORTED MURDER OF COLONEL STEWART.

CAIRO, FRIDAY.—A telegram has been received here from Lord Wolseley stain g that no further confirmation of the reports of Colonel Stewart' death has been received. Major Kitchener telegraphs from Ambukol that according to ru- mour current there three Europeans. with a Dragoman, have been taken prison rs by the rebels. If this rumour is correct, the Europeans may be presumed to be Colonel Stew- art, Mr Power, and M. Ilerbin, French Consul at Khar- toum.

Colonel Stewart realised from his Irish estates a rental of £5,000 or £3/100 a yetr. The 11th Hussars, the re- giment which he commanded, is quartered in Dublin, and his reputed murder has caused great grief amongst the soldiers. Before General Gordon was appointed to pro- ceed to the Soudan, Colonel Stewart had recently returned from visiting Khartoum, and meeting him in a London club, Gordon selected him as his companion. A Central News Wady Haifa telegram says :—Nothing further has transpired respecting Colonel Stewart, and the story of his murder is now doubted.

div.head: 13RITD,H PROFECFORAJE OF NEW GUINEA.
div.p: 13RITD,H PROFECFORAJE OF NEW GUINEA.

The Central News is authorised to state that, in accor- dance with the statement made by Mr Gladstone in the House of Commons at the end of last session, steps have been takel for proclaiming the British Protectorate all over the southern coasts of New Guinea to eastward of the 141st meridian of east longtitude. Instructions have been sent by telegraph to the Commodore on the Australian steamer to proceed to New Guinea and proclaim the protec- torate which will include Islands adjacent to the southern part of New Guinea. Settlement within the Protectorate will not at present be permitted.

DARESBURY lIIGHWAY B ARD. A. meeting of this Board was held in the Court House,. Dareebury, on Thursday afternoon. There were present— Messrs J Cliff. (in the chair), J C• oper, J Mayer, J Knowles, J Mclntyre, P Percival, W Bradford, J NV Had- dock, T Bennett, A. K,nworthy, P Darbvshire, H Houghton, P Tickle, T Baguley, C T Whitley, T 8 Burgess, W Turner, J Barber, and 11 Linaker (clerk). THE SURVEYOR'S ILLNESS.—A letter was read from the surveyor (Mr Darby:Aire) stating that he was ill, and that the doctor had forbidd him to go out of the house. At a eubsequent stage of the meeting it was agreed that the sur- veyor's brother should be appointed to look aftr.r the books, he., during the illness.

Ex CRA.ORDINAUY Tn.s.Frfo.—The Clerk read some Caln' municarions that had pa,rsed between him and the town clerk of Liverpool with respect to the extraordinary traffic in pin of tha Board's distric c tused by Mr Walker, one of the Corporation contractors. The Corporation, it WU stated, did not accept any liability for the payment of dam- age caused by the extraordinary traffic, but the Water Com- mittee were willing to allow their engineer to look into the matter on Mr Walter's behalf The town clerk also com- mented upon the charges made by tho Board, which he con- sidereeexcessive, and suggested th it 4a 8d would be a reasonable compensation for the datna.e.—fhe chairman, vice-chairman, ant the chairman of the thance c Immittee were appointed a committee to deal with the matter en the recovery of the eurveyor.

ESCAPE OF WATER, AT STOCKTON HEATH.—Some corres- pondence was read with regard to the escape of water from the Bridgewater Navigation Company's canal at Stockton Heath, which ran on to and datnaged the road. The Sur- veyor reported that the water was still running, on to the road, and it was agreed that the clerk shoot write and in- form the c3mpany of that fact, and ask them to apply a remedy. Tan LEVEL Cnossmos —The Clerk said he hid written to the London and North-Western Bailway Company with respect to the complaints as to the stoppages caused to traffic at the level crossing at Latchford. In reply he bad received a letter from Mr Shaw asking for instances, and this letter he (the clerk) forwarded to Mr Long, who made the compiaints at the previous Board meeting. Mr Long. in his answer, said he could not give the exact dates, but could bring plenty of proof that these delays had occurred. Mt Long said another point which shoUld be impressed upon the company was that the normal position of the gates ought not to be across the turnpike, but open to the road and closed across the line. This letter had been forwarded to Mr Shaw, who replied that be would give the matter his best attention.—some of the members expressed the opinion that there had recently been some improvement with regard to the gates, but that there was still room for further iifl-. provement.—The subject then dropped. FINANCE.—The Clerk stated that .£271 171 13 had been received from the county surveyor towards the main road expenses. He had also forwarded a claim of £l6O from the Government grant in aid of the main roads.
